title: Moving Past Traditional Data Approach Mentalities
text:
Building a Versatile Tech Stack for Supply Chains Means Parting with Old Ways
Organizations today face many challenges when optimizing their Maintenance, Repair and Operations (MRO) data with their current technology stack, which may include a mix of ERP software and supply chain tools. A big problem is “Garbage In, Garbage Out, " or GIGO. Technology challenges include inefficient processes that amplify hidden costs, system inefficiencies from using outdated MRO software, and sticking too closely to a data cleanse-first mentality.
Fortunately, there are ‘go-around’ ways to help improve MRO needs. Taking a different approach can work. In this article, you’ll learn about existing challenges in current MRO practices, procurement, and operations; how to let go of the arduous and costly ‘data cleanse’ mentality; and how companies can enhance those current systems with AI and purpose-built solutions.
ERP/EAM/P2P are systems of record and transaction
Companies using traditional ERP and EAM systems for MRO optimization often need help with their existing tech stack. These conventional systems frequently miss the mark for optimization in areas like data dependency, rising costs, unacceptable downtime, and a decreasing bottom line. They simply weren’t built to optimize MRO and spare parts inventory and impact operations teams, dragging them into a quagmire of inefficiency.
Outdated technology stacks have issues with:
- Data fragmentation: Data is siloed, dirty, and inconsistent, making it difficult to unify and optimize parts inventory across multiple suppliers;
- A lack of visibility: Traditional systems struggle to show what parts are already in stock and what needs to be ordered, hindering proactive optimization;
- Difficulty with M&A integration: Mergers and acquisitions can lead to multiple, incompatible data sets that are expensive and time-consuming to integrate.
Companies can use MRO-specific tools to bolster their tech stack versatility and offset these issues. Here’s an analogy: using apps like Teams, Zoom, and Slack enhances team productivity and works alongside existing software like Microsoft Outlook but does not seek to replace it. In the same way, MRO-specific tools complement ERP systems by filling the critical gaps in their functionality.
An example of this is spare parts criticality assessment. Traditional methods like ABC analysis can be time-consuming, especially after disruptions like the pandemic. A large portion of inventory and spend are held as insurance materials that become slow-moving, obsolete, and overstocked (SLOB). AI can be used to analyze and improve the accuracy of criticality assessments, ensuring parts are classified correctly based on their impact on business operations. This helps ensure critical parts are readily available to minimize downtime and risks.
Challenges for MRO Practices, Procurement and Operations
First among several challenges is data fragmentation in asset-intensive organizations. The data is often very dirty, incomplete, and inconsistent, considering the hundreds of thousands of MRO parts being housed. These parts usually come from a broad supplier base, so it's difficult to unify and streamline a system for them.
Organizations may be held back by the limitations of traditional systems of record in handling MRO data and outcomes. In fact, these systems can negatively impact optimization efforts. These systems are designed for direct materials and finished goods, so they struggle to accommodate the specific needs of MRO parts with unique data requirements.
Data in these systems is also siloed, further slowing decision-making. For instance, some companies with traditional ERP/EAM systems cannot see what’s already in-house versus what they need. Just to analyze a single MRO part, companies may have to pull together data from 10-18 different screens in SAP and/or Maximo. Or they may have two different SAP instances, customized and configured in two different ways. This data segregation with multiple data sets across clients and systems can block visibility for stocking policies, lead times, and overall optimization efforts.
Negative financial impacts
The limitations of ERP and EAM systems in handling MRO materials data can negatively impact inventory, procurement and risk optimization efforts leading to financial impacts on unstructured MRO data, particularly for duplicate parts.
One example is a Fortune 200 oil and gas company that identified $37 million of duplicate parts in its global inventory. Neither they nor their suppliers knew these parts were the same. This resulted in unnecessary warehouse space usage costs, increased carrying costs (estimated at 15-20% more on top of the part value), potential tax implications on the duplicated inventory, and reduced profitability and business inefficiency.
Clearly, traditional systems and approaches are designed for direct materials and finished goods. However, they are ill-equipped to handle the specific needs of MRO parts and their unique data requirements. ERP/EAM systems lack the right intelligence and automation to manage MRO materials data efficiently, which causes teams to struggle with maintaining optimal inventory levels and procurement/risk strategies.
Ditch the ‘data cleanse’
One misconception in MRO is that data quality needs to be perfect before using AI for MRO optimization. You can almost hear someone yelling, “We need a data cleanse, pronto!”
However, this old way of thinking assumes that “dirty data” necessitates data cleansing as a prerequisite before implementing AI solutions, which is not the case today.
Modern AI data solutions have been trained to handle messy and unstructured data while simultaneously recommending business outcomes and executing efficiency gains across multiple functions. AI can work with imperfect data while delivering value through optimization and cost savings while balancing the risk of downtime.
Centralizing and organizing MRO data is crucial for effective search and analysis, even though there are some inconsistencies that AI can help address.
Using Purpose-Built Tools with AI Capabilities
Purpose-built tools with AI can complement existing ERP systems, enabling faster, more efficient MRO optimization and better decision-making around resource allocation. Traditionally, manual review of spare parts and assigning criticality levels would take months or even years. For an energy company with 500,000 spare parts globally, an internal company estimate revealed an estimated 1,000 hours to complete manual review and assignment of criticality levels.
There’s a better answer. Purpose-built MRO material optimization tools powered by AI can significantly reduce this time by automatically analyzing historical data, usage patterns, and business context to assign appropriate criticality and service levels. Hundreds of hours can be turned into mere minutes all while ensuring accurate classification and prevention of the disruptions caused by misclassified critical parts.
AI in MRO Optimization
AI-driven MRO optimization ultimately is a win-win for the entire organization. It can improve procurement and operations by ensuring data accuracy, optimizing inventory management, and ultimately driving cost savings and profitability. AI in MRO improves collaboration between procurement and operations teams through better data visibility and shared goals. Sourcing spare parts at scale means more accurately confirming demand down to the item level and then following trusted demand signals from that point on. If you haven’t already, maybe it’s time to examine how your current tech stacks are holding your company’s MRO strategy back.

title: Dynatrace Stock Down 17%. Generative AI Could Boost Shares 33%
text:
While many companies are talking about generative AI, very few — notably Nvidia, SuperMicro, and Vertiv — are getting enough of a revenue boost from supporting the AI chatbots to reward investors.
There are many software companies now aiming to deploy generative AI in their services on behalf of customers.
The modest stock market performance of such AI software companies in my generative AI stock index, according to my June 15 Forbes post, suggests investors could be disappointed with how much AI is contributing to their revenue growth.
A case in point is $13 billion (market capitalization) Waltham, Mass.-based Dynatrace, a provider of a platform for monitoring the performance of companies’ cloud-based applications.
Dynatrace stock has fallen 16% in 2024 as of June 25 — as investors seemed disappointed with Dynatrace’s fiscal year 2025 revenue and earnings per share guidance.
Yet my June 13 interview with Dynatrace CEO Rick McConnell suggests the stock could rise — especially if the company’s AI-powered service bring in more users which propel the company’s revenues above muted expectations.
Dynatrace’s Mixed March 2024 Quarter Results And Forecast
Dynatrace reported mixed results last month for the quarter ending March 2024. Revenue grew rapidly — exceeding expectations while the company forecast revenue and earnings per share that fell short of investors’ estimates.
Here are the key figures:
- Fiscal Year 2024 Q4 revenue: $381 million — up 21% and $200,000 above analysts’ estimates, according to Investor’s Business Daily.
- Fiscal Year 2024 Q4 annual recurring revenue from subscriptions: $1.5 billion — up 21%, IBD wrote.
- Fiscal Year 2024 Q4 adjusted earnings per share: 30 cents — matching estimates, IBD noted.
- Fiscal Year 2025 revenue forecast range midpoint: $1.651 billion — $30 million short of estimates, IBD reported.
- Fiscal Year 2025 earnings per share forecast range midpoint: $1.275 — five cents a share short of estimates, according to IBD.
Dynatrace was pleased with its performance. “We had a fantastic quarter ending in March,” McConnell told me. “It is a good starting point. fiscal Q4 leads into our fiscal year 2025 with momentum.”
How Generative AI Could Boost Dynatrace’s Revenue Growth
When it comes to generative AI, most businesses are holding back. Roughly 5% of companies in the U.S. are using the technology, according to a Census Bureau survey featured in a report by The New York Times.
Given the small number of businesses deploying generative AI, it should come as no surprise that few suppliers of AI-powered services are reporting significant revenues from the technology.
Companies with the greatest potential to do that are at the summit of what I call the value pyramid — a set of three broad uses for AI chatbots whose adoption by companies is less common as you approach the top, according to my new book, Brain Rush: How to Invest and Compete in the Real World of Generative AI.
The generative AI value pyramid has the following three levels:
- Overcome creator's block At the base of the pyramid are the many ways people use AI chatbots to get started on an activity — such as writing an email or a report, creating a photo or video, or coding software. By helping overcome creator's block, AI chatbots can increase people's productivity. This is the easiest way for businesses to get value now. However, since other companies can do the same, the advantage from using AI to overcome creator’s block is fleeting.
- Boost customer service and sales productivity The middle layer of the value pyramid can increase a company’s productivity. For example, in the temporary job placement industry, generative AI can reduce significantly the number of candidates a recruiter sends to a company before finding a match. AI chatbots can also help a company to resolve customer questions more rapidly. It is unclear whether companies will be willing to pay enough for such applications to enable their suppliers to grow profitably.
- Create new growth curves. The top level of the pyramid is the most valuable one. AI technology suppliers aspire to create new growth curves for their business by helping their customers grow faster. In general, if generative AI can deliver faster growth, that growth will drive up the company’s stock price — thus making companies more willing to pay a high price for the technology.
Dynatrace Operating At The Peak Of The Value Pyramid
Dynatrace is operating at the third level of the value pyramid. That’s because the company can demonstrate the relationship between the technical performance of its clients’ customer-facing application and key financial metrics — such as revenue growth and cost reduction.
“Customers are not just using our product for digital transformation and moving their workflow to the cloud,” McConnell told me.
“They are asking ‘What is the business outcome? What is the business value?’ The business outcome is not just technical. It affects revenue generation, growth and cost savings,” he added.
The conversion rate from a web page visit to a purchase drops from 18% to 1% when the time to load a Web page rises from 0.5 seconds to 5 seconds, he told me, according to my February Forbes post.
Dynatrace can help its customers achieve faster growth and higher profitability thanks to Hypermodal AI. “Hypermodal AI combines three AI techniques,” he said.
“The first is causal AI which does root cause analysis — Why did it break? How to fix it? The second is predictive AI which anticipates where the system is about to break and fixes it before there is an end-user impact. Those are not new.”
Dynatrace’s latest kind of AI — generative — makes information easier for non-technical users to access. Those managerial users could expand Dynatrace’s revenues. “What is new — we introduced it over the last six months — is generative AI,” McConnell told me.
“End users can ask a simple question. The quality of the answers is limited by the efficacy of the underlying data. Without good data, you end up with legal briefs not based in reality. The value of Dynatrace’s generative AI is in accessing deterministic data leading to 100% trust. Generative AI will enable us to expand to more people.”
How Dynatrace Helps Improve Airline Travel
Dynatrace helps one airline operate much more effectively by diagnosing and solving the problems causing flight delays. “I was speaking with a global airline that is a Dynatrace customer,” he told me.
“There are over 160 applications that must be working for an airplane to take off. In the terminal, an application tells passengers which gate to go to and whether the plane is on time. These applications — covering booking tickets, posting the right gate, loading the airplane, and taking off — are all interconnected,” he added.
Dynatrace enables airlines to identify what is causing the problem and solve it. “Before Dynatrace, if something went wrong, more than 100 people in charge of those applications would be on a call to identify the problem,” he explained.
“Most of them would be saying, ‘It’s not my fault.’ With Dynatrace, the airline has radically reduced the time needed to restore normal performance. There has been an impact to on-time departures, the number of tickets sold, and user experience ratings,” he concluded
Will Dynatrace Stock Go Up?
Investors see considerable upside in Dynatrace stock. Based on 20 Wall Street analysts offering 12-month price targets, Dynatrace stock could rise 33.2% to reach the average $58.33 per share, according to TipRanks.
One analyst explained his reasons for optimism. “We have a positive outlook on Dynatrace’s prospects in the observability space,” wrote Morningstar analyst Malik Ahmed Khan.
“The firm’s products benefit from secular tailwinds driving an accelerating increase in data for enterprises to monitor and analyze. In our opinion, the firm’s sticky product portfolio, broad swath of products that cover the entire IT stack, and increased penetration in its target market have enabled Dynatrace to form a narrow economic moat around its business,” he added.
Dynatrace sees a bright future ahead due to market growth and a strong product. “The market for observability and application security is growing rapidly,” McConnell told investors in May, according to the company’s Q4 2024 Earnings Call Transcript.
“Our end-to-end platform differentiates us and puts us in a strong competitive position. And finally, we have a solid business model that continues to deliver a strong balance of growth and profitability,” he concluded.

title: Why F5 Is Taking The Long View On AI
text:
While many technology vendors are stumbling over themselves to hype AI, infrastructure provider F5 has been taking a more realistic and data-based approach. In fact, recently released survey results show the company is downright circumspect, highlighting the many risks of AI.
F5’s survey data shows that enterprises are bedeviled by AI difficulties ranging from GPU procurement to data quality and security. But that doesn’t mean AI isn’t a long-term trend. It shows that F5 sees AI as a new application with high data and throughput demands, so it will need a more secure and distributed infrastructure to support it. Not only is this the conclusion of F5’s survey research, but it also synchronizes with our own view at Futuriom.
Moving Slowly Toward AI’s Promise
In a global survey of over 700 IT professionals, along with an in-depth survey of another 75 AI decision-makers in North America and the UK, F5 reported that a majority (77%) may be enthusiastically embracing AI, but 72% have had issues with data quality and scaling. These companies also struggle to obtain AI skillsets, build and operate infrastructure, and—sadly—trust the results of their efforts. A stunning 77% of those surveyed said they lacked a single source of truth for their organization’s data.
If firms can’t trust their AI, they’re not going to deploy it strategically. And that seems to be what’s happening: With a few exceptions at very large and very rich companies, AI deployments consist of a scattering of chatbots and copilots that could be of minimal benefit compared to the outlay of effort they require. As a result, companies aren’t yet using generative AI (GenAI) in live apps: A full 69% are still researching use cases, and 63% are working on proofs of concept.
All of this has been leading F5 to take a long-term view of AI and what it means for the future of infrastructure.
“We overestimate what will happen in the next twenty-four months, but we underestimate what will happen in the next ten to twenty years,” F5 CEO François Locoh-Donou told me in an interview with me earlier this year. “There’s a bit of overestimation for the next twelve months. There's a lot of hype. We are a couple of years away from seeing the real deployments and five years from how enterprises build their infrastructure.”
Locoh-Donou describes AI as a long-term transformation which will lead to big adjustments by enterprises as well as vendors. At its annual AppWorld conference held earlier in the year, the company unveiled its strategy to create an end-to-end suite of app delivery and security capabilities. This type of infrastructure will be key to supporting AI, which will generate enormous amounts of data and demand high-performance, secure connectivity.
“We think we have entered the world of distributed applications,” F5 CEO François Locoh-Donou. “AI accelerates the distribution of networking and accelerates the need for secure multicloud networking.”
AI Security Issues Loom Large
The F5 survey points out that the data struggle is taking place even in the 53% of companies that claim to have a data strategy in place. But those strategies often don’t align with the needs of AI. Companies successful in implementing mission-critical AI have defined a separate AI strategy targeting specific use cases, and they’ve done their homework in researching technology approaches and setting up trials. In contrast, the laggard firms appear to have approached AI projects in the same way they’ve always worked with data, throwing solutions at the AI problem that worked with business intelligence and other “legacy” applications.
“Our report highlights a concerning trend: Many enterprises, in their eagerness to harness AI, overlook the need for a solid foundation,” said Kunal Anand, EVP and CTO at F5, in a press release. “This oversight not only diminishes the effectiveness of their AI solutions but also exposes them to a multitude of security threats.”
For enterprises undertaking AI projects, security is a many-headed monster. There are internal threats, such as increased corporate liability as a result of AI (reported by 27% of F5’s sample as a top concern); data privacy (23%); and data leakage (21%).
But the potential for AI-powered external attacks was reported as the chief concern of AI security among 29% of enterprises in the F5 study. As a result, 42% of companies surveyed are adding API security; 39% are adding DDoS protection for AI models; and 38% are adding bot protection for models. Overall, respondents are planning to spend 44% more on security over the next several years as AI implementations grow, according to the F5 survey.
Source: F5’s 2024 State of AI Application Strategy Report.
The need for tighter security for AI workloads also should lead to market innovation, according to F5. “AI will accelerate the distribution of workloads. It will accelerate the need for securing APIs,” said CEO Locoh-Donou in my interview with him. “There will be some AI-enabled security capabilities that will be table stakes quickly. After that, AI will cause new applications services to emerge. Things like AI gateways might be mainstream application services.”
Turning to the Cloud
The trouble with AI deployments is pointing enterprises toward AI models and attendant services offered by public cloud providers such as AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud. While open-source models are also favored, it seems that models from the likes of Microsoft that include integral authentication, security, and monitoring are gaining in popularity. To quote from the report: “It’s not only the model itself that’s important; it’s the availability of a robust ecosystem of services that support access to the model and integration with it.
The report also notes: “This is why the most popular AI models are often offered by cloudproviders. The providers already deliver a rich set of services that support applications of all kinds to greatly simplify adoption of their models.”
Why AI Will Accelerate Hybrid Cloud
While AI models and services are increasingly available from key public cloud providers, there’s evidence in F5’s survey that in the future, customers will continue to deploy a hybrid cloud approach supporting both on-premises and public cloud services. But they will increase the use of SaaS solutions: Today, 49% of those surveyed by F5 said they preferred SaaS as a delivery model for AI, but in two years 64% expect to favor SaaS for AI.
At the same time, use of public cloud is expected to dip slightly, with 65% of respondents reporting use today, and 56% anticipating public cloud use for AI within two years.
Conclusion: Better Data, Tighter Security Is Needed
None of the problems cited in F5’s study is putting off corporate buyers. Indeed, survey respondents reported that 18% of their IT budgets are being spent on AI today; and a full 94% expect that percentage to increase over the next two years.
To realize workflow automation, however, companies will need to get a handle on the quality and maturity of their data sources. Absent this, they can expect to fall short of the hoped-for solutions AI promises.
As AI workloads straighten out and move past trials, security will become tighter and more granular, particularly in the area of APIs, which are the primary means of enterprise interaction with SaaS solutions, the preferred vehicle for AI delivery.
Overall, F5’s survey offers yet another indication that the enterprise world is still struggling to grasp the fundamentals of AI applications, and it will be at least a couple of years before tangible results are widespread.

title: Transforming Saudi Arabia: Embracing AI For The Future Of Work
text:
By Joseph Hammond
In this century, data will play a central role in geopolitics, much like oil did in the previous century. This will change jobs like never before and result in a massive change in labor markets around the world.
"A.I. is like a beast that can consume endless amounts of data, no matter how much data you have," said Ahmed Al Yamani, a Saudi expert on digitalization and the CEO of Takamol, a Saudi government-owned company.
The transition from petroleum to data will fuel the jobs of the future and the world's largest oil exporter is thinking hard about that transition.
Saudi Arabia has committed to massive investments in artificial intelligence which will make it both the largest player in the Middle East and a globally important one. A Saudi tech fund was announced earlier this year with the participation of American banks which will fund to the tune of $40 billion.
"This is creating unprecedented value and investments in data. Nvidia and other chipmakers are only going to see demand double. I don't see any new technology currently or even on the horizon that will match the ability of AI and data to fuel the next era of global prosperity [and jobs]."
Al Yamani pointed out that the founder of Intel, Gordon Moore, famously predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double roughly every two years with a minimal increase in cost. While Moore initially forecasted that this trend would continue for another decade, Al Yamani notes that the trend has continued to the present. Furthermore, the time has fallen to 18 months between cycles.
The Saudi government founded Takamol, in part, to diversify Saudi Arabia’s hydrocarbon-heavy economy with the understanding that labor mobility is key to a 21st-century economy.
Takamol has worked with the Ministry of Labor and the Ministry of Investment to ensure that government agencies weren't working in silos. Tasks like compliance and upskilling for workers have become areas in Takamol that have taken the lead. In research and discussions with investors — including American companies — Takamol has found that the most significant hurdles aren't from government services but from logistical issues like finding labor and office space. Takamol has put together a platform where such information is readily available. In the past, such information was only available on narrow, industry-specific platforms such as oil and gas.
Traditionally, most Saudis, like Arab workers in other countries, have sought government jobs.
“[I]f given a choice, only about one in five Saudi national adults (19%) polled by Gallup between 2013 and 2015 would opt for a job in the private sector; the vast majority (75%) would prefer employment in the public sector,” said results of a Gallup poll in 2015.
By standardizing these processes, Takamol aims to make opportunities more open and fairer for Saudis of all stripes. Attitudes in Saudi Arabia towards the private sector are also changing in line with large scale investments.
"Migrating all services into the cloud to hyper scalers and entering the Saudi market with their requirements and improving their footprint within the government - Microsoft, Google, Amazon - all cloud services in the country are investing $10 billion here,"
Saudi Arabia is drawing on a strategy from the rise of the Asian Tiger economies but with a twist. In East Asian countries like Korea, China, and Taiwan, rapid growth was driven by special economic zones (SEZs). Local governments set these areas aside to produce goods, originally the industry in question textiles, for export. However, that model has since been applied to a variety of industries in a variety of contexts.
Saudi Arabia's focus on digital services means the new generation of SEZs won't be tied to the oil fields either.
"We have [an SEZ] right here in Riyadh that is focused on the digital economy, which is where the clients and demands are," said Al Yamani.
Al Yamani believes that American companies will play a significant role in the the next phase of the future of work in Saudi Arabia from AI to other areas as well
"One opportunity for American companies is to develop infrastructure, particularly digital infrastructure for cloud hyperscales. There are few companies that can do that, and many of them are American. The opportunity is here: 60% of the construction currently in the Middle East is in Saudi Arabia," Al Yamani said.
Under the Saudi Vision 2030 plan, a third of all cars in Riyadh are supposed to be electric vehicles. The city will also soon see heavy investment as Riyadh will host both the 2034 FIFA World Cup and the 2030 World Expo. The AI transition will be key for goals both municipal and national in Saudi Arabia.
“The AI transition is coming; that is no longer up for debate,” wrote Jad Haddad a digital economy consultant in a local Saudi media outlet,” Generative AI is about to change the game – and this is happening at a time when the Kingdom is in the unique position of being able to invest heavily in its future.”

title: The Prompt: Dario Amodei On Anthropic’s Most Intelligent AI Model Yet
text:
Welcome back to The Prompt.
Amazon is secretly working on a ChatGPT competitor, code-named Metis (likely after the Greek goddess of wisdom), powered by an in-house AI model called Olympus, Business Insider reported. The AI assistant can provide up-to-date answers from real time sources and is being developed by the retail giant’s own AGI team, which is working on building artificial intelligence that can think and learn like humans.
Now, let’s get into the headlines.
BIG PLAYS
For months, the AI community wondered about the whereabouts of OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, especially after he participated in Sam Altman’s brief ouster from the company in late 2023. The question “Where’s Ilya?,” which at one point trended on X, was answered on Wednesday when Sutskever announced that he is starting a new venture called Safe SuperIntelligence, a research-oriented company with “one focus, one goal and one product” — to build safe AI systems. The company claims it will “not do anything else” nor get distracted by selling AI products, until it has achieved safe superintelligence, Sutskever said in an interview with Bloomberg.
Apple has been talking to rival Meta about integrating Meta’s generative AI models into Apple Intelligence, an AI system that will be available on iPhones and other Apple devices, according to the Wall Street Journal. Apple, which is already partnering with OpenAI to bring ChatGPT to its devices, has also held similar discussions with AI startups Anthropic and Perplexity. Apple could help distribute these AI models to its more than a billion iPhone users and drive up their subscription revenues.
ETHICS + LAW
A group of the biggest record labels including Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment are suing two music-generation AI companies, Suno and Udio AI, for alleged copyright infringement on a “massive scale” and for using their content for AI training without consent.
Plus, AI search startup Perplexity appears to be accessing and scraping content from websites like Wired and other Condé Nast-owned publications through a secret IP address after developers blocked its web crawler Perplexity Bot from stealing its content, a Wired investigation found. On multiple instances, Perplexity’s AI search engine conjured false quotes and attributed them to real people. Leading startups like OpenAI and Anthropic have also been disregarding an established web standard that allows publishers to exclude their content from being used for AI training. Earlier this month Forbes found that Perplexity had plagiarized journalistic work from Forbes, Bloomberg and CNBC through a feature called Perplexity Pages.
REGULATION
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and the founders of 140 AI startups signed an open letter opposing California's new AI regulation that would require the makers of AI frontier models to conduct risk assessments of their systems and hold developers legally liable for misuse of the technology. While the bill applies to AI model builders that have spent over $100 million to train their systems, nascent startups that have dubbed themselves “little tech,” said the bill could hinder the state’s ability to retain AI talent.
AI DEAL OF THE WEEK
Chip startup Etched AI has raised $102 million in Series A funding at a $500 million valuation. Founded by three Harvard dropouts, the startup is building a custom chip and software that is designed specifically for transformer models, the technology behind ChatGPT and other generative AI. CEO Gavin Uberti, a former mathematics world champion, said existing hardware like Nvidia GPUs are slower and less efficient because most of the power is used to move memory around the chip rather than carrying out AI tasks. “If you're willing to run one model architecture onto the chip, you can take out the vast majority out of that memory movement and fit way more compute onto the chip,” Uberti told Forbes.
Also notable: AI video generation startup HeyGen has raised $60 million in a round led by Benchmark at a $500 million valuation. The company, which allows users to create AI avatars, said it has crossed $35 million in annual recurring revenue and has 40,000 enterprise clients.
DEEP DIVE
On Thursday, Anthropic unveiled its most intelligent AI model yet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which the company claims is cheaper, faster and has better performance than rival AI systems like OpenAI’s GPT-4 in terms of coding, writing and interpreting complex instructions. The model is part of a new family of AI models that will include a smaller size model (Haiku) and larger one (Opus), both of which have not yet been released. Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which generates responses at twice the speed of Anthropic’s previous model, Claude 3 Opus, can also better understand humor and nuance. The model has already been integrated into a number of applications including Quora’s chatbot Poe and clinical documentation company Deep Scribe’s medical scribe.
I spoke to Anthropic CEO and cofounder Dario Amodei about his ambitions for the next iteration of Claude models. (This interview has been edited for clarity and conciseness.)
Rashi Shrivastava: What prompted you to create a new family of AI models, beginning with Claude 3.5 Sonnet?
Dario Amodei: Three months ago we released the Claude 3 family of models. And there's a technological trade-off curve between the intelligence of a model versus its speed and cost. Each of those models is on a different point on that trade-off curve and serves a different set of business needs. What Anthropic generally wants to do is push out that tradeoff so that the high end models of today can be served for much lower cost and while being much faster.
Shrivastava: You say that this model is significantly better in terms of understanding nuance and humor. Can you give an example of what that looks like?
Amodei: I think just recently there was a lawyer who assigned Claude 3 Opus to make Supreme Court decisions and he said it was surprisingly thoughtful, moderate and balanced and sometimes makes better decisions than the Justices. And for everything that Claude 3 is kind of good at, Claude 3.5 sonnet pushes that a little bit more.
Shrivastava: How were you able to improve the model’s performance? Would you say it was better training data or scaling compute, or a mixture of both?
Amodei: The name of the game here is we're always trying to improve our models by improving every ingredient that goes into them, the architecture and algorithms, the quantity and quality of data that goes into them, the amount of compute that's used to train them. I think the general scaling hypothesis continues to hold, although we're also getting better at getting more out of a given amount of compute to train the models.
Shrivastava: Do you anticipate that these models could be used differently from previous versions? How so?
Amodei: As the models get smarter and also as they get more affordable and faster for any given level of intelligence, that makes a much wider set of applications more economical. So for example in biomedical areas, today we're using them for better clinical documentation, but as the models get smarter, they're going to increasingly be used for the core of the field.
YOUR WEEKLY DEMO
As companies continue to train their large AI systems on public data, you may want to protect your Instagram posts and personal data from seeping into training datasets. Experts suggest trying to use tools like ChatGPT in incognito mode or engaging with models through the company’s API. If you’re based in the U.K. or Europe, you can opt out of Meta using your content for training purposes.
QUIZ
The CEO of this company told shareholders he is on a mission to usher in artificial superintelligence.
- Softbank
- Tesla
- Amazon
- Meta
Check if you got it right here.
MODEL BEHAVIOR

title: Perplexity AI Vs Journalism: The Risks We Need To Anticipate
text:
There are ethical and legal disputes running between AI companies and content publishers, but nothing comes close to a flashpoint like Forbes’ recent accusation about Perplexity AI. This is a unique moment in 2024 because the spat is about journalistic labor and form. It began earlier this month with Forbes complaining about Perplexity AI stealing language from the former’s paywalled scoop on Eric Schmidt’s stealth drones startup. Articles have since been flying back and forth as multiple news outlets – Axios, AP, Semafor, Wired, Short Cut and Fast Company – have all chronicled the dispute.
What’s missing in all the back and forth about the adequacy, or not, of citations, traffic referrals, and rights is a discussion on a fundamental question: What is the future of the journalistic form? Paywalled or not, are we headed to a future where journalists are merely laboring to supply tokens (pun intended) to large language models and their applications?
The significance of authentic journalistic form
AI engineers eager to produce the next extractive content aggregator are missing a core emotional point. Journalists who care about digging up realities that lurk beneath the surface also view their work a labor of love. Their final product has a form associated with the work, presented on a web page that stands for the work.
This classic form, whether the truth-telling is done by traditional professionals or volunteers or social media creators, may seem simple: a page with a headline, the creator or author's name and title, the story’s topic, key words, the story itself. And thanks to reform movements in journalistic culture, these pages are increasingly carrying additional context about the sourcing and methods used in stories. Readers or viewers have the opportunity to know that human beings became their eyes and ears, dug into the real world on their behalf, went back into archives, tracked people and experts down, and relayed truths, facts, values and frames through a story.
A fantastic example of journalistic form and labor at work is the new investigative series released this month, 40 Acres And A Lie, published by Mother Jones, in collaboration with the Center for Public Integrity and Reveal. It is on one of the oldest broken promises of reparations in American history. “A government program gave formerly enslaved people land after the Civil War, only to take nearly all of it back a year and a half later,” goes the intro. The team of named journalists themselves marshaled artificial intelligence “to track down the people, places, and stories that had long been misunderstood and forgotten, then asked their descendants about what’s owed now”, says the series introduction.
Journalistic form has value for democracy. It represents journalists' intervention into democracy’s discourse. It lets ethical journalists defend their work in public to questions about their story selection, sourcing, verification, corroboration, etc. The form is key for people in democracy to try to hold journalists accountable to ethical standards. There will be contestations over facts, representation, unaccounted-for stakeholders, amplification or salience to illegitimate controversies and so forth.
In sum, this form that manifests on journalistic pages is the face of journalism and journalists who undertake truth-telling. Despite the field’s continuous grappling with ethics, it is this form that makes journalists and journalism visible to the public.
Large Language Model-curated news needs scrutiny
Perplexity AI’s Pages feature is designed to look like news articles and not your personal Q&A with your preferred LLM chatbot. It explicitly lets its users “curate” new articles with headlines using generative AI summarizations of other articles. Each page automatically includes numerical (like Wikipedia) and logo-based citations to original sources. If Perplexity AI’s Pages feature succeeds, it will mean other competitors will follow. And we will have “curated generated content”, or CGC, (I’m coining this here), for the generative AI era. This is akin to user generated content or UGC that emerged with social media companies.
Perplexity AI has also taken on a publisher-like role in pushing newsy content to its audience with a newsletter. As more startups and services follow, streams of newsy summary articles answering contemporary questions will enter the online sphere every day. They will be “curated” by “users” like you and me. What happens when recycling begins? How will we differentiate between the human journalists who invest time and money in digging up real stories and the mix of humans and machines who come later?
Most worrisome is Perplexity AI’s news podcast Discover Daily which produces 5-minute generated audio summaries of the news of the day. The audio has no spoken inline credits to the original publishers or journalists it relies on. Credits are only made in text in the show notes. If you only listened to the audio and did not see the credits, you will have no idea who reported the stories and how. Compare this with Apple News Today. As the show’s hosts summarize the latest stories and the questions answered in the news reports, they usually say the names of the media outlets each time. You can hear which publisher reported or exposed what, or which outlet explained something.
Generative AI companies’ have an opportunity
Genuine news publishers cannot be faulted if they are wary about promises of audience expansion from links through generative AI answers.
On the economic front, the good news is that newer revenue sharing or royalty models are emerging to let AI answer engines reward original sources to the degree their material is used for a given subscriber query. Tim O’Reilly made a case for a method to apportion payments to original sources in this recent piece on how to fix AI’s original sin. “By creating an algorithm that attributes the content referenced for an “answer,” we’re able to allocate a royalty to the original creators. Which is an important advancement in bringing AI models to market”, wrote O’Reilly. Semafor reported Perplexity AI’s claims that they are working on revenue sharing. Revenues are indeed a key component of recognition of authentic creative work, but not all.
But the critical challenge and opportunity for AI companies in handling journalism is more than revenue share. The designers of large language models and their applications need to invest more time in catching the differences between original, value-added and recycled journalism that often run in the same news cycle. They need to find ways to distinguish news publishers or journalists who actually broke the original story from those who publish rapid derivative rewrites within minutes. Original reporting brings new knowledge into the world relative to other types of secondary and follow-on writing.
In line with that, generative AI-curated current affairs content needs a standard for richer credits that respect journalistic form. Numerical, reductive, and tiny logo-based citations will not cut it. This is a design problem that needs to be worked on together by news publishers and generative AI companies.
We need to anticipate the risks
It is not my case that journalistic form is already being done to death because of LLMs and generative AI applications. But if the current direction of generative AI-powered news applications solidifies in the name of “extracting knowledge,” we must anticipate the risk of journalistic form losing its force altogether. With the Internet revolution, publishers lost control of news distribution as search, social, and digital aggregators took over. But the journalistic form largely remained. With generative AI-powered answer engines relying extractively and reductively on journalism, we have to ask ourselves, in caution, where this road is headed.
We need a way for human reporters and investigators to be visible as the people who are doing the real work so that they can defend it in the public domain, whether or not machines aggregate their findings as knowledge.

title: Chinese Dissident Artist Ai Weiwei Speaks About Free Speech And His Love Of Lego
text:
Ai Weiwei insists that he’s simply a troublemaker rather than an artist. “I’m the kind of person who makes trouble, but in a smart way,” he states. “Art is just about making trouble, but not big troubles. The art world is too fragile if you make big troubles, just small ones. So I don’t really create artworks; I just make little troubles.” As the most high-profile Chinese artist and human rights activist living today, he filled the Turbine Hall at London’s Tate Modern with 100 million porcelain sunflower seeds meticulously hand-crafted and painted by 1,600 Chinese artisans as a metaphor for both the downtrodden, conformist Chinese populace and the power of the masses, and made the documentary Human Flow following the plights of millions of displaced persons across 23 countries through intimate interviews of individual refugees and drone footage of vast migrant camps. Conducting his own citizen investigation after the devastating 2008 Sichuan earthquake, he berated Chinese officials for their negligence that resulted in the deaths of thousands of students in collapsed public schools owing to substandard construction. This probe culminated in the installation “Remembering”, which saw the façade of Haus der Kunst museum in Munich covered with 9,000 colorful children’s backpacks arranged to form a quote in Chinese by an earthquake victim’s mother.
Time and again, Ai has proven that he’s unafraid of saying the “wrong” thing. In his eyes, creativity is the power to act and to change the status quo. Convinced that an artist must also be an activist, he firmly believes in the role of art in challenging authoritarian regimes and advocating for freedom of expression. “I think freedom of expression is the condition of so-called art because only by encouraging freedom of expression can we find an unpredictable result,” he says. “Other things, like mathematics or physics, are logical and rational, but humanity is not just about the logical and rational. There is a huge area of who we are where that we don’t really have the answers to. Before, of course, we had religion to take care of some answers, but now we cannot answer the most essential questions: what’s the purpose of life, to be rich, comfortable or problem-free, or is there a more profound meaning? Or do we really just spend this time without knowing anything, then leave? So I think those are worthwhile questions.”
Born in 1957 in Beijing, Ai spent the first two decades of his life in semi-military labor camps in the remote Chinese villages of Heilongjiang and Xinjiang. Shortly after his birth, Communist officials had accused his father, the great Chinese poet, Ai Qing, of being an anti-revolutionary Rightist during Chairman Mao’s anti-intellectual campaign, and the family was only allowed to return to Beijing in 1976 at the end of the Cultural Revolution. “In my father’s generation, a lot of very talented artists and professors all had no jobs and were criticized as the bad guys,” he recalls. “My father was pretty angry with me, saying I should go to the countryside to work instead of staying home. I didn’t want to work in the countryside because I grew up in the countryside. It didn’t mean anything to me; it was just hard labor. So I was kind of ashamed of myself because all my classmates started working as farmers. My father never really want me to become an artist, as being an artist was like committing suicide because you were already on the other side: you were against the Revolution.”
Self-taught (Ai dropped out of the Beijing Film Academy after two years and Parsons School of Design in New York after one semester), he works in multiple disciplines and in between them, refusing to define his practice as sculpture, installation, architecture, design, photography or film. Living in exile has become a way of life for the nomadic artist, who spent 12 years in the US from 1981 to 1993, and has been based in Europe since 2015, when he left China. Fearing for his safety, after being severely beaten by the police and imprisoned in 2011, he was granted asylum in Germany. Now he has moved to the Portuguese countryside, an hour’s drive southeast of Lisbon, where he has built a massive new studio, while maintaining spaces in Berlin and Beijing.
“Since young, I’ve been full of bad ideas, and I have the ability to bring them to life,” Ai points out. “I naturally know how to do things. It takes a long preparation time to investigate, organize people or write reports. A lot of people share my ideas, but it’s not planned – it’s by intuition. Maybe this afternoon, I’ll think something is funny, then we will start making it. We don’t calculate the cost or analyze, so that gives us a kind of liberty.” Guided by instinct and circumstance, his team in China is currently sewing countless buttons onto a series of textile panels. Upon learning that a button factory was closing down and the buttons were going to a landfill, he purchased 30 tons of buttons on a whim. “I became the king of buttons,” he proclaims. “Then it took us years to figure out what we had: 9,000 types of buttons with different names, sizes and designs. Now finally, I’ve found a way to put them together to make an artwork.”
In 2015, when Lego rejected Ai’s request for a bulk order of bricks on the grounds that it didn’t want its products used for political purposes, he mobilized his fans through social media, who donated millions of their own Lego blocks to him via mail and official collection points in a sign of solidarity. The Danish toy firm later admitted that it had made a mistake. Taking on Western art history, Ai has reinterpreted Claude Monet’s “Water Lilies” using 650,000 Lego pieces, and his fixation with the toy bricks is now abundantly on display in his solo exhibition “Neither Nor”, on view through September 1, 2024 at Galleria Continua in San Gimignano, a walled medieval hilltop town in Tuscany, southwest of Florence, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In a former movie theater converted into an art gallery, Continua is hosting 35 of Ai’s works. Some may view Ai’s Lego installations replicating some of the world’s most venerated paintings as a provocation, but his art is never just a carbon copy, there’s always an addition. In “Neither Nor”, a mysterious coat hanger appears in Giorgione’s “Sleeping Venus” in reference to brutal, self-induced abortions before they became legalized, a panda clings on to a horse in Rubens’ “The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus” as a symbol of contemporary Chinese state power, a refugee materializes in Georges Seurat’s “Un Dimanche Après-Midi à l’Île de la Grande Jatte” in response to the ban on the burkini in France, the locust invasion that destroyed entire crops in Pakistan in 2020 is superimposed over Vincent van Gogh’s “Le Semeur au Soleil Couchant” and Leonardo da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa” is smeared with cake, recalling the vandalism perpetrated by environmentalists against the Louvre’s most prized possession. However, the real showstopper is the 6.84-meter-long “Last Supper”, inspired by da Vinci’s magnum opus that’s considered the most important mural painting in the world. Ai has surreptitiously inserted himself into the composition, replacing Judas’ face with his own.
“Legos are used to convey personal messages and contain stories related to me, my childhood and my upbringing,” Ai explains. “Pixels, digitization, segmentation, fragmentation and disconnection provide a unique freedom for reproduction, enabling a qualitative and quantitative breakthrough in image formation that moves away from the widely used order, method and composition. It is similar to the use of ancient mosaics and the presentation of fabrics and carpets, which have a lengthy history. The existence and logic of using Lego as a structure are surprisingly consistent with the logic of my expression on social media, including tweets and Instagram images. Both include temporal and spatial factors, the flattening, fragmentation and expropriated continuity of media and reality, including existence itself, ideologies, politics and events, and linguistic approaches to culture and dreams.”
Ai’s deep bond with ancient Chinese culture and scale is palpable in “Neither Nor”, and manifests itself in two large-format installations in the garden. An oversized version of the game “Pick Up Sticks” is a nod to Chinese fortune sticks used for oracular practice, while “Pillar” consists of two-meter-tall porcelain vases that have overcome the limits of the processing of this material considered the highest expression of Chinese craftsmanship. As Ai is a master of accumulation, some 3,000 wooden stools from the Ming and Qing Dynasties and the Republican Era that he collected from the villages of northern China, lined up in rows, fill the auditorium directly in front of the stage that were once the stalls. The exhibition concludes with “Huantou Guo”, a floating mythological beast made of bamboo and silk in the manner of traditional Chinese kite making, which was inspired by the Classic of Mountains and Seas, a 4th-century Chinese text.
Considering your engagement with the world and involvement with architecture, design, curation and activism, do you ever think about not being an artist? Do you ever lose faith in what art can do?
Firstly, I don’t have that fate, so I’m not worried about losing faith. Secondly, I always tell people I’m a fake artist, but people still don’t believe it. So I still associate myself with art activities, and I’m happy people tolerate what I’m doing. I’m almost 67 and I think I can call myself an artist because artists have some kind of practice. I started when I was very young. My father was a writer, a poet, and although I cannot call myself a writer yet, I would still prefer to be a writer than to be called an artist.
You’re saying that because of your father, the famous Chinese poet Ai Qing, you feel you can’t be a poet?
I’m not very skillful. A poet needs to be in a purer and more innocent condition, so I think I’ve already messed up, but in my heart, I believe in poetry and I believe life is not just absolutely rational or logical. There are many things beyond rationality and logic, and those all can be mysterious and beautiful. I can’t even tell why we are here and what is the chance we’re not going to disappear, so all those things are very confusing. I think only poets can deal with emotions or feelings and use language, which also is very limited. Our language is just like Lego pieces, which have only 40 colors, but they create completely different structures and statements.
What made you specifically use Lego rather than other toys or materials?
I think that any medium is not a medium unless you successfully use it, so we started using porcelain. Porcelain took a few thousand years for people to model and fire it, different glazes, temperature, type of control. It takes so many years to come up with a beautiful Chinese vase that we cannot match it today. And also other things: carpentry, poetry, language. It takes a person his whole life to try to polish or to refine very simple structures. Lego has the same quality. We have 40 colors and the company has been around for a very long time. They told me they didn’t want to sell to me because of political reasons. So I said, “Hey, that’s a political statement.” They didn’t even realize they had made a political statement by not selling me the Legos, so of course I won the case and now I can freely use them.
When Lego refused to sell you their plastic bricks for a time, as they said they didn’t want to get involved in anything that makes a political statement, there was a kind of protest and your fans worldwide were invited to donate their own bricks to you at Lego collection points set up in different cities, so you got them in the end. You called Lego out for censorship and discrimination and the Danish toy maker made a U-turn on its policy. However, Lego bricks are expensive and you’re spending a huge amount on the company, so why not use a different kind of material? Are you using Lego because you won the case?
Firstly, art is priceless, so it doesn’t matter whatever you use, it’s really undervalued. You can use gold or diamonds, but still art is priceless. That’s what I believe in my heart. Secondly, when they told me I cannot use Legos, that encouraged me to do something that seemed impossible. But I got really broad support from my galleries and friends. When I see children look at my Lego works, I look at their expressions and how much they are surprised that Legos can also be used in this way. Of course, every work I do is not just for childish play. It has a childish quality. I love that quality, but at the same time, there’s a very profound political or personal meaning or artistic argument behind my works.
Describe your current exhibition “Neither Nor” at Galleria Continua in San Gimignano, which explores the concept of ambiguity and contradiction.
The title actually comes from a Jasper Johns’ work called “Neither Nor”, but nobody knows it. It’s about an area in between, which I’m always interested in. There’s too many political correctness. It doesn’t allow people to think outside of the cage because as humans, we can think freely, we can ask questions, but in many societies, even universities, we’re not allowed to do that. So I think that’s something wrong with our immune system because we are addicted to a certain style, which is not good for our thinking, our mind or our emotions. “Neither Nor” shows my mental condition. It’s something that’s hard to explain because we cannot just say “yes” or “no”, but very often, we say “neither nor” because the situation is so complex.
You’re showing some of the great works of Western art history, particularly the Italian cannon, but you’ve altered them. For example, why did you put yourself as Judas in your Lego painting of “The Last Supper”?
Actually, I have a little story about why I did this painting. It’s because when I was very small, I read a poem written by my father when he was in jail, sentenced for six years, during the 1930s. He wrote about the moment that Jesus became a sacrifice, who betrayed him and all those stories of enlightenment. I read it when I was very young, but I didn’t understand it at all. In the story, my father told me that Judas sold some information and betrayed Jesus for a small amount of money, and put pressure on religion. His betrayal made Jesus become Jesus because of his sacrifice. I think that this is a very funny story because for me, a story needs someone like this. So I put myself as Judas because I want to tell people not to trust me.
There’s a coat hanger in the foreground of the Giorgione “Sleeping Venus”, which has become one of your motifs, and it goes back to the Duchamp profile that you saw in a Jasper Johns painting when you were first in New York. You looked at it as a design object and the resonance it had for you when you were in prison.
It was really when the US had a big debate about women’s right to abortion. So this is an old topic, a classic argument. We all know how the coat hanger played a function in a very brutal, symbolic way for the women of that time. So when I made this painting, I asked an American friend, and he wrote to me, “Weiwei, you cannot do that.” I said, “Why? It’s just a coat hanger.” He said because this would be too controversial and I would never escape this argument. That made me so excited, and I said, “That’s not what your argument should be. We cannot hide our arguments. We should always encourage arguments.” So I did the coat hanger.
You treat the coat hanger and art history as readymade objects in a very Duchampian way. What was the trigger for your works? Did you start by thinking that you want to express your concerns around abortion and women’s rights, or did these things just morph out of the process of found objects and what those objects might tell us?
My political position is never clear. That’s why the exhibition title “Neither Nor”. I’m not defending any rights except freedom of speech, which I think is an essential human right. Freedom of speech means you’re not just saying the right thing; it gives you the possibility to say something wrong or that can be called wrong, so you can have a debate. If you don’t allow this kind of so-called wrong, then you’re in a most dangerous society that won’t allow something beyond your understanding or your so-called value judgement. Humans have the right to speak out. It’s hard. I can be poor, I can have a very narrow mind and be completely wrong, but human society is still growing and it never really reaches maturity, even if it is fast developing scientifically. I think we’re very immature as humans.

title: Facebook, Instagram are using your data to train AI: Learn how to protect it
text:
Meta may have paused its plans to train artificial intelligence models for the lucky ones living in Europe, where laws protect people using Facebook and Instagram better than Americans. Here in the good ole USA, both Facebook and Instagram have already been combing through public posts from U.S. accounts to train and improve its AI capabilities, including its chatbot, since last year.
The proposed privacy policy update for European Union and U.K. users, originally scheduled for June 26, would have allowed Meta to use publicly shared content for AI training. However, users and regulatory agencies opposed this plan, leading to its indefinite postponement in those regions.
In contrast, Meta has been incorporating public data from U.S. accounts into its generative AI features without offering an opt-out option. But I’ve got some privacy tweaks for you to make on both social networks we will get to in a second.
We reached out to Meta, and a company spokesperson provided us with this statement: "Across the internet, public information is being used to train AI. This is not unique to our services. We’re committed to building AI responsibly and believe it’s important that people understand how we train the models that power our generative AI product."
GET SECURITY ALERTS, EXPERT TIPS - SIGN UP FOR KURT’S NEWSLETTER - THE CYBERGUY REPORT HERE
What you need to know about Meta’s AI training
AI chatbots and other large language models, such as those creating images, use your personal data for training. Companies like Google and OpenAI trained their AI models using data shared on the internet. It's important to note that these companies did not feed your social media data directly to AI. Instead, they relied on data posted by publishers and small websites. They also made agreements with large publishers and companies like News Corp and Reddit to use their content legally.
However, Meta’s AI training is different. The company will use every personal detail of your life that you posted publicly. This includes photos and videos in your feed and captions on your posts and Reels. Meta can only use this information if you have a public account. Private accounts, Facebook and Instagram stories, and Threads data will be spared. Meta says it also doesn’t use anything from private, direct messaging on Facebook and Instagram, even for people with public accounts.
Users in the U.S. and other countries without national data privacy laws don't have a sure way to stop Meta from using their data to train AI. Interestingly, people in the U.S. might never have known that Meta is using their personal data to train AI if it weren't for the European Union (EU). The EU has laws that make companies disclose how they get, use and keep data – and offer opt-outs. Because of these laws, Meta had to email EU users about the policy change.
DON’T FALL FOR THAT ‘LOOK WHO DIED’ FACEBOOK MESSAGE TRAP
How to stop Meta from using your data to train AI
You can’t stop Meta from training its AI on your personal data unless you make your Facebook or Instagram account private. The other option to stop the social media giant from using your personal data is to delete your public posts. Deleting stuff might be a little too much, but below, I show you how to make your account private on both Instagram and Facebook.
If you have a Facebook account:
Open your Facebook account on your phone or computer. Note: I am using my phone for this tutorial.
- Select the Menu
- Tap Settings & privacy
- Select Settings
- Scroll to where it says Audience and visibility
- Click Posts
- Then select an option other than Public, such as Friends or Only Me
If you have an Instagram account:
- Select the profile tab in the bottom right
- Tap the three lines in the top right corner to open Settings and activity
- Tap Account privacy and toggle your account to private so it appears blue
How to remove data from the internet
While you can stop Meta from using your data by making your account private, other tech companies can still use your publicly available data. Invest in a data removal service to remove your data online. No service promises to remove all your data from the internet, but having a removal service is great if you want to constantly monitor and automate the process of removing your information from hundreds of sites continuously over a longer period. Remove your personal data from the internet with my top picks here.
Kurt’s key takeaway
Tech companies are chasing after your data to get ahead in the AI race. Google already uses data from multiple platforms to train its AI, and OpenAI was one of the first to do this. Meta wants in on the action by using your Facebook and Instagram posts. This isn’t fair, and U.S. users should have the same control over their data as those in the EU. It's time for the government to introduce stricter data protection laws to stop big tech giants from exploiting Americans' data.
