title: Council Post: Generative AI Killer Applications For The Enterprise
text:
Muddu Sudhakar, Investor, Board Member and CEO of AISERA, Inc., an AI Service Management (AISM) Company.
Killer applications are breakout software systems that prove the core value of a larger technology such as a platform, operating system or gaming console. They are essential for driving growth and adoption. They also mark a sharp change in the direction of the technology industry.
During the 1980s, the killer applications were for the PC platform such as spreadsheets and word processors. As for the 1990s, it was the internet that took center stage with Amazon's e-commerce juggernaut, the Yahoo portal and email. Then in the mobile era, the killer applications were Uber, WhatsApp and Instagram.
As of today, the new platform is generative AI. This was sparked with ChatGPT, which has helped boost OpenAI's market value to about $80 billion.
What about the other killer apps? Interestingly enough, they are mostly not in the consumer space. Rather, they have emerged in the enterprise. This is due to the inherent capabilities of generative AI. The technology is particularly good at handling natural language, reasoning, automating tedious processes and interpreting huge amounts of data. These capabilities can lead to significant improvements in productivity, cost savings and even revenue opportunities.
Keep in mind that generative AI has emerged as one of the top priorities for executives. This is highlighted by a recent IDC report that predicts spending on the technology will go from $16 billion in 2023 to $143 billion by 2027. This is a 73.3% annual growth rate. Predictions are far from foolproof, but there is certainly significant momentum.
Let's take a look at some of the early killer applications for generative AI in the enterprise.
AI-Assisted Coding
In June 2022, Microsoft's GitHub launched Copilot for AI-powered code generation. According to GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke: "When you type code or comments, GitHub Copilot suggests the next line of code. But it's not only a single word or line of code. GitHub Copilot can suggest complete methods, boilerplate code, whole unit tests, and even complex algorithms."
Copilot would go on to be one of Microsoft's fastest-growing applications. In Q2 2024, the company announced that there were over 1.3 million paid users, up 30% on a quarter-over-quarter basis. There are over 50,000 organizations that use Copilot, like Goldman Sachs, Etsy, Autodesk and Dell Technologies.
Other megatech companies such as Google and Amazon have aggressively launched their own AI-powered code generation tools. There are also numerous startups in the market like Cursor, Tabnine and Replit.
The value proposition for AI-assisted tools is clear. A 2023 McKinsey study showed that developers could create code 35% to 45% faster. It also has been shown to effectively onboard new developers to projects. With severe shortages of technical talent and the strategic importance of creating applications, generative AI can be a force multiplier for an enterprise.
Cybersecurity
There continues to be significant growth in the number of cybersecurity threats. In 2023, the number of global data breaches soared by 72%. The average cost of a breach is about $4.45 million, according to research from IBM.
Generative AI can be critical for mitigating the risks. After all, a breach can happen within minutes or even seconds. There needs to be a sophisticated defense system that can act in real time and is highly adaptable. Generative AI's ability to decipher complex patterns can be instrumental. It can also learn at high speed, allowing for the defenses to anticipate problems.
Additionally, generative AI can help alleviate the severe talent shortage for security professionals. On a worldwide basis, the shortfall is expected to reach 3.5 million by 2025. The technology can help automate many of the tedious processes while also bolstering employee training.
According to a 2023 survey from KPMG, 63% of IT professionals say that generative AI in cybersecurity will have the greatest impact on their organization, and 64% expect to use this technology within the next six to 12 months.
Then again, the productivity gains can be substantial. For example, Checkpoint Software's cybersecurity copilot has saved 90% of the time on common security tasks. According to a Microsoft whitepaper (download required), its offering has improved security professionals' speed by 22% across all tasks. As for security novices, they were 44% more accurate.
Customer Service
For many years, chatbots have been mostly a disappointment. One of the main reasons is that they have generally been preprogrammed with scripts and decision trees, meaning chatbots cannot understand certain queries. They can also be impersonal and not effectively take into account a user's background information. Then, there are the issues of making handovers to human agents.
However, generative AI is poised to change the game. Consider the case with Klarna, which is a fintech startup. The company partnered with OpenAI to use generative AI to create an AI assistant for customer service.
One month after the launch, the company announced that its tool could handle about the same amount of work as 700 full-time agents and that satisfaction scores were roughly at the same levels. The AI assistant also had a more accurate resolution rate, which meant a 25% drop in repeat queries. Klarna estimated that the technology would result in a $40 million profit improvement.
Conclusion
Unlike previous technological shifts, which were primarily consumer-focused, generative AI has become fertile for killer applications in the enterprise. As spending on generative AI software skyrockets, these early applications are just the beginning of a wider and deeper integration of AI technologies in the enterprise—signaling a major shift in how businesses operate and compete in the digital age.

title: Latest Trend Of Mindless ‘Raw-Dogging’ On Flights Gives Way To Mindful Generative AI Taking Up The Slack
text:
The latest trending buzzword is the catchphrase of “raw-dogging” during a commercial flight (the clean version), namely that you opt to do nothing as a flying passenger other than staring straight ahead for the entire duration of the flight. You intentionally and devotedly allow your mind to be free of any of the usual accompaniments such as no audiobooks, no earphones-pumped music, no in-flight movies, no videos on your smartphone, and not even any old-fashioned paper-based books or newspapers.
That’s right, you sit there and seemingly act like a human vegetable.
Furthermore, those of the purest form of this activity, or shall we say non-activity, would eschew any water, food, candy, or any other valuable or useless nourishment. You are trying to minimize any kind of physical exertion. You are also aiming to reduce or minimize any form of external stimulus that might get your mental juices going. The assumption is that by avoiding using headsets and not watching or listening to entertainment or infotainment, and by not reading regular books or e-books, your mind is getting a vital respite.
Let’s talk about it.
As you will shortly see, though this is a hot trend right now, I predict that one means of overstepping this newly identified mindless approach to flying is going to ultimately and soon enough give way to the use of generative AI during your flying journeys. I suggest that you can have your cake and eat it too, consisting of remaining relatively motionless and yet stirring your desired mental emptiness into fruitful mindfulness via the likes of modern-day generative AI and large language models (LLMs).
We will proceed by first looking more closely at this hot trend. I will then introduce to you the aspects of how generative AI is going to disrupt the emerging approach. AI, as you know, seems to be a mighty disruptor, and I claim that the same will be true in this particular use case.
Hang in there, I’ll explain why.
Before we leap into the fray, allow me to go into my customary opening remarks. For my ongoing readers, in today’s column, I am continuing my ongoing series about the impact of generative AI in the health and medical realm. The focus this time is once again on the mental health domain and examines whether those seeking mindlessness might instead favor augmented mindfulness.
I have previously examined numerous interleaving facets of generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Other vital background includes my in-depth coverage of mental health chatbots which have been bolstered by generative AI (see the link here) and the rapidly changing nature of the client-therapist relationship due to generative AI at the link here. I explored where things are headed regarding the levels of AI-based mental therapy autonomous guidance at the link here, and showcased the importance of the World Health Organization (WHO) report on global health and generative AI at the link here, and so on.
Unpacking The Matter Of Flying In Today’s Nutty World
I dare say that many flyers will often opt to bury themselves into their assigned seat and then try to turn away from the rest of the chaotic world. Nowadays, the tussle and verbal arguments on flights are nonstop and altogether exasperating. You want to just have your own tiny spot of turf for the next few hours and hope that nothing untoward delays your flight or disrupts your desired peace and quiet.
If you hide by not making any motions or garnering any possible attention to your actions, you might avoid attracting some nutjob who wants to pick a battle with you. Keep your eyes averted from the eyes of others. Don’t be using anything that someone else might ask what you are watching or reading. Don’t tempt someone to look at you to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing what you are doing.
Remain as invisible, unobtrusive, and uncontroversial as you humanly can. Hide in plain sight. Do this by eliminating any motion such as eating, drinking, talking, etc. Make yourself like one of those startled animals that freeze in the woods and pray that no predator perchance spots them. The most microscopic movements, such as watching an in-flight video and smiling or expressing sadness, will send blaring visual signals to nearby passengers, and the next thing you know, others are verbally entering your so-called private space.
Not everyone who goes this vanilla toast route of being a passenger on planes is necessarily doing so to keep from getting picked on or drawn into a fracas onboard the flight.
They might be simply relishing a moment of oneness.
You are a stranger to everyone else who is confined in the same tight space as you are. In a sense, that’s a rarity of sorts. You see, you don’t have to carry on a conversation. You don’t need to make small niceties with others. At work, you must do so. With friends, you have to do so. Here, stuck on a plane for a few hours, there is no statutory requirement that you engage in dialogue or seek to be a part of the humanity surrounding you.
The ticket you purchased is focused on getting you and your body from point A to point B. That’s it. The airline doesn’t tell you that you have to be responsive to the person seated to your left or right. About the only time you are supposed to do anything is when the flight attendants or crew members ask you a question. Usually, that only happens if you are seated in a row that includes responsibility for the exit hatches. Most of the flight, you are well within your rights to remain in your own little bubble.
Something else about flying is notably special.
There is no escape. Everyone including you is locked into a kind of cone or shell and there is no substantive control that you have over things once you sit down. You are padlocked in place and time, waiting for the arrival at your destination, so you can scoot out of the iron-clad confinement and make your way back into the real world (versus the artificial world of being ensconced in an airplane).
You’ve Paid For A Moment Of Isolation So Use It
I’ve got a twist for you.
Maybe this doesn’t fit your mental model of flying, but it could be said that you are buying a moment of isolation when you purchase that airborne going ticket. People that you know will understand and realize that you are going to be on a plane for a few hours and generally unreachable. You’ve bought yourself time to do some self-reflection and graciously avoid any interruptions.
Try arranging that in almost any other mode of life. It’s hard to do so. If you were to go to a movie theatre for a couple of hours, few would consider that an uninterruptable endeavor. You can always be called and asked to leave the movie for a moment to take a brief or urgent call. There is nothing that seems to constrain you from being available, other than common courtesy.
Being on a plane is a blessing in disguise.
Of course, this is eroding as a proposition due to the expanding bandwidth of Wi-Fi while on a plane, allowing you to be just as in touch as if you were sitting in a hotel room. No excuses will eventually be the standard retort if you haven’t texted someone or called them, despite being on a plane. Employers will fully expect you to engage in work activities, including ones that aren’t just the silent efforts of noodling on spreadsheets. Your being seated in a plane won’t absolve you or prevent you from taking calls, making calls, reading emails in real-time, responding in real-time, and so on.
Right now, while the moment still exists, each time you get onto a plane you should be saying to yourself how you want to use that carve out of special time.
I realize that most people perceive the time on a plane as a time waster. They desperately want to fill up the time. If you are on a seven-hour flight, you might watch three movies back-to-back, trying to fight the boredom. Your stored audio podcasts can be a salvation. The Wi-Fi on the plane is your rescue line. The use of any modern-day digital contrivance to keep your mind employed is a breath of fresh air. Using a paper-based artifact is fine too. You used to be able to depend on various worn torn magazines in the back pocket of the seat in front of you. Regrettably, that’s typically no longer your final lifeline (the pockets are normally empty now, other than a flimsy flight safety instruction sheet; the reading of which only lasts a minute or two).
There is another side to the coin of how to use the time.
Rather than a time waster, you can be optimistic and see this as a time to do the things you’ve not had a chance to otherwise do. A movie that you’ve not been able to squeeze into your busy schedule is now watchable while you are otherwise unoccupied while on a plane. No one can reasonably decry your having used the time to watch a movie solely for entertainment purposes (well, some might, such as pressures from work or maybe someone who has asked you to help with this or that problem-solving task).
You can go beyond the pale and momentously turn the time into a grand positive by learning something new while on the flight. A podcast that covers an area of interest in an instructional fashion is a nice twofer. It uses up time. It boosts your skills. That is quite defensible to others that you know. It surely is defensible in your own mind, such that you cannot silently berate yourself for wasting a precious clump of time; instead, you have put the time to amazingly productive purposes.
Good for you!
The Time Can Be Used For Nothingness If You So Desire
Into this morass of either being a time waster or a time embellisher comes the rise of the motionless dead-stare.
The deal is this.
A conscious decision is made to craft a modified variant of a sensory deprivation tank. You don’t watch movies simply for the sake of chewing up time. You don’t watch movies, even educational documentaries, to use the time to self-educate. In short, you don’t watch movies. Period, end of story. Nor do you engage in conversation. You don’t eat, drink, or do any similar consumption.
Instead, you use the time for complete and utter barrenness.
You paid for it.
It’s yours to use as you wish.
The difficulty is that those around you don’t necessarily see the world from that same viewpoint. They think of you as their buddy. They think of you as someone to be entertained by. They see you as handy-dandy fodder for their effort to fill the time. What is that person watching? What is that person listening to? Why is that person smiling? Why is that person grimacing?
In fact, some people believe that the purpose or at least a side benefit of flying is to be amidst your fellow humankind. What a wonderful moment to make new friends or foster acquaintances. You cannot just usually walk up to someone on the street and start a conversation out of the blue. On a plane, it is not only readily possible but also widely accepted.
If someone on a plane doesn’t respond to an attempt at human connection, they are usually seen as anti-social. That’s a dour person. Must be a hermit. Must be a rotten person. How can they not engage with their new onboard neighbors? What’s their deal? The irony is that oftentimes this will perhaps prod those such provocateurs into wanting to talk with someone more so than otherwise. They want to figure out the puzzle. They want to turn you into a social butterfly, all by getting you to open up on a few-hour-long flight. Miracles can be made to happen, so they earnestly believe.
Flying used to be a lot like that.
You would be a business flyer and make a human-to-human in-person connection that landed you a new job or led to selling whatever product or service you were hawking. It was stupid to not leverage the trapped connections onboard a flight. People that you wouldn’t normally expect to return your cold calls could be enchanted with your sales pitch over drinks on a flight. Flying was a goldmine.
The same went along with making new friends. The person seated next to you might live in the same geographic region as you. This made sense because either the departure locale or the destination locale could be something the two of you have in common. The next thing you know, you’ve made a friend and will keep in touch forever. Nifty that a flight managed to bring the two of you into contact. Was it fate or luck? Doesn’t matter since the outcome was divine.
Given the craziness on today’s flights, people have generally gotten used to the idea that the odds of anything fruitful occurring on a social basis are lower than the odds at a Las Vegas casino. You are best to wear a hoodie or some such clothing, take your seat, put yourself into your own world by wearing a headset, and watch the clock until your flight arrives at your destination.
Sorry that this seems anti-social and unlike the days of yore, but that’s where we seem to be nowadays.
Expanding The Nothingness Proposition
Assume for a moment that you are interested in being a prospective member of this new trend entailing doing nothing, as much as feasible, while on a flight.
The good news is that you don’t have to buy anything or make any special arrangements. Just show up to your flight on time and without any fuss or muss, don’t carp about the flight, sit quietly in your seat, avoid making any indications that you want to converse, politely rebuff others if they try to engage or invade but do so without getting their dander up (this is a rough challenge, for sure), respond to the flight attendants or crew (don’t call upon them, but do make sure to respond to them promptly and courteously), do not eat or drink, do not use your smartphone or any such devices, do not read a book or any materials, do not use the in-flight entertainment services, and keep to yourself.
Whew, that seems like a lot, but it isn’t quite as hard as it might seem.
A satirical conspiracy theory making the rounds is that this is precisely what the airlines want us to do.
How so?
The beauty of this trend is that passengers become (according to some) complacent sheep that will be herded without any added effort by the airlines. No more backtalk to the flight crew. No more having to deal with people wanting to switch seats. Just get them onboard as though kindergarten is in session. They won’t be whining about the meal selections. They won’t complain if the Wi-Fi is down. No one will bemoan the in-flight movies available. The reason is that none of those extras will be needed or utilized.
Maybe the airlines are secretly spurring this new trend, some exhort. Makes sense for them to want to do so. The flights will proceed more smoothly. A plane ride becomes a focus on transporting people, akin to transporting baggage. Even if the airlines aren’t pushing this, they would seem to undoubtedly silently welcome it. Anyway, let’s not go down the conspiracy’s abyss here.
Getting back to being a lump on a log, there are a lot of people who would dread such a predicament.
What in the world am I going to do for those excruciatingly long abysmal hours on a plane if I cannot be entertained by one thing or another?
The answer is that you are supposed to use your mind.
You can go one of two major routes about your mind:
- (1) Empty your mind (mindless mode). Go into a Zen-like mental mode, allow your mind to be barren of thoughts or emotions. Let your mind be free of any need to think.
- (2) Be thinking (mindful mode). Without having to rely on any external stimulus, engage your mind into thinking about whatever you want to think about. Maybe the issues of the day. Perhaps the meaning of life. You name it. Allow your mind to chew on a bone of your choosing.
The reaction by most people is likely one of shock and doubt.
Is it possible to empty your mind for hours at a time non-stop?
Doesn’t seem possible.
Is it feasible to fill your mind with your own devised thoughts for hours at a time non-stop?
Doesn’t seem feasible.
Can’t be done.
An alternative that people will quickly gravitate toward would be to simply fall asleep. Sleeping during a flight seems to achieve the same desired ends. You won’t eat or drink while sleeping. You won’t be watching movies or listening to podcasts while sleeping. As an aside, some would argue that they cannot go to sleep without at least having those various other engaging options to lull them to sleep but let’s put that out of bounds for now. Go with the flow on the concept that sleep is seen as the hoped-for answer.
I am about to say something that might be triggering. You are forewarned.
In this hot trend, you are not allowed to sleep.
Sleeping is cheating in this case. You can only score top points for attaining nothingness if you are awake. It is a cheap and disdainful idea that you would use sleep to tide you over. Just about anybody could sleep their way into mental oblivion. Forget about sleep mode as a sneaky alternative. If you fall asleep, you’ve lost the gambit and are out of the game. Those are the rules, live with it.
I will acknowledge a small tip of a different nature that might help.
You can certainly shift back and forth mentally from the emptiness avenue to the thinking avenue. There is nothing wrong with that approach. Maybe for a half hour, your mind is mindless. The next hour, your mind is mindful. Then, you take a mental break, and your mind is mindless for another half hour. Finally, you reach your destination and turn your mind back into an active mode for real-world interaction.
Some people will contend that the added rule of variability allowed doesn’t do anything for them. They just cannot do any combination of mindlessness and mindfulness that will get them through an entire flight. They will simply go mentally mad. Their minds will break. Who knows what might then transpire?
Generative AI Might Change The Proposition In A Clever Way
I trust that you are intently mulling over whether you have what it takes to succeed in this latest flight-going herculean quest.
Some vital caveats come into the matter.
The truth of the situation is that you are going to still be encountering stimuli. This is not truly a sensory deprivation tank. You can look here or there while in your seat, thus you are receiving all manner of visual information that your brain can be processing. You can smell or detect odors, which your brain can process. The sense of touch is still with you, such as being able to feel the plane rocking or the toughness of your seat. You can hear sounds and process the words being spoken around you by the chattering of nearby passengers, likewise, the music that you overhear from their sound-leaking headsets, and so on.
In that manner, you are not bereft of things to think about. Everything happening around you during the flight is widely available for your mind to ponder. Few people probably today give those little moments or myopic bits much thought while flying. If you enter into this needed hyper-aware mode, it is possible that you could fill your mind with a constant stew of things to think about.
Admittedly, you will likely need to have sharpened your mind to do so, akin to Sherlock Holmes's attentiveness, but the bottom line is that you can fill hours upon hours of mental wonderment by using your senses while confined to your seat. One supposes that if you want to go the other route of mindlessness, you are going to have to fight against the surrounding stimuli. In that instance, you might put on blinders, plug your ears, and reduce the stimuli as much as you can. Remember though, no sleeping is allowed, therefore do not let the lack of stimuli lull you into slumber. That’s a no-no.
Is it fair to look at the screen on the back of the seat in front of you?
The general rule seems to be that as long as you aren’t using a headset, and you aren’t changing the channels, you can stare at the screen. This might mean that you will see a menu of options for the whole flight. Or you might see ads. Some turn the screen to show the map of the flight, which depending upon your opinion is acceptable to look at, while some say it is a type of cheating if the map wasn’t already on by default. Any overt act to do anything with the screen is considered a cheat.
I am going to once again forewarn you about something else that might be triggering. Ready yourself.
Is it fair game to look at other people’s screens?
I know that sounds creepy. Allow me a moment to explain what this is about. There you are, in your assigned seat. You are able to look around. A person in the row ahead of you and to your left is displaying on the seatback screen a movie. You cannot hear it. But you clearly can see it.
In theory, you could watch an entire movie by simply looking at that screen. Since the person’s back is to you, they might not know that you are doing so. If they knew you were doing so, this would likely seem eerie and creep them out. They might be tempted to tell the flight attendant. Things could get ugly.
Putting the dangers aside, from the perspective of this gambit, does that seem like a reasonable part of the rules? You might argue that if you are allowed to look at the screen directly in front of you, the idea of looking at someone else’s screen seems equally fair game. The retort is that the screen in front of you is to remain untouched. The screen of another passenger is being controlled by that person and thus a human effort is now drawn into the gambit. Aha, the retort to the retort goes, the person in the gambit is not doing anything to impact that other person and the screen they are watching. It is merely a part of the environment in which you are confined.
The overall gist is that there are lots of potential exceptions or indeterminate rules that come into this game. It isn’t strictly tied down to a list of definitive dos and don’ts. The whole kit and kaboodle are somewhat loosey-goosey.
That’s where I want to introduce you to the role of generative AI.
I’d dare suggest that the loosey-goosey rules might accommodate generative AI, or, failing that possibility (which some would adamantly insist is far outside the allowed rules), we might change the game and encompass generative AI as part of the game.
Intrigued?
I hope so.
Read on.
Squaring Up Generative AI In The Gambit
First, let’s talk in general about generative AI and large language models (LLMs), doing so to make sure we are on the same page when it comes to discussing the matter at hand.
I’m sure you’ve heard of generative AI, the darling of the tech field these days.
Perhaps you’ve used a generative AI app, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing caliber.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
The matter at hand is that we are playing the nothingness game while enduring an entire flight from one place to another. Remember that the nothingness game doesn’t require that your mind be blank during a flight. Indeed, you are welcome to have a fully engaged mind. That is a completely allowable part of the milieu.
You cannot have a conversation with a human. Doing so is abundantly outside the rules. The only conversation permitted as exceptions would be emergencies where a dialogue is the only sensible way to proceed, or if a crew member engages you in discussion for flight operations purposes.
I ask you this, would it be permissible to carry on a conversation with a machine, such as generative AI?
Interesting proposition.
Give that some thought.
Let’s for the sake of discussion say that yes, conversing with generative AI is within the bounds of this matter. The nice thing about this is that generative AI would readily occupy your thinking processes for the duration of a flight. You could start a discussion and do the heavy lifting by keeping the conversation going. Alternatively, you could tell generative AI to keep the conversation active, for which the AI would then continually try to find new topics to cover or ask questions of you that prod you to proceed further.
If you only want to do some lightweight chatting, all you need to do is instruct generative AI to remain on easygoing topics. The AI will avoid asking mind-bending questions of you. If you steer the conversation into the latest theories of quantum mechanics, the AI will subtly demur and move to some other simpler topics.
Generative AI can be used for entertainment purposes, such as having the AI play tic-tac-toe with you or tell you fanciful stories. The same generative AI can be used for educational pursuits. You might tell the AI to teach you about how to become a world-renowned chef. Imagine that during a flight from one city to the next, you come up-to-speed with the best cooking techniques and practices of world-class sous chefs. Nice.
During a flight, generative AI is not only aiding you in using up the otherwise dismally boring time, but the AI can enhance your knowledge of a wide variety of subject matters. You will step off the plane as a better person. You used the time fruitfully. Via AI, you were totally mindful rather than mindless. All around success.
In that sense, your overall mental health could be improved too.
There is another angle to this. As I’ve extensively covered, people are using generative AI for mental health guidance, see the link here and the link here, for example. On that two-hour flight that otherwise would be dull, you could bring up the personal issues you are having at home and work.
Maybe discuss the bout of depression that you’ve recently experienced.
Assuming that you are interacting with generative AI via a text-based mode, no one else around you would be aware of what your conversation consists of. You might be baring your soul, meanwhile, thankfully, no one else knows what you are undertaking. On the plane, you can have whatever AI conversations you want to have. A complete therapeutic advisement session can occur right under the noses of your fellow passengers.
You can also start and stop the conversation as you please. With humans, you typically have to go through various contortions to civilly end or at least temporarily pause a conversation. Not so with generative AI. Just stop entering prompts, or if you like, tell the AI you want to take a pause, and will get things restarted when you wish to do so. Conversations with generative AI are said to be frictionless, meaning that the usual human-to-human friction of chatting can be reduced to near zero.
Seems like we have a winner-winner chicken dinner in our hands.
Gotchas Regarding Generative AI Usage In This Guise
I don’t want you to get a misimpression that generative AI is the silver bullet here.
First, generative AI is not sentient, and you have to be mindful to not overstate what the AI can do. Conversations are decidedly part and parcel of any good generative AI package. The trouble is that there are limitations and constraints that any lengthy conversation will almost always encounter. Remember that the conversation is an artificial one and not one with a fellow human.
Second, generative AI can at times make errors or generate what is commonly referred to as AI hallucinations, see my coverage at the link here and the link here. I disfavor the terminology of saying that AI hallucinates since it is an improper anthropomorphizing of AI. In any case, the point is that the AI can suddenly make up something that is groundless and fictitious. You might not realize that you are being fed a falsehood. That’s bad.
Third, people tend to assume that their conversations with generative AI are entirely private and confidential. That’s typically not the case. The AI maker often retains the right to examine whatever you have entered or done in the generative AI, including that they can reuse that info to do further data training of the AI. Be wary of what you enter into generative AI, see my details at the link here.
Fourth, the matter of whether generative AI is doing a good job of advising on mental health is still unknown and an open question, see my coverage at the link here. It could be that the provided mental health advice is going to shoot our collective societal foot, namely that on a large-scale population-level basis people will be getting off-the-wall therapeutic guidance. This could be happening insidiously, person by person, such that across the board we don’t realize that the AI is taking us down the wrong mental health path.
I believe you can see that we must be cautious in using generative AI, overall, and when it comes to being used during a flight, we ought to have some suitable reservations in hand (a pun there).
Let’s envision this.
You are sitting on a plane and everyone around you is engaged in a “private” conversation with their generative AI app. The whole flight consists of the passengers quietly text-wise chatting with generative AI. The passengers do not eat or drink, as per the stated gambit of nothingness. They don’t sleep. They do not use any other digital device, other than what is needed to engage with generative AI. We might go so far as to restrict the AI to not show any movies, not play any music, or do anything else of a similar nature.
We will restrict the generative AI to text-based conversations on a one-on-one basis.
This solves the problem of those people who are scared out of their wits of what to do with all that nothingness time. Generative AI is their flight buddy. No one must use the generative AI. Some passengers will merely allow their minds to go blank for the duration of the flight. Others will have the mental fortitude to entertain their own mind. The rest will either use generative AI because they believe they will otherwise go bonkers, or AI will be used by those who believe they didn’t need to do so but that it would be a nice added plus.
Problem solved; gambit achieved.
Conclusion
Whoa, some will be yelling defiantly, using generative AI as part of the nothingness trend is quite obviously skirting the rules. If you can’t use the in-flight entertainment and can’t use podcasts, it seems to stand to reason that you cannot use generative AI. Don’t try to pretend otherwise.
I hear you.
Allow me to briefly pursue a different tack.
Before I do so, and slightly via a shifting of gears, it is worthwhile to note and acknowledge that the trending catchphrase has morphed from an earlier-in-time meaning associated with the moniker (a somewhat indelicate meaning). Unfortunately, the catchphrase is being reused. I only used it briefly and then aimed to be descriptive rather than use the particular phrase. It would be better for all if a different term was formulated for this new usage. I hope that will happen.
Just wanted to make that known.
Let’s get back into the groove of generative AI and the future.
I am betting that the use of generative AI for tiding you mentally over during a flight is going to happen whether it fits into the rules of the game or not. The game will not bear fruit on its own. If you are willing to toss generative AI into the game and bend the rules (if that’s what it takes), the rest of the game has a chance of surviving.
Setting aside the game entirely, you can make a surefire bet that people are going to be using generative AI while on flights. I already do so now, and I’ve seen fellow passengers doing likewise. They are just the tip of the spear, the early adopters, the movers and shakers.
Gradually, generative AI is going to be used while you are on a plane, on a train, in a car, in a bus, and pretty much wherever you are. I suppose you will use generative AI while in a box and with a fox, and while eating green eggs and ham (head nod to Dr. Seuss).
Have fun on your next flight and see whether you can take on the nothingness challenge. Try it without the use of generative AI. On your return flight, go ahead and try it with generative AI. You be the judge of what seems fair and appropriate.
I’d wave at you during the flight if I’m also onboard, but then again, that’s not within the rules of the game, so just assume I would have waved had I been permitted to do so. Thanks for playing along.

title: Council Post: AI Innovation: Keeping Pace Or Propelling?
text:
Alejandro Martinez is CEO U.S. & Canada of SDG Group. Sharing insights on How Data & Analytics Generate Business Impact and Value.
As every day brings more options for embedding AI into your company’s overall strategy, business owners who want to see better outcomes should consider their choices carefully. AI solutions are becoming increasingly accessible—from Microsoft's Copilot to databases with embedded LLMs—which means business owners face a critical decision: play it safe or push things forward? Just as a modest return on a savings account barely outpaces inflation, cautiously adopting AI might keep you afloat, but it won't necessarily propel your business ahead of the competition.
As the CEO of a company at the forefront of AI, data analytics and digital transformation, I've seen how transformative strategic AI implementation can be. But navigating this strategy requires more than just plugging in the latest tech. Here’s how you can use it as a catalyst to move your business forward.
Take A Bird’s-Eye View
The first thing companies should do is take a step back and get a 360-degree view of their processes. You need a comprehensive understanding of your entire operation to identify where AI-driven improvements could help the most. This is crucial because the AI world is always evolving, and businesses need to re-evaluate their processes constantly to keep up. Patchwork solutions without a comprehensive underlying understanding can lead to inefficiencies and missed opportunities.
Take the time to analyze your entire operation from all angles, including assessing workflows, identifying pain points and understanding inefficiencies. For example, in manufacturing AI can optimize supply chain logistics and enhance quality control. In customer service, AI-powered chatbots can handle routine inquiries and free up human agents for more complex tasks.
Taking a holistic view goes beyond applying piecemeal solutions, which might address specific pain points but not align with your overall business goals. It’s a strategic approach that ensures AI solutions integrate seamlessly with your existing systems.
Find A Guide
Keeping pace with the rapid evolution of AI is just one part of the challenge. The other is a company’s own lack of internal expertise. Understanding the complex landscape of potential solutions can be overwhelming. This is where an advisor or “pacer” can be extremely helpful. This person isn’t just a contractor hired to develop the solution, but a partner and an experienced guide who can explain complex concepts and recommend suitable solutions based on your specific needs and goals.
A pacer’s main job is to translate cutting-edge concepts into actionable steps. Think of them as a translator who can coach your team, act as an analytics translator or design workflows. This tailored approach streamlines the entire process of AI adoption and includes keeping the company informed of the latest trends and advancements, maximizing the benefits and minimizing the risks that AI adoption can bring.
To successfully navigate the AI revolution, business owners need to make strategic choices. By taking a comprehensive view of your operations, carefully calibrating your risk tolerance and partnering with an AI guide, you can help ensure that your adoption of AI is a well-informed and strategic process.
Risky Business
In the financial world, investors need to be clear about how much risk they’re willing to take with their investments. We should do the same when it comes to incorporating AI into our workflows. Consider your risk tolerance carefully. The AI landscape is a spectrum: some solutions are well-established and carry lower risks, while others are potentially more disruptive but come with a higher degree of risk.
One critical measurement when investing is a risk aversion score. We should apply a similar approach to our AI game plan that defines the level of risk we're willing to take. As we do so, it's important to remember that just implementing what everyone else is doing is simply keeping pace. To truly propel your business forward, you need to identify strategic areas where you want to increase your competitive advantage and differentiation.
By understanding your risk profile, you can make informed decisions about which AI solutions to implement. There's no magic formula. You can choose to keep pace with the pack by adopting proven solutions, which should ensure slow but steady improvement. Or you can take a bolder approach by venturing into riskier but potentially groundbreaking territory, and gain a competitive advantage in the process. Either way, defining your risk tolerance—how innovative you want to be—helps you make calculated decisions.
Forbes Business Council is the foremost growth and networking organization for business owners and leaders. Do I qualify?

title: Council Post: The Evolution Of Customer Understanding In The Age Of Digital Transformation
text:
Brian Enright is the CEO and Managing Director of DP World Americas.
In today's rapidly evolving marketplace, the importance of deeply understanding and engaging with your customer has never been more critical. This is particularly true for the logistics and supply chain sectors, where maintaining strong customer relationships is essential for navigating the complex landscape of global trade.
And yet amid the whirlwind of digital transformation, a surge of new artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled solutions like virtual assistants, chatbots and automated response systems are revolutionizing how we interact and engage with customers.
As a CEO, I advocate for the ongoing digital transformation, recognizing that these advancements are overwhelmingly positive by enabling businesses to venture into new markets and roll out new services and solutions. However, it's vital to recognize that these digital solutions are driving significant shifts in customer engagement strategies.
So, this begs the question: What does this transformative era mean for customer engagement in the digital age? Will digitalization diminish the personal touch in customer relationships, or will it enhance interactions to new levels?
Digitalization Enhances Expectations
Digital technology has transformed traditional business, ushering in an era where customer expectations are at an all-time high. Customers adopting an “on-demand” service culture reinforced by services such as Google Search, Alexa, Siri and more are driving businesses to accelerate and expand digital transformation programs.
In fact, more companies like Amazon, Marriott and Progressive are using chatbots and customer service platforms for instant communication, resolving issues or answering inquiries immediately. In just a few taps on a smartphone, we have on-demand transportation (Uber, Lyft), food delivery (DoorDash, UberEats) and accommodation (Airbnb, Hilton), while digital payment solutions such as Apple Pay, Google Wallet and PayPal have revolutionized how we send and receive money.
Customers today seek instant gratification, personalized experiences and seamless service across all touchpoints. To stay competitive, businesses must adapt their strategies based on these customer journeys and leverage cutting-edge technological solutions to amplify their human capabilities. But we cannot forget that at the end of the day, the customer we serve and who makes our businesses grow is a person.
The Importance Of Human Connection In The Digital Era
My decades of experience working with customers have taught me that people desire recognition and understanding. Technology undoubtedly makes it easier for us to connect, but technology alone cannot always fulfill these needs. The human element remains irreplaceable across the customer journey.
Here’s a recent example where the human connection really played out. Last month, we engaged with an automotive OEM during a sponsored customer event. This potential client was interested in integrating an online shopping cart but was uncertain about our geographical fit. We engaged in detailed discussions to fully grasp their specific challenges and identify suitable logistical solutions.
Following this, we conducted an operational analysis and found that our contract logistics office in Olive Branch, Mississippi, could not only meet their initial requirements but also offer a more comprehensive service package. This win came down to taking the time to connect in person and identify potential solutions—together.
In this digital era, we leverage analytics and big data to better understand our customer behaviors, preferences and needs. This is particularly important in the logistics and supply chain sectors, where customer needs vary dramatically. We use predictive capabilities to preemptively address customer needs, enhance communication and integrate digital solutions such as IoT and AI to optimize operational efficiency and customer satisfaction.
Digital solutions undoubtedly provide a competitive advantage—generative AI shows great potential in personalizing customer service for a broad audience, allowing human representatives to focus on more complex and sensitive issues. Moreover, technology can assist businesses in monitoring customer behaviors and preferences, enabling them to better tailor the customer experience.
While digital solutions offer competitive advantages and the potential to enhance service, they require us to rethink our interaction with customers. It's not merely about keeping up with trends but about meeting customer expectations, improving operational efficiency and being part of a team.
Recently, a procurement leader representing a Fortune 100 company described the importance of relationships and the shared vision between supply chain solution providers and their clients as an extension of ourselves and understanding the full spectrum of our needs. From sustainability and efficiency to brand and more, this awareness takes time to develop, and once established, it can feel risky to disrupt a positive working relationship.
Embracing Digital Transformation For Enhanced Customer Engagement
How we balance technological efficiency with human connection will define the quality of our customer engagements.
Digital transformation is not just about adopting new technologies; it's about transforming our approach to customer engagement to be as dynamic and forward-thinking as our markets. How can we balance technological efficiency with that sense of human connection to create a compelling customer experience?
Firstly, leaders need to focus on the seamless integration of AI capabilities with human insight. This begins with a robust understanding of customer data. AI tools can be used to analyze large volumes of data to identify trends and preferences that help inform personalized customer interactions. But technology alone isn't enough—we must also maintain a balance where technology enhances service, without replacing the essential human elements of empathy and understanding.
Specific actions to integrate AI and human capabilities include developing a workforce that is both technologically proficient and adept at interpersonal relations. How? By empowering your employees to use technology as an aid rather than a substitute. Provide training programs to enhance their skills in managing AI tools and establish collaborative platforms where AI and human input converge. For example, while AI can predict customer behavior and automate responses to common inquiries, human agents are better suited to handle complex situations that require nuanced understanding and emotional intelligence.
Challenges such as resistance to technological adoption, ethical concerns regarding AI and potential data breaches can obstruct these efforts. Leaders can address these challenges by fostering an organizational culture that values continuous learning and innovation. title: Council Post: Why Global Enterprises Should Care About Equitable Access To AI
text:
Pamela Maynard, CEO of Avanade, a leading digital innovator on the Microsoft ecosystem and global leader in technology business solutions.
Start talking about tech and see how long the conversation takes to turn to AI. Thirty seconds? A minute? Of course, it’s a hot topic. We’re at the start of a revolution, with generative AI set to change the world like calculators, mobile phones and the internet once did.
AI has been around for years, but the advancements in generative AI over the past 18 months—including large language models, small language models, ChatGPT and products like Microsoft Copilot—will revolutionize how we work, collaborate and create by democratizing the technology, putting it in the hands of everyone.
But will it really be in the hands of everyone? Reality suggests otherwise. In October, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres launched a High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence, citing AI’s power for incredible potential as well as incredible harm. He mentioned concerns like misinformation, bias, the invasion of privacy and fraud. But one remark in particular caught my attention:
“As things stand, AI expertise is concentrated in a handful of companies and countries. This could deepen global inequalities and turn digital divides into chasms.”
Guterres is not alone in this viewpoint. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) suggests that countries with developing economies “don’t have the infrastructure or skilled workforces to harness the benefits of AI, raising the risk that over time the technology could worsen inequality among nations.”
So, the disparity is clear, and it threatens to get worse. But why should leaders of global enterprise organizations care? From my experience as a CEO in the tech industry, I can see three clear reasons:
1. It’s better to be proactive than reactive, especially on issues that align with corporate values.
Just two weeks after the murder of George Floyd set off global protests in 2020, Gartner identified a “new urgency to employee and public demands for more diversity and inclusion in the workplace.” Corporations could not invest in diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives fast enough, with the "chief diversity officer" becoming the C-suite title with the fastest hiring growth in 2020 and 2021, according to a LinkedIn study. During one of the hottest talent markets in recent memory, employees were looking to companies to “uphold their stated values,” as Gartner put it.
Responsible AI—which factors in not just bias, misinformation and privacy but also the inclusivity and accessibility of the technology—will be part of similar conversations. We’re all talking about how the success or failure of AI depends on whether we get these first critical steps right, and that is not limited to our organizations; the responsibility extends to our broader society and world. If we get it wrong, we’re facing digital divides that have widened into chasms.
Like the chief diversity officer was once brought in to make a more intentional strategic impact, corporations could tap a chief AI officer to set an ethical AI strategy, build a responsible AI framework, collaborate with legal to iron out data privacy concerns and more. Rather than hiring a chief AI officer when things start to go awry, don’t we owe it to our customers, employees and ourselves to have better foresight and put the right leadership in place now?
2. Moving the needle requires a robust ecosystem of support that we can’t create alone.
Corporations have a responsibility to manage the risks presented by AI, but they cannot be successful in a vacuum. Throughout history, we’ve seen that meaningful transformation occurs when a diverse and interconnected network of collaborators—governments and policymakers, NGOs and nonprofits, activists and citizens—works together toward a common goal. Whether advocating for racial justice or championing environmental sustainability, the power lies in collective action.
It's a positive sign that we are seeing events like the AI Safety Summit in the UK bring together corporations and governments to discuss international cooperation to manage the challenges of AI, but NGOs and nonprofits are often absent from these conversations. These organizations are actively addressing issues like bias and inequality that AI may exacerbate and can add the necessary perspective to create truly thoughtful regulation.
The nonprofit sector is marked by what many call a “sharing culture,” meaning they are open to collaborating and freely offering their learnings to others. Bringing nonprofits and NGOs to the table will ultimately enable many more. This is critical to pursue fairness, inclusivity and the equitable distribution of AI benefits.
3. Equitable access to AI empowers NGOs and nonprofits to pursue equity in other areas, too.
If we ensure equitable access, AI has the potential to allow NGOs and nonprofits to significantly increase their impact. Generative AI empowers nonprofits to achieve their missions. It enables them to create new solutions, services and products that can positively impact the world. We are already seeing many organizations use AI to create more focused campaigns to target donors and aid fundraising and to make chatbots more user-friendly and enabled with more languages for their beneficiaries. Now, with Microsoft Copilot for Microsoft 365, there are ample ways to empower employees and volunteers with copilots to make them more impactful and responsive.
We are in a unique position we will never be in again: On the cusp of AI changing our world. And we have the power to shape that change for good. I challenge leaders of the global enterprise to commit to broadening the circle of those who have access to AI by investing in responsible AI, bringing all stakeholders into AI discussions and having candid conversations about the impact of this work. If AI solutions are developed with and by those most impacted by it, we can ensure this technological advancement is groundbreaking for all, not just the few.

title: ActiveCampaign: How Is This Chicago-Based Unicorn Using AI?
text:
In the heart of the Midwest, a new wave of business leaders is spearheading the adoption of cutting-edge AI strategies. I validated this through conversations with a variety of leaders participating in Omaxn*, a Midwest AI forum. From proof of concepts to customer-facing solutions, these visionaries are reshaping the business landscape.
Recently, I had the opportunity to catch up with Jason VandeBoom, the innovative founder and CEO of ActiveCampaign*. This Chicago-based startup has captured the industry's attention with its remarkable journey to unicorn status.
For those unfamiliar with ActiveCampaign, it's a company that helps small teams power big businesses with intelligent marketing automation. Their platform does everything from automatically sending your customers a welcome email when they fill out a form on your website to automatically engaging with a prospective customer during the right stage of the sales process.
Through email and marketing automation, ActiveCampaign customers can better communicate with their own customers at scale, sending personalized messaging to each customer—all through automation. ActiveCampaign's CRM and sales engagement automation handle lead prioritization and contact management so that the sales team can spend their time doing what they do best: closing deals. I know some businesses use ActiveCampaign as their sole sales and marketing team—with 100% of their monthly revenue growth being directly touched by ActiveCampaign automation.
Since VandeBoom knows the power of an automation platform, the evolution and use of AI naturally came up in our discussion. Right off the bat, VandeBoom explained that he and most of the technology and product folks at ActiveCampaign will say that AI isn't new, and it's more than ChatGPT and large language models—it's about evaluating the right model for the right problem. He shared that models like Gemini, Anthropic, and Open AI are not distinctive enough. They all provide similar benefits and are pretty competitive, so it's about using what best suits the business. He also shared that they use cutting-edge open-source technologies like LangChain to interact with the models, speeding up their delivery of new features.
At ActiveCampaign, they do not force AI into experiences where it doesn't work; rather, they experiment with AI to determine what customers find helpful or ineffective and iterate as necessary. For example, for a period of a few months, ActiveCampaign was testing out AI onboarding for customers, meaning AI was responsible for onboarding new customers and getting them started on the platform. VandeBoom was very candid in explaining that customers struggled to engage with it. Where they thought the open-ended questions would help customers better describe their needs, customers wanted to avoid explaining themselves to a robot. Therefore, ActiveCampaign stopped with the AI questions and returned to what customers had already connected with. The key to their success is talking to customers, figuring out their preferences, and working alongside them to meet their needs.
"When thinking about implementing an experience for our customers led by AI, our first question is always: Does it provide real value?" said VandeBoom. "So many businesses are extremely focused on getting that next flashy AI capability in front of their customers, but what's flashy often doesn't actually solve the problems our customers have. We just don't do things to sound impressive on paper. That is not going to best serve our customers. That's never what we've been about."
ActiveCampaign's AI capabilities fall into three main buckets: personalization, suggestion, and validation.
ActiveCampaign's platform makes the experience for the end customer hyper-personalized. For example, with predictive sending, all customers have to do is check a box, and the ActiveCampaign platform sends their emails to each recipient at the time they are most likely to engage with that email. AI is used to analyze past engagement data and send communications to each person based on the optimal time for them. Their AI content Generator allows marketers to generate content and iterate on their feedback, with options such as making it shorter or funnier and even changing the entire tone of the content. The generator uses this feedback to make smarter recommendations based on the brand and what will resonate with each of their segmented audiences.
The platform suggests opportunities, inspiring marketers to achieve more than they ever thought possible. When marketers want to send emails, ActiveCampaign's platform suggests automation recipes they should use that are already built out for them so that they can make sure their email marketing is a part of the entire customer journey and that messages are sent when key actions are taken. ActiveCampaign's AI Automation Builder transforms customers' business goals into automated customer journeys. This AI tool understands their objectives and desired outcomes and helps convert them into actionable automations.
AI is also used to help validate business decisions and offer a perspective on what others in their industry are doing and finding success. ActiveCampaign customers receive automated emails powered by data analytics that show what other automation people use in their industry or how successful their campaigns are compared to others with a similar-sized business to constantly help their customers gain more revenue and grow.
I was curious how AI helps ActiveCampaign's business internally, and the answer was that they use it to better help their customers. ActiveCampaign uses AI internally to predict customer churn and issues before they arise. Using data analytics, they can see how people are using their platform. For instance, customers are given product adoption scores that show how much they use the platform, which features they use, whether they are having issues, and so on. If the churn predictor flags a customer as high risk for churn, their team contacts that customer to see if they are having trouble getting set up or figuring something out. Instead of sitting in frustration, AI can identify issues, and ActiveCampaign's team can address these issues proactively.
The one thing I found really interesting is that the entire executive leadership team at ActiveCampaign reads every single customer review that comes in daily. VandeBoom speaks passionately about staying close to the customer and how it’s easy for companies to stray from their feedback, but this is something he and his team have done since day 1 that will remain a constant. And while he reads every customer review, there are still support conversations with customers and chat conversations the team doesn't see. That's why they use AI to generate summaries of support conversations that help them spot issues, refine processes, and identify gaps where customers need help. They use the model Claude by Anthropic for this.
ActiveCampaign is committed to customer privacy. VandeBoom explained that any information that customers input to these models is anonymized, so no personal information is shared or stored. "While we want to ensure we are innovating and providing growth through our product, we would never put our customers at risk," VandeBoom said. "Any way that we incorporate AI into the platform is done so in an extremely privacy-conscious way."
In the rapidly evolving realm of AI-driven business solutions, ActiveCampaign emerges as a prime example of an organization that balances technological innovation with a focus on delivering genuine customer value.
*Disclosure: Wilkins is the founder and executive director of Omaxn. ActiveCampaign is an Omaxn Sponsor.

title: Quantum Now?
text:
Like the hapless tramps in Samuel Beckett’s play Waiting for Godot, the world has been waiting – not for the mysterious Godot, but for quantum computing, which is much anticipated but has yet to arrive. But while the ghostly Godot never does show up, quantum is beginning to materialize.
It’s about time. Global powers, led by China, have invested more than $55 billion in the promising technology and we are closer than ever to realizing the $500 million to $1 billion in gains that quantum promises to deliver to businesses over the next fifteen years. The quantum market is already estimated to be worth more than $1 billion this year, even though quantum computers are not yet very useful.
In Europe, Germany has launched an investment plan of more than $3 billion by 2026, and France has announced an investment of nearly $2 billion, aiming to train 5,000 quantum-ready engineers and create 30,000 jobs. In the United States, the National Quantum Initiative Act has authorized $1.2 billion in funding over five years for quantum computing research and development.
What are we talking about? Computers that could be a billion times faster than conventional computers for solving certain complex problems.
Classical computers, such as the one you’re likely reading this article on now, rely on binary bits to store and process information as strings of zeros and ones. But quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in a superposition of states, allowing for an exponential number of simultaneous combinations of zeros and ones. Don’t bother trying to visualize this - no one has ever seen a qubit. It’s all math.
Nonetheless, this superposition can be measured, enabling quantum computers to perform complex computations at an exponential speed.
Several technologies at the boundaries of current physics are being tried to make this work: superconductivity, neutral atoms, trapped ions, and photonics.
Are they used in businesses? Not yet. At this stage, quantum supremacy, meaning that a quantum computer is more efficient than a conventional computer, has only been established for algorithms without truly useful applications, such as verifying that a die is not loaded (Google, 2019).
But progress in developing quantum computing has been steady, and many people believe quantum computers will be a practical reality within a few years. IBM, the leader in quantum computing hardware, predicts that quantum computers will outperform classical computers in specific tasks by 2027.
Quantum supremacy is expected to first materialize for "native" quantum problems, which lend themselves particularly well to quantum modeling. They fall into four categories: modeling physicochemical reactions to discover innovative materials, new proteins, and future drugs; optimizing complex systems to improve flow management or the design and engineering of complex systems; generating synthetic data to train AI models; and finally, cryptography.
So, is it too early for businesses to be building their quantum muscle? Absolutely not. It takes time to build a team that understands how to use the burgeoning technology, and the future will belong to those who can harness the power of quantum computing early.
Banks, hedge funds, and car manufacturers are recruiting specialized quantum teams. They are tackling the construction of algorithms coded in qubits for their strategic applications. They are forming partnerships with quantum computer manufacturers - IBM, Atos, Pasqal - and academic research centers. These companies will be ready for the day when manufacturers offer sufficiently powerful machines. The aim is to increase the number of high-quality qubits and reduce error rates, eventually multiplying the power of the best current prototypes by a thousand.
The first challenge will be cybersecurity: with quantum supremacy, many of our security devices will become instantly obsolete. Businesses should start now to shift to quantum-hardened encryption technologies. The American National Institute of Standardization and Technology (NIST) is working on developing and standardizing post-quantum cryptographic algorithms and plans to impose a schedule for using encryption solutions capable of resisting quantum attacks.
But quantum computing has the potential to help mankind solve some of its biggest problems - mitigating climate change, for example, by accelerating the development of new materials for carbon capture, more efficient catalysts for hydrogen production, better batteries for electric vehicles, and optimized power grids that can handle renewable energy sources.
Quantum computing is also expected to accelerate drug discovery, enabling the development of personalized medicines and more effective treatments for diseases. And quantum algorithms could be used to optimize logistics and supply chain management, reducing fuel consumption and increasing efficiency. The list goes on.
AI can complement and enhance quantum computing, helping to develop error correction techniques for quantum hardware, for example, one of the main barriers to practical quantum computers. Quantum computers, meanwhile, can simulate complex natural processes, like the behavior of molecules or weather systems, much more accurately than regular computers.
Scientists collect relatively small amounts of data from experiments with such natural processes, but this isn't always enough to train AI models effectively. Quantum computing is expected to be able to generate additional, high-quality data to fill in the gaps, making the simulations more accurate and reliable. This, in turn, can help AI make more precise predictions about natural phenomena.
And quantum computing can generate synthetic data to train generative AI models when real-world data is scarce or difficult to obtain. While GenAI does not directly use quantum algorithms, hybrid algorithms that combine classical and quantum computing can leverage the strengths of both computing paradigms, potentially leading to more powerful and efficient AI models.
And if quantum doesn't come? In Beckett's play, when Estragon asks this question to Vladimir, the wise vagabond replies: "We'll come back tomorrow." Businesses will do the same and remain busy with generative AIs.
—-
Here are five steps that business leaders can start implementing today:
Build Quantum Expertise:
Working with quantum computing requires deep expertise, including quantum software developers and quantum hardware engineers who can design and optimize quantum circuits and algorithms for specific business applications. Quantum computing will initially augment rather than replace classical computing, so quantum teams will also need traditional software developers who can integrate quantum solutions with existing classical systems. And companies will need people who can translate complex business problems into quantum algorithms.
Since quantum computing is still an emerging field, companies will need to collaborate with academic institutions, technology providers, and quantum research organizations to keep up with the latest advancements and integrate cutting-edge solutions. Building a multidisciplinary team with these areas of expertise takes planning and time. While this may not be something smaller companies can undertake, large companies should start now. Because quantum computing is a new computing paradigm, hiring and developing talent capable of harnessing it in conjunction with company domain expertise will be the winning combination. But quantum scientists and engineers will be in short supply when quantum advantage will trigger interest, not dissimilar to what happened in AI in 2015 and GenAI now.
Develop Quantum Use Cases:
Companies need to identify and develop specific quantum use cases that align with their business goals. This involves exploring how quantum computing can solve industry-specific problems, such as molecular modeling in pharmaceuticals or portfolio optimization in finance. Conducting proof-of-concept projects and pilot studies ahead of time will help refine these use cases and demonstrate their potential value.
Harden Security Protocols:
Companies will need to implement post-quantum cryptographic algorithms (PQC) to secure data and communications. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has been developing these algorithms designed to withstand quantum threats. Companies large and small should track these developments and start integrating PQC algorithms into their security frameworks to ensure their encryption is hardened against quantum computer attacks.
Foster Strategic Partnerships:
Companies should begin forging strategic partnerships with quantum technology providers, research institutions, and other industry players. These alliances will facilitate knowledge sharing, accelerate innovation, and ensure access to the latest advancements.
Monitor Regulatory Developments:
Navigating the regulatory landscape is crucial for the successful adoption of quantum computing. Quantum computing is considered by governments as “dual-use” technology and critical for national security and competitiveness. Transitioning away from RSA to PQC protocols will a massive undertaking on a scale larger than the Y2K bug. Business leaders should stay informed about emerging regulations, mandates and standards.
Preparing for quantum computing is not a one-time effort but an ongoing commitment. It requires vision, strategic foresight, and a willingness to invest in the future. The rewards, however, will be immense for those who are prepared.

title: AI dataset licensing companies form trade group - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 2 min read
AI dataset licensing companies form trade group
The emergence of generative AI technologies that can mimic human creativity in recent years has triggered an outcry from content creators and a string of copyright lawsuits against tech companies like Google, Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI, which is backed by Microsoft.
By Katie Paul
NEW YORK: Seven content-licensing sellers of music, image, video and other datasets for use in training artificial intelligence systems have formed the sector's first trade group, they said on Wednesday.
The Dataset Providers Alliance (DPA) will advocate for "ethical data sourcing" in the training of AI systems, including rights for people depicted in datasets and the protection of content owners' intellectual property rights, the companies said in a statement.
Founding members include U.S. music dataset company Rightsify, image licensing service vAIsual, Japanese stock photo provider Pixta and Germany-based data marketplace Datarade.
The emergence of generative AI technologies that can mimic human creativity in recent years has triggered an outcry from content creators and a string of copyright lawsuits against tech companies like Google, Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI, which is backed by Microsoft.
Developers have been training models by feeding them vast quantities of content, much of it scraped from the internet for free without the consent of those who created the works or own rights to them.
Tech companies, which claim the usage is legal, are also quietly paying for access to private collections of content both to fulfill needs for particular types of data and to hedge against legal and regulatory risks.
The prospect that demand for licensed data will grow if copyright owners prevail in their legal fights has prompted the emergence of a nascent industry of companies that package content and sell access to it for use by AI systems.
As a result, groups have been formed to establish ethical standards for that trade, like Fairly Trained, a non-profit founded this year which certifies models that have not used copyrighted materials without a license.
The DPA targets the content of those transactions, requiring, for example, that its members agree not to sell text data obtained by crawling the web or audio that features people's voices without their explicit consent.
A heavy focus will be to push for legislation like the NO FAKES Act, a U.S. bill introduced last year to create penalties for generating unauthorized digital replicas of people's voices or likenesses, said Alex Bestall, CEO of Rightsify and its licensing subsidiary GCX, who led the founding of the group.
"Advocacy will be a big part of it because everyone's taken their positions on AI and copyright, but a lot of these battles are yet to be solved and it's going to take a while for them to be," said Bestall.
The DPA also will press for more training data transparency requirements like those in the European Union's AI Act and a similar U.S. bill introduced in April, the Generative AI Copyright Disclosure Act, he added.
The group plans to publish a white paper outlining its positions in July, he said.
