title: AI's hunger for power can be tamed - ET CIO
text:
- Artificial Intelligence
- 4 min read
AI's hunger for power can be tamed
Tech firms investing in AI must prioritize energy-efficient algorithms to combat environmental impact and rising power consumption, shifting away from current energy-intensive models towards more sustainable practices.
The artificial intelligence hype that made Nvidia Corp. the world’s biggest company has come with a price for the world’s climate. Data centers housing its powerful chips are gorging power and belching carbon dioxide, and sobering figures now reveal the extent of the problem. Data centers will use 8% of US power by 2030, compared with 3% in 2022, according to a recent report from Goldman Sachs Group Inc., as their energy demand grows by 160%.
Register for the ET MSME Day 2024 here.
Add this all to the growing discontent about generative AI tools. To not only stem the tide but also uphold their goals of building AI “for humanity,” tech firms like OpenAI, Microsoft and Alphabet Inc.’s Google must grow their teams addressing the power issue. It would certainly be possible. A few signs of progress suggest the trick may be to redesign their algorithms.
continued below
The good news is that these “engines” could get smaller with greater investment. Researchers at Microsoft, for instance, have developed a so-called “1 bit” architecture that can make large language models about 10 times as more energy efficient than the current leading systems. This approach simplifies the models’ calculations by reducing values to 0 or 1, slashing power consumption without sacrificing too much performance. The resulting tech isn’t the most capable, but a good example of a “contrarian” approach that can immediately reduce AI’s cost and environmental impact, says Steven Marsh, founder of Cambridge, UK-based startup Zetlin Ltd., which is working on building more efficient systems.
Marsh says he’s making progress. His team recently trained a neural network-based AI model on an Nvidia graphics processing unit (GPU), and the system heated up so much that they had to bring fans into the room over five days. When they ran the same model with their proprietary, non-neural network technology, it used just 60% of the power. The current approach, Marsh says, is “like putting a rocket engine on a bicycle."
Nvidia has also taken promising steps toward addressing the energy problem. A couple of years ago, it developed a new format for its chips to process AI calculations with smaller numbers, making them faster and less power hungry. “Just that little tweak on the silicon saved a lot of energy,” Marsh says. If companies designing AI systems take better advantage of that tweak, they could save energy eventually.
It doesn’t help that AI companies are in an arms race. OpenAI and Anthropic have raised $11.3 billion and $8.4 billion, respectively, according to data provider PitchBook. Much of that money isn’t going to recruitment (they each have workforces of just a few hundred people). Instead, it’s being poured into running servers that can train and run their models, even as their investment leads to diminishing returns. (There is evidence that the latest text- and vision-reading systems are showing smaller advancements in areas like accuracy and capability.)
Those companies, along with Google, Microsoft and Amazon.com Inc., should devote additional money to refashioning their algorithms to save energy and cost. Collectively, it’s been done before. Data centers managed to keep their power demands flat between 2015 and 2019, even as their workloads tripled, because their operators found ways to make them more efficient, according to Goldman Sachs.
OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman has talked up nuclear fusion as an answer to the problem, having personally invested $375 million into an enterprise called Helion Energy. But he might be creating hype around an energy technology that won’t be commercialized for several decades.
Rather than outsource responsibility to a futuristic energy source or superintelligent AI that doesn’t exist yet, tech firms should put greater focus on making their models more energy efficient now. After all, breaking away from established and inefficient systems was how this revolution was kicked off in the first place.

title: DataStax Underpins Base Blocks In AI Application Lifecycle
text:
Software has a lifecycle. Our apps are code-based entities created inside what the IT industry likes to call the software application development lifecycle, or SDLC. Code is laid down, put through testing and debugging, released to live production and then augmented, enhanced, maintained and extended. In the longer term, some applications hang on to graduate to legacy status (a term usually used pejoratively, although at least these are apps that still work) and some are refactored, retired, decommissioned and killed off.
We could add in more steps and stages here, but the point is made i.e. software has a lifecycle. Now that the tech industry has thrown itself into the current artificial intelligence renaissance, we can talk about AI lifecycles as well.
What Is An AI Lifecycle?
The AI lifecycle starts with infrastructure, which will encompass everything from the large language model being used to the logic in an AI engine and onward to the analytics power of the cloud computing service that the development team decides to sign up for. It will also include the database provisioning process, the networking and connectivity layer to join microservices and form bonds to external applications and services through application programming interfaces. At the upper level, the AI lifecycle sees us focus on compute processing, the throughput of data itself and the delivery of intelligence to end users via chatbots or other smart software functions. Again, this is not an exhaustive list, but it provides some idea of the circulatory flow that exists.
DataStax has eyes on making a good portion of the backend part of the lifecycle equation easier so that developers can focus on application development, rather than infrastructure management. Now styling itself as an AI platform company, DataStax has focused on generative AI development with extensions to make retrieval augmented generation simpler. Much-loved by AI purists who want AI to get real, RAG provides a means of injecting externally ratified data into an AI process, often belonging to datasets that the company using the deployment owns.
The Lowdown On Langflow
In April this year, DataStax acquired Langflow, an open source visual framework for building RAG applications. Now, DataStax is releasing Langflow 1.0, which includes a version of Langflow hosted in the DataStax Cloud platform. This technology has a drag-and-drop interface, with plenty of of integrations with the most popular generative AI tools: LangChain, LangSmith, OpenAI, Hugging Face, Mistral and others so that developers can set up, swap and compare all the major large language model and embedding providers.
The company says that this gives developers the flexibility to compare different providers and their results. They can now make major changes quickly instead of having to learn new APIs and work on re-coding their applications. As part of the Langflow 1.0 open source release, developers can now use LangSmith’s observability service to trace an application’s responses for more relevant, accurate LLM-based applications.
“The generative AI stack and its lifecyle is a big and complex ball of technology that many are working to get their arms around. We’re focused on helping developers stay true to their roots so they can do what they do best: build and develop, rather than worrying about application infrastructure,” said Ed Anuff, chief product officer, DataStax. “From the launch of Langflow in Astra [DataStax’s serverless, multi-model database], to bringing the largest ecosystem of embedding providers together in one place, we’re delivering on our promise to make generative AI application development as fast and simple as possible so organizations can get their apps in production quickly, for immediate impact.”
Ready-To-Bake AI Data
As part of its current news stream, DataStax also notes a new partnership with Unstructured. This is a no-code platform and cloud service helps convert almost any document, file type, or layout into LLM-ready data and “stands up” a generative AI data pipeline from transformation and cleaning to generating embeddings for a vector database. The partnership is designed to enable enterprises and developers to easily make their enterprise data ready for AI, handling the data ingestion and chunking (use of a so-called data chunking algorithm helps break data down into smaller and more manageable chunks) across data types: PDFs, Salesforce, Google Drive etc. to use in AI applications.
Once again, this is the company aiming to take care of more backend lifecyle heavy lifting.
At this point, AI developers get data ingestion through quick conversion of large data sets and common document types into vector data. This new integration then enables these embeddings to be quickly written to Astra DB for relevant generative AI similarity searches.
Infrastructure Offloading
“Developers want to work with generative AI and find out how they can use it in their applications - they are under pressure from their business to discover what they can achieve and what the options are to innovate,” said DataStax’s Anuff. “However, this area is so new, there are developments and new launches taking place all the time. Developers are finding it difficult to keep up, because there are new versions of tools being launched and these updates can affect or break applications. Engineers are essentially spending more time on building infrastructure than they are building software or solving problems.”
To get over these hurdles, we know that software teams are looking at ways they can remove or reduce the infrastructure overhead around generative AI. This helps them to concentrate on business issues, rather than on IT problems and getting things to work together.
“For the majority of developers around generative AI, reducing or eliminating the integration overhead around applications ensures they can focus on business logic and application design, which creates the most value for the business. For developers implementing new techniques like RAG, getting accurate performance data across the whole application lifecyle can find bottlenecks that are affecting response times and show where different options can improve results,” explained Anuff.
Shaping The AI Lifecycle
Every company building with generative AI right now is looking for the most effective way to implement its toolsets and extensions (generally with RAG as well) within their applications. Being able to break apart the AI development process into frontend backend upper and lower tier elements across the AI lifecycle at this point in the still-embryonic nature of this technology (arguably) helps us to think about the crucial component parts of AI in more manageable terms.
We can think of the AI lifecycle as cyclical, obviously, but as we build it, technologists will usually call it an end-to-end process, which in this case means infrastructure-to-user. If we get our heads around this notion, even with all the AI hype that surrounds us, then we can stand on firmer intelligence foundations.

title: Can AI-Powered Smartphones Solve Our Focus Crisis?
text:
For the last 15 years, cellphones have been buzzing and dinging incessantly — summoning us to the next work email, the latest team chat, or yet another breaking news alert — the line between indispensable tech and intrusive tether has blurred. For professionals worldwide, these devices swing like a pendulum between being a lifeline to productivity and an anchor of distraction. Against this backdrop, a pivotal question emerges: Will the next generation of AI cellphones restore the balance, turning what was once a disruptor into a catalyst for concentrated productivity?
The Distraction
Today, the impact of this technological encroachment is stark. Employees lose approximately 720 work hours per person each year to distractions, translating into significant financial losses for businesses. Smartphones, leading the pack, compel the average user to check their device 150 times a day — that’s about once every six waking minutes.
With all this in mind, I recently had the opportunity to speak with Sudhir Chadaga, Motorola’s Global Head of B2B, about the convergence of future work dynamics and technological advancements. Our discussion reinforced the notion that tech-induced distraction is still an uphill battle. According to a recent Motorola survey, 55% of employees report frequent distractions from non-work-related smartphone use.
However, there's a beacon of hope on the horizon. Innovations in AI technology may soon offer a solution, promising to redefine our interactions with these indispensable, yet disruptive, devices.
AI Is Coming To Phones, And It’s A Game-Changer
The mobile industry is on the brink of a transformative shift, thanks to advancements in AI. "Artificial intelligence will bring about great change in the mobile industry and in the way we live," T.M. Roh, president and head of Samsung's mobile experience business, stated on stage during a recent event.
This change is evident in the development of AI features across the big players in phone technology. The latest roll out of advanced search features, photo editing, and in-ear language translations are just scratching the surface. New AI is also delivering standout features and essential tools for productivity and focus.
How Can An AI Cellphone Solve Focus Problems?
Leading smartphone manufacturers have integrated functionalities that enable users to enter a specific mode to minimize notifications; upon exiting this mode, AI assists in managing and filtering missed notifications. This prevents the overwhelming flood of alerts that typically bombard users, ensuring a smoother transition back to connectivity. Here are just a few examples currently available:
- Apple's Focus Mode: Apple has introduced a feature called Focus Mode in its iOS operating system, which serves to help users tailor their notification preferences based on their current activity. This mode allows users to set custom filters for different times of the day or specific contexts — like work, personal time, or sleep — limiting notifications to only those that are deemed important. Upon deactivating the mode, the system uses AI to summarize the missed notifications, helping users catch up efficiently without feeling overwhelmed by the backlog.
- Motorola’s Moto Unplugged: Motorola’s new “Unplugged” feature allows users to disconnect and then, upon reconnecting, uses AI to filter and prioritize important messages. Such innovations aim to enhance focus and efficiency by managing the digital noise that clutters our devices. Sudhir Chadaga notes that this feature plus the new Razr’s purposely small screen offers “a very unique way in which the user can actually enjoy the hardware without feeling commoditized by every app and advertisement.”
- Samsung's Bixby Routines: Samsung offers Bixby Routines on its Galaxy smartphones, which leverages AI to automate various tasks and settings based on the user's behavior, location, or time of day. This feature can be configured to automatically turn on Do Not Disturb mode during meetings or while at specific locations, such as the office or a library, effectively minimizing disruptions. When the routine ends, Bixby can provide a summary of important communications or actions missed during the period, ensuring that users stay informed without constant interruptions.
The Future Of AI Cellphones Is Bright
Looking ahead, the future of intelligent phones addressing the focus crisis is promising. With AI-driven features specifically designed to enhance user control and minimize distractions, smartphones are evolving in ways that may restore the boundaries we've lost to digital encroachment. As these devices grow smarter, they have the potential to transform from being a source of constant interruption to a key tool in our quest for focused productivity.

title: Council Post: What’s Keeping CMOs Up At Night?
text:
Mark Emond, CEO, Demand Spring.
Since returning in February to my role as CEO at Demand Spring, I have been spending a lot of my time meeting with B2B CMOs and senior marketing executives inside and outside of our client base. I have been asking them two primary questions to re-immerse myself into the mindset of today’s marketing leaders.
1. What’s keeping you up at night?
2. What opportunities for growth in B2B marketing do you see?
The Focus On Growth
After years of growth, the last 18 months have not been easy for B2B CMOs. Growth, spending and digital transformation was a hallmark of the pandemic from 2020 through to the summer of 2022. Organizations suddenly found their digital infrastructure to be sorely lacking, while buyer behavior continued to change precipitously.
A Gartner study validated that B2B buyers were spending more time researching solutions independently, through digital and offline channels, than engaging with vendor sales organizations. Buoyed by ongoing economic expansion and a digital transformation agenda, CMOs had their foot firmly pressed down on the growth gas pedal.
Then, the U.S. Federal Reserve and central banks throughout the world began to raise interest rates. The economy started moving sideways. And CFOs got worried. Marketing spending declined, with organizations showing both concern for a potential recession, and a preference for profitable growth over growth at all costs.
Since the fall of 2022, B2B CMOs have had to do more with less. The size of many B2B marketing organizations has shrunk significantly, as have marketing budgets. What hasn’t changed are growth expectations from the C-suite.
Common Concerns Among CMOs
My conversations with CMOs have reflected three common concerns.
1. The Growth Imperative In A Sideways Market
Strategic projects have been shelved for opportunistic actions that drive results now. At the same time, many marketing teams are now extremely lean. CMOs have had to cut out all the fat and focus squarely on actions that are driving sales pipeline initiation and influence.
A major challenge is breaking through all of the noise. There is so much content, and buyers are inundated with so much outreach in every channel (social, email, paid search, phone) that breaking through has become hard. Many of the CMOs I’ve spoken with also expressed real concern about the declining productivity and effectiveness of their sales development teams.
2. Measurement And Attribution
A struggle dating way back has always been how to properly measure marketing’s contribution. Many CEOs and CFOs continue to want to see the ROI data that shows the singular marketing tactic that is responsible for initiating a long, complex B2B sale that has many touches.
Many CMOs spend a lot of time educating and advocating with their peers for a broader set of metrics that reflect marketing’s contribution to overall financial performance, including sales pipeline influenced using a multi-touch attribution model, revenue, the cost of customer acquisition and customer lifetime value.
Complicating the challenge for many CMOs is the reality that B2B marketing organizations are often the ugly toad at the analytics ball. While finance, sales and supply chain departments are often organizational leaders in analytics resourcing and capabilities, many marketing teams struggle to get the resources they need to properly measure and manage performance.
3. AI Anxiety
Most of the CMOs I have spoken with have expressed uncertainty with respect to how AI will transform marketing practices, processes, roles and technology. They rightfully view AI as a potential answer to their business challenges. But most lack a strategic plan for prioritizing where to apply AI in the short, medium and long term, how to develop and train their teams to innovate using AI and how to consider AI as part of their operating model alongside their employees and agencies.
Moving Forward With Resilience
But it’s not all doom and gloom for CMOs. They are a resilient lot, and generally one that views the world through a glass half full approach. Even through the challenge of lean times, lean budgets and high growth expectations, I've found they see value in focusing their teams on core campaigns, programs and projects that are based on good business fundamentals.
CMOs see opportunities to drive competitive advantage by getting tighter on their messaging, innovating more with their creative to cut through the noise, better aligning their efforts with sales and breaking down silos that developed within their own marketing teams as they grew and hired rapidly prior to the slowdown.
After 18 months of austerity, many are also starting to see their budgets come back a little bit as CFOs realize that a little more fuel is needed to drive pipeline growth.
In light of the concerns, I think there are three key things CMOs should be doing at this time.
1. Ensure that analytics is optimized throughout the organization. Closing the performance visibility gaps that make it really hard to measure and manage campaign performance and attribution is essential to proving value and advocating for increased budget.
2. Have the tough conversations at the C-suite table about the impact of spending on marketing in an uncertain economy. It's often wiser to take a scalpel than an axe to the marketing budget in uncertain economic times. While paring back the marketing budget can contribute to short-term profitability, it can also erode competitiveness in the short and long term.
3. Embrace AI in both an opportunistic and a strategic manner. Opportunistically, there are some quick wins to become a more productive marketing department (e.g., content ideas and first drafts). CMOs should also think strategically about AI, creating a three-year plan for how to optimize your operating model within marketing using AI to make better use of your human capital.
While many B2B CMOs (in a role with an average tenure of 4.4 years) seldom sleep entirely soundly, they have really struggled to get quality Z’s in the last two years. For their sake, let’s hope that the hints of growth we are starting to see are real and that the efficiencies gained throughout this period form the basis for the next wave of marketing-led growth.

title: Will AI Replace Freelance Jobs? The Rise Of Complementarity In Human-AI Collaboration
text:
In a recent article, the Wall Street Journal posited that AI is poised to replace freelance jobs, creating a sense of inevitability about a future where machines dominate work previously performed by humans. However, this narrative overlooks the nuanced and transformative potential of AI to complement and enhance human capabilities rather than supplant them. The reality is far more complex and hopeful, emphasizing collaboration over replacement.
AI as an Enabler, Not a Replacement
The assertion that AI will replace freelance jobs oversimplifies the multifaceted role AI can play in the workforce. As highlighted by Invisible Technologies, a company at the forefront of operational innovation, the most significant benefits of AI emerge when it is integrated with human expertise. This synergy between AI and human intelligence allows for solving complex process problems and achieving outcomes that neither could accomplish alone. Invisible's proprietary process orchestration platform, blending advanced AI with a skilled global workforce, exemplifies how AI can amplify human potential, not diminish it.
The Rise of Internal Talent Marketplaces
Furthermore, the integration of AI into the workforce is reshaping how organizations manage and deploy talent internally. Internal Talent Marketplaces (ITMs) enable organizations to align company needs with employee preferences, increasing job satisfaction, reducing turnover, and fostering a culture of continuous learning and development. These marketplaces utilize AI to match workers with roles that best suit their skills and career aspirations, enhancing overall organizational agility and resilience. This model demonstrates that AI can facilitate better human resource management rather than replace human jobs.
The Open Talent Economy
The future of work is not a zero-sum game between humans and machines. As we discussed in our HBR article, "Do You Need an External Talent Cloud?" the open talent economy represents a paradigm shift in how companies access and utilize skilled professionals. Digital platforms enable organizations to tap into a global pool of freelancers, providing flexibility and access to specialized skills on demand. This approach is not about replacing jobs but about creating a more dynamic and efficient workforce that leverages AI and human talent in tandem.
Freelancers Want Your Work, Not Your Job
Additionally, the notion that AI will wholesale replace freelance jobs fails to consider the evolving preferences of skilled professionals. Many highly skilled freelancers seek flexibility and autonomy, valuing project-based work over traditional employment. Companies are increasingly unable to attract these professionals into full-time roles, as they prefer the diverse experiences and independence that freelancing offers. This shift in worker preference underscores the need for businesses to adapt by integrating freelancers into their talent strategies, supported by AI-driven platforms that enhance, rather than replace, human contributions.
Complementarity in Human-AI Collaboration
A comprehensive study by Hemmer et al. (2024) at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and the University of Bayreuth provides further evidence that AI and humans can achieve complementary team performance (CTP)—a level of performance neither could attain individually. The research introduces the concept of complementarity potential, highlighting how different sources, such as information asymmetry and capability asymmetry, can be leveraged to achieve superior team outcomes. For instance, in real estate appraisal, humans utilized unique contextual information to complement AI's data-driven insights, while in image classification tasks, heterogeneous capabilities between AI and humans led to enhanced decision-making. This underscores the importance of designing AI systems and collaboration mechanisms that maximize the strengths of both AI and human team members .
Embracing a Collaborative Future
The fear that AI will replace freelance jobs is rooted in a misunderstanding of AI's role in the future of work. Instead of displacing human workers, AI is poised to become a powerful tool that, when combined with human ingenuity, can lead to greater efficiencies, innovation, and job satisfaction. By embracing AI as an enabler of human potential and integrating it into flexible talent strategies, organizations can navigate the complexities of the modern workforce and thrive in an increasingly digital world. This collaborative future promises not the obsolescence of freelance jobs but their evolution into higher-value, more fulfilling opportunities.

title: Making Peace With Gen AI As Job Killer
text:
A report published by the IMF calls for fiscal policies to soften the pain of employment transitions resulting from generative AI. The big idea is captured in a graphic projecting five years of rising joblessness followed by accelerating job creation plateauing at a lower level of unemployment. Along the way, those losing jobs are expected to live less well during the transition but end up 10% better off in the long run.
I have been asked about this report by several supply chain leaders over the past two weeks, many of whom believe they own a big chunk of this challenging transition. The question is how to navigate technology adoption when it is obvious that jobs will be lost while business output grows.
Everyone Gets a Super Smart Intern
Some have described Gen AI as a tireless intern that can help knowledge workers get a quick start on almost any task, provided they are asked the right questions. Compiling, for example a first draft of SKUs to trim in an assortment simplification effort, or suppliers to upgrade to strategic status, or risky ports to avoid are natural Gen AI use cases that could also be handled by a smart intern.
Applications like Aera Skills implemented at Mars Wrigley, for instance uses AI to ferret out details behind out-of-stocks that in SAP are simplified down to a handful of “reason codes”. Just like a great intern, this system helps supply chain team members dive deep on why shipments go wrong so they can figure out how to make the process better.
Before AI, such root cause analysis was slow, manual, and error prone. With AI, people skip the drudgery and go straight to problem solving, which is more valuable to the business and more rewarding for most people.
Less Work, More Purpose
The takeaway from the intern analogy is that leaders are increasingly in position to elevate job design from the dehumanizing approach made famous by Frederick Taylor in 1911. Taylor said of his Scientific Management theory, “in the past, man has been first, in the future the system must be first.” He may have been right about system productivity gains, but the resulting mindless work has been parodied by everyone from Charlie Chaplin to Lucille Ball.
Job elimination through AI is certainly a concern as chronicled in research by McKinsey and others. But it is also a powerful transformer of jobs, shifting hours spent away from rote tasks in favor of more creative work. BCG’s most recent survey on AI at work, for instance found that over 80% of employees surveyed said that Gen AI freed up more time for strategic work, and decreased time spent on administrative tasks.
Own the Transition with People Development
For supply chain leaders facing the tug of war between investors expecting labor cost savings and employees worried about job security the best answer is leaning into the transition. This means investing time, money and credibility in educating teams about AI and its uses.
Intuit, for example offers lunch-and-learns, online courses and in-person boot camps to train employees in AI and data science. They have also created a seven-month apprenticeship program open to non-technical people looking to build skills in areas like machine learning and software development.
PepsiCo is another example of an organization that bets big on training. It launched the Digital Academy in 2022 providing integrated digital learning, segmented by role and level, complete with certification and badging. Alibaba takes it farther still, offering an internally developed Gen AI engineering course meant for employees externally, to its customers and partners.
Speak Truth to Power
Beyond training people and looking for ways to design better work, supply chain leaders should also be honest about the impact of AI on jobs. The IMF’s report was written by and for economists whose mission is to recommend taxes and social welfare spending to ease the transition for displaced employees.
Economists need, but often lack the practitioner’s view of how technology changes specific jobs. Sharing your plans and challenges publicly may influence policy while building trust and transparency in your own organization.
There is light at the end of this tunnel.

title: Serpentine Artistic Director Hans Ulrich Obrist On AI, Art And The Role Of Cultural Spaces
text:
Artists have long engaged with new technology. Notably, in the 1960s, engineer Billy Klüver collaborated with artists Robert Rauschenberg, Robert Whitman and Fred Waldhauer to co-found Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.), a non-profit that played a pivotal role in merging technology with art. Contemporary artists are similarly immersed in cutting-edge tech, but they now face even more pressing issues as generative AI embarks on its own expansive and unpredictable journey.
Serpentine is acutely aware of the challenges facing not only artists, but also the public. For over a decade, the London cultural institution has been deep diving into the ocean that is AI. Through Serpentine Arts Technologies research body and Creative AI Lab, a collaborative project with King’s College London, it has been investigating the impact—positive and negative—of new technology on the arts and artists.
In recent years, the Serpentine galleries have staged numerous exhibitions highlighting the work of some of the most interesting and diverse digital artists of our time, including Brazilian artist Gabriel Massan and Los Angeles artist/designer Refik Anadol. This fall the gallery welcomes Berliner artists and technologists Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon (named by TIME magazine among the 100 most influential people in Al) who are imagining the art institution as a laboratory for finding new technologies through an artist-led Al system.
The exhibition coincides with the publication of “Future Art Ecosystems 4: Art x Public Al,” Serpentine’s latest strategic briefing which sets out to break down the implications of Al for the cultural sector and offer strategies for claiming greater agency within Al-driven economies.
I took the opportunity to speak with Hans Ulrich Obrist, curator, critic and art historian, and artistic director at the Serpentine. I wanted to understand why the cultural institution is so involved with the art of AI, and how he views the potential and perils of the technology.
Why is it critical for a cultural institution like yours to be involved directly with artists who work with cutting-edge technology like AI, and to help realize their projects?
It is important for art institutions to engage with technology, which is why we’ve been developing our technology department in the last 12 years. In the 1960s Billy Klüver and E.A.T worked with the leading tech company of that time Bell Lab, who made it possible to create projects that would have otherwise not have happened. We have a similar situation today with artists who want to work with technology. To give you an example, the young, brilliant Brazilian artist Gabriel Massan, wanted to do a video game (for “Third World: The Bottom Dimension,” exhibited at Serpentine North in 2023). Working with our technology team of five curators, we were able to produce that.
Your Creative AI Lab initiative forms spaces for research into AI systems, with the data and findings available to other cultural institutions and artists. Why does Serpentine invest in an open-source research project?
One part of what we do is to activate and enable artists who want to work with new technologies. The second point, which is very important to us, is to think beyond the confines or the walls of Serpentine—to consider the whole sector. The Creative AI Lab offers a research platform and it is a space to investigate AI systems from a cultural perspective. It generates a solid foundation for leadership for the entire arts. Our alliances are crucial. Knowledge production is very important to us.
Is this why you invest in these in-depth reports, and make them readily available for all to view?
As a cultural institution, we want to be useful for the artist as well as the whole art sector. So far we’ve published four reports, available for anyone to download. The latest, “Future Art Ecosystem: Art x Public AI”, looks at AI and is a strategic briefing which breaks down the topic and makes it accessible for the cultural sector. It offers strategies for greater agencies for the art sector within the AI economy.
What is the potential of working with a self-created dataset—open-source AI models like the one artist Refik Anadol has been developing alongside Smithsonian and National History Museum, and through his own data gathering in the Amazon rainforest?
We think artists can not only show us how to positively use these technologies, but also show us the dark corridors of technology, the dangers, which is equally important. Refik Anadol shows us that art can intermediate between culture, technology, society, ecology etc. Artists can make the invisible visible. Another important aspect is, of course, the question of how we source the data, how we can ethically source archives, and who owns these datasets. We think that this is a negotiation.
Anadol’s work is very much about connecting us to nature through technology—through his immersive AI art he reveals the possibilities of our interconnectedness with the rest of the environment, what we can see and what we can’t. We saw this vividly and viscerally in “Echoes of the Earth: Living Archives” staged at Serpentine North this winter. Can you speak of how the ecological message sits within your vision at the gallery?
We can use technology for fostering attention to the natural world. We need to look at how tech can create a spiritual connection with nature to make sure we are communicating with the environment rather than continue this colonial separation from nature, which is destroying the environment. It is about expanding the possibilities of how art can act as an intermediate between culture, technology and society, and how art can liberate us from becoming stuck in a quantified world, which is very dangerous.
As a curator, is it exciting, perhaps sometimes even daunting, to work with AI artists who are working in very different fields, with different expressions, some of which are new to us all?
That’s a very interesting question because we learn from each artist we are working with enormously. And these artists enter the DNA of the organization since an institution is a learning system. Their work is very collaborative, and they bring with them all their own partners, an entire ecosystem. Gabriel Massan, for instance, brought a whole interdisciplinary crew of people to create their video game. We are always listening, we are learning, we are transforming, we are changing. What’s also interesting is their lifespan. Whereas an exhibition would typically stay for a few months, these digital artworks are like a living organism. They never end.
Visiting these digital exhibitions, what strikes me is the diversity of audience and visitor engagement. Do these exhibits and interventions impact on Serpentine as a gallery and a learning space?
Absolutely. We want to be constantly evolving. With the artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg we created (“Pollinator Pathmaker,” April 2022 to March 2024), a living sculpture on Kensington Gardens for pollinators rather than humans, which became one of the longest lasting outdoor public projects in London. She was able to create this work in collaboration with AI with which she gathered data on plants which love to pollinate for an exhibition that encourages a multi-species dialogue. These are longer duration projects which are interesting for a gallery.
Exhibitions such as Gabriel Massan’s led to new audiences. Many were young teenagers who brought along their parents. In my experience of 30 years of museum practice, it’s always the other way around! These exhibitions can help connect a younger audience to the museum.
What do you see as the role of museums and cultural institutions in engaging the public in understanding the impact of AI on our lives, acting as a bridge to almost demystify it for the public?
Our role is to build bridges between cultures, technology, science and society. In this fragmented world we need more bridgebuilding, and we hope through our work we can contribute to this. Technology often creates separation. Social media creates filters. With art we can hopefully break that filter bubble, and be an intermediator between culture, art, science, technology. It’s about togetherness.
Read my interview with Refik Anadol, see digital artist Cao Fei’s “Duotopia” at Sprüth Magers in Berlin, and read why French gaming artist Sara Sadik is exploring loneliness through gaming.

title: Council Post: Why It’s Time For HR Departments To Get Up To Speed With AI
text:
Jâlie Cohen is the chief human resources officer for Radiology Partners.
Artificial intelligence is rapidly gaining traction in the business world, but many human resources departments aren’t embracing it. If HR leaders continue to delay AI adoption, then there is a risk that HR as a function will fall behind the industries we support.
Many HR Departments Are Behind In Embracing AI
According to a 2024 Gartner survey, only 38% of HR leaders indicated that they “are piloting, planning implementation, or have already implemented generative AI.” That’s a 19% increase from June 2023, Gartner noted. But consider another finding from the survey: 67% of HR leaders stated that adding generative AI-related roles in their departments isn’t on the roadmap for the upcoming 12 months.
Additionally, a survey conducted by Human Resource Executive in 2023 revealed that almost “two-thirds of HR teams have yet to embrace artificial intelligence in their operations.” The survey also found that over “60% of respondents shared that HR teams at their organizations aren’t using AI and its counterpart, gen AI, for any functions, including talent sourcing, interviewing, onboarding, learning and managing employee leave.”
I find these statistics alarming. AI is already here, and to better support candidates and employees, it’s time for HR leaders and their teams to lean into using it.
Instead Of Strict AI Regulations, HR Leaders Should Create Guardrails
It’s understandable that some HR leaders are hesitant to embrace AI. AI has a number of risks, and in HR, the consequences of improper AI usage can be particularly severe. Some risks include the leaking of employee data, bias during the recruitment stage and employee disengagement, as noted in an HRMorning article. However, in light of these issues, HR leaders shouldn’t opt for blanket bans of AI or hard-and-fast rules about its usage. Given how quickly AI is evolving—and how it’s becoming increasingly popular in the business world—neither blanket bans nor hard-and-fast rules are likely to stick with the workforce.
Instead, HR leaders should implement guardrails—boundaries that people can work within. The first step leaders should take to put systems in place is to make people accountable for the outcomes of AI usage. For instance, if an HR associate uses AI to draft an employee handbook and turns in a product that’s fraught with errors, then they would be held accountable for that. HR team members need to know that using AI is a tool, not the be-all and end-all, nor is it an excuse for having inaccurate or incomplete work. Accountability and ownership are key. After the submission of a draft of any work product, there needs to be a clear owner to review, edit and sign off on the final product.
Another step leaders should take is to determine which tasks on their teams are off-limits for AI usage and which tasks are okay to use AI for. For instance, after having discussions with their staff, a CHRO could conclude that it makes sense to use AI to draft policies, employee handbooks and performance goals, but that AI can’t be used to write employee performance reviews without incorporating any human input. Given AI’s rate of change, over time, these use cases might transform. It’s important that HR leaders periodically review their AI use cases and update their use case guardrails accordingly.
Leaders should also strategically navigate using AI in recruiting. AI can be a powerful tool to use in recruiting, but leaders need to be careful about avoiding bias. Using an inclusive lens when building guardrails can help facilitate diversity in hiring.
HR Practitioners Should Function As AI Advisors
HR leaders and their staff should take a listen-and-learn approach to AI. They should be diligent about educating themselves on AI and gaining a strong understanding of the technology before rolling out initiatives. At my organization, for instance, we’re at the forefront of clinical AI and have incorporated several AI tools into the radiologist workflow to improve patient care and outcomes. While these AI implementations are driven by our clinical experts, our HR team continues to lean in and learn from our clinical colleagues as we explore nonclinical AI solutions to improve support processes across the practice.
Additionally, when it comes to AI implementation, HR teams have a dual function—one, applying AI in their own departments, and two, helping other departments identify how to most strategically use AI. HR practitioners should function as AI advisors at their organizations, providing guidance on the best use cases for AI, recommending guardrails for other departments and so forth. They should partner with other department heads, such as CMOs and CFOs, to proactively explore AI solutions that make sense for individual teams. And once those tools are in place, HR leaders should emphasize ongoing education and training for everyone. Foundational knowledge about AI is crucial, but it isn’t enough to keep up with the changes.
Ultimately, when HR leaders and their team members do their part to continually learn about AI, they can effectively weave it into their tasks—and influence the rest of their organizations to do the same, ushering in new waves of innovation.
Forbes Human Resources Council is an invitation-only organization for HR executives across all industries. Do I qualify?

title: Apple’s ‘Privacy-Focused AI’ Gets Seal Of Approval From Investors
text:
Apple’s AI features have gained the seal of approval from an investment firm, which says the iPhone maker’s privacy-focused Apple Intelligence platform could help it to gain marketshare.
New York-based investment bank Rosenblatt Securities made the announcement after issuing a survey that found privacy was a top feature desired by US consumers in AI, investment-focused site Investing.com reported.
Of the 500 survey respondents, 17.8% said privacy was their most desired feature, choosing from a list of 15 smartphone features. This was 5.6 percentage points higher than the next-ranked feature, insight.
“Given that Apple has uniquely flagged Private Cloud Compute as core to its approach, building on a recent history of stronger advertising privacy safeguards in its app store and contrasted with AI privacy mishaps from rivals, Apple appears positioned to gain brand interest and AI market share from its out-of-the-gate focus on strong privacy,” Rosenblatt analysts said.
Taking this into account, Rosenblatt upgraded the iPhone maker’s shares to “buy,” effectively giving Apple Intelligence its seal of approval. Other research analysts concur—Bank of America restated a buy rating and issued a $230.00 price objective on Apple shares in a research note on June 12, according to Marketbeat.
Tigress Financial raised its price objective on Apple from $240.00 to $245.00 and gave the company a strong-buy rating in a report on May 30. DA Davidson upgraded Apple from a neutral to a buy rating and raised its target price for the company from $200.00 to $230.00 in a research report on June 11.
Interestingly, some of the elements that help Apple’s AI to be more private and secure including specialized large language models (LLMs) and Apple silicon, could help shield the iPhone maker from the cost pressures affecting rivals, the Rosenblatt analysts said.
They noted that Apple’s spending was not increasing at the level of rivals such as Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. “So Apple can have its cake (healthy margins) and eat it too, by using integration via Private Cloud Compute with third parties to offer the benefits of these companies' massive investments,” the analysts said.
The Truth About Apple’s Privacy-Focused AI
This latest news will be a boon to the iPhone maker, which has long differentiated itself with its privacy focus.
Apple has been seen as being late to AI compared to its tech giant rivals, but the firm’s privacy focus has impressed experts. This is despite Apple’s deal with OpenAI to include ChatGPT on iPhones in iOS 18, which some commentators say could pose privacy issues.
Apple Intelligence and its Private Cloud Compute appear to be very different to the AI privacy features offered by rivals, with the iPhone maker allowing users to have as much privacy as possible when using the technology. Even when AI features are more resource heavy, Apple claims its PCC offers the ability to process data in a uniquely secure and private way, in a private cloud environment.
“When AI algorithms are designed, it is extremely important that privacy is baked in,” says Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at ESET. However, the amount of data that is harvested and analysed to produce a good standard of quality is “extortionate” and “can sometimes leak personal data,” he adds.
Apple’s continued emphasis on robust privacy is “clearly trailblazing its competitors” with few offering the same level of protection, says Moore. He thinks the iPhone maker’s AI strategy “could possibly lead to a much needed increase in market share which may in turn force others to follow suit.”
Concern around AI privacy continues as the technology is rolled out at speed by all tech giants. But with initial surveys confirming privacy is important for consumers using the technology, Apple could have hit the mark with its AI strategy.

title: HP’s CIO Seeks To Boost Productivity And Remove Digital Friction
text:
HP Inc. is on a mission to drive growth and improve customer satisfaction by innovating faster, streamlining processes and delivering seamless user experiences. For Chief Information Niall Johnston, who joined the company from GE late last year, that means finding new ways for technology to make life easier for HP’s customers, employees and partners.
“My role is really about productivity for the end users and customers,” Johnston said in an interview. “It’s all about removing digital friction and creating new experiences.”
It’s difficult to talk about productivity today without mentioning artificial intelligence. HP is all-in on AI copilots for Office365 and GitHub, Johnston said, and experiments with code generation and AI-enabled chatbots in call centers have shown promise.
He described the company’s approach to AI as a pyramid, with reliable data and infrastructure as the foundation. Training and education comes next, along with clear ways to choose and prioritize the use cases that will deliver the most value to the organization.
As new AI opportunities spring up across the company, Johnston has worked closely with data and analytics chief Scott Hallworth, as well as HP’s business unit leaders and process owners, to build momentum for new initiatives.
The accessibility of generative AI tools has spurred a more democratic approach to innovation. “There is so much potential that you can’t innovate centrally,” he said. Much of the value from AI comes from individuals connecting their understanding of the tech and the knowledge specific to their roles.
Johnston joined HP amid a multi-year digital transformation effort that will allow it to thrive in an era of AI and hybrid work. In addition to becoming more agile, streamlining complex workflows and developing new digital experiences, the company is also embracing a standard, reusable set of “digital building blocks,” such as tools that make it easy for both consumer and business customers to subscribe to new services.
HP recorded $12.8 billion in revenue in the second quarter, slightly below the same quarter a year prior. The company sees growth ahead as it introduces AI PCs and other devices.
In his first six months in the role, Johnston has taken a broad look at the technology organization’s back office technology, approach to product development, talent strategy, governance and more to identify opportunities for improvement. The goal is to make sure that the operating model allows teams to deliver their best, he said.
Along with driving productivity, Johnston said he wants to help the technology organization better understand its impact on customer experience. Rather than just monitoring the performance of a given product over time, for example, teams are looking deeper at the customer journey to identify points of friction and remove them.
“It’s about how you rate the experience of the people who are navigating your ecosystem rather than just reporting the statistics of how it’s functioning,” Johnston said.
That process is made easier in part because HP’s IT group uses those products and services internally. Being “customer zero” for the company’s offerings strengthens relationships with product managers and allows for quicker feedback loops. It also strengthens ties with sales teams by allowing the IT group to serve as a showcase for current and future customers.

title: Randy Travis, wife Mary talk country singer's AI music comeback, American Music Fairness Act
text:
Randy Travis, wife Mary talk country singer's AI music comeback, American Music Fairness Act
"Forever and Ever, Amen" singer Randy Travis and his wife, Mary Travis, met with lawmakers and testified on Capitol Hill on Wednesday regarding the American Music Fairness Act (AMFA).
Speaking as the "wife and voice" of her husband, who has aphasia and can’t speak, Mary Travis testified in D.C. on why the AMFA is important.
"What would sheet music sound like without a voice, and what would radio sound like without a song?" she said. "This piece of legislation is essential to correct a hundred-year-old issue regarding artists and nonpayment for their work performed on the most prominent music platform in America -- one of which they helped to build and sustain."
A bipartisan bill, the AMFA seeks to ensure music creators are fairly compensated when their songs are played on AM/FM radio.
Radio broadcasters argue that the new performance royalties would financially jeopardize many radio stations, forcing them to cut back on programming, and could lead to stations playing less music and only the most popular songs.
Artists are currently paid on other platforms, including satellite, cable and internet, when their music is played -- but not radio. Songwriters, on the other hand, are paid on all of the aforementioned platforms.
The bill aims to help these artists recover the hundreds of millions of dollars in royalties they are currently losing out on every year.
During the testimony, Mary Travis said she likes to call artificial intelligence "artistic intelligence" because it enabled her husband to release a new song utilizing the technology "in its most authentic and artistic way."
Randy Travis suffered a massive stroke -- among other health issues -- in 2013 that left him with aphasia, robbing him of his ability to perform live and speak.
Mary Travis said her husband’s song "Where That Came From" is "the first song ever recorded and released with full artist consent and involvement in a studio setting" using AI.
"This is good AI, but there is bad -- no, there's terrible -- AI out there, and it's increasing exponentially daily," she added.
In an interview with "Good Morning America," which aired on Thursday, Mary and Randy Travis sat down with ABC News' Rachel Scott, and Mary Travis recalled how she felt when listening to her husband’s voice through the song.
"I might still cry just thinking about it," she said.
Mary Travis also discussed the importance of speaking out at the Capitol with her husband.
"There [are] some changes that need to be made, and Randy felt like he was the one that has kind of been tapped to do that," she said, to which her husband agreed.
She continued, "After his stroke, we depend more on royalties because he can't tour; he's not out there on the road. That's where your money was made because they don't have CD sales or album sales anymore. So you depend on the royalties."
At the Capitol, the couple also called for more regulation around AI and music.
On Monday, major record companies sued AI song-makers for copyright infringement.
Kristin Robinson, a senior writer from Billboard, spoke to "GMA" about the concerns raised by the technology.
"The music industry is very worried right now about different AI music companies potentially scraping the Internet for copyrighted material so that they can train their AI models to produce music that will directly compete against human artists," Robinson said.
Discussing what she has learned throughout this whole process, Mary Travis said, "You learn that you can do a lot of things you never thought you could do. … This may be one of the most important things he does."

title: PegaWorld Themes Speak To The Top AI Implementation Challenges
text:
Given the rapid evolution of technology in the customer engagement space over the last year, and after attending a few other vendor customer events in recent months, I was keen to hear about Pega’s latest thinking and the advancements they had made to their platform at this year’s PegaWorld, given that they are leading player in this space.
Now, amidst all of the usual keynotes, customer stories and announcements, two things stood out for me:
1. A Pragmatic Approach To Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Unlike many other vendor presentations where every other sentence is peppered with references to Generative AI (Gen AI) and how it is going to solve many of the world’s problems, Pega’s approach felt refreshingly pragmatic.
That’s not to say that Gen AI wasn’t mentioned, isn’t being used or doesn’t feature within the advancements and new functionality within their technology.
Not at all.
Gen AI features heavily in the development of the Pega platform and it’s new functionality.
But, what stood out for me was their left-brain, right-brain framing of how to think about applying AI to a business challenge.
For example, if a business encounters a problem which requires an analytical solution that needs to be understood, audited, and defended, then that would be a left-brain problem, and the business should choose an AI technique, like machine learning or predictive analytics.
Conversely, if a business encounters a problem that requires some creative thinking, like creating text or images or generating ideas for new apps or processes, that would be a right-brain problem, and the business should consider using an AI technique like Gen AI.
Now, that does not mean that organisations may not combine the two types of thinking to solve a problem.
But it is a useful starting point and will help enterprises and executives make sense of and cut through the Gen AI hoopla and noise that is dominating the market right now and make sure they select the right tools for the right jobs.
As one Pega executive quipped when I spoke to them at the event, many customers come to us asking about implementing GenAI, but we end up implementing a predictive AI solution for them once we have better understood their challenge and have decided what would be the most appropriate approach.
The value of this type of approach is only likely to get more relevant in the coming years as the number of AI techniques that are available to businesses increases.
To put that into context, according to Pega’s AI experts at a roundtable at the event, we are currently only scratching the surface of the number of techniques that are potentially available to us or will become available to us in the coming years. In fact, it was posited that we are only using 3-4% of the possible tools and techniques that potentially are in the AI toolbox.
2. Making It Easier To Get Started
The second thing that stood out for me was hearing Pega CEO Alan Trefler say that they are not the easiest platform to use or to get started with during his opening day keynote.
Now, while the Pega community and the wider marketplace have long understood that Pega may be one of the best platforms in the customer engagement platform space, they also understand it is not an easy lift.
But, once in place, the returns and value that customers get are enviable.
So, with that declaration from Trefler in mind, the announcement of Pega GenAI Blueprint™ and Pega GenAI Socrates™ at PegaWorld made complete sense.
- Pega GenAI Blueprint™ is essentially an app design-as-a-service tool that allows organizations to imagine what a best-in-class workflow or process would look like. The tool starts by asking the user to describe their app concept. It then crafts tailored workflows based on best practices, Pega’s decades of industry experience and generative AI to design the required components in seconds. This could be anything from processing insurance claims to handling credit card chargebacks to managing patient care. Moreover, if the user is a current Pega client, these ‘blueprints’ can be imported into their Pega environment and quickly turned into a prototype for testing and further development.
- Pega GenAI Socrates™ is a generative AI tutor that helps users learn Pega faster and more effectively while retaining more knowledge, resulting in a more deeply skilled workforce. Inspired by the time-tested Socratic teaching method, Pega GenAI Socrates educates students through a two-way conversation interspersed with open-ended questions on each learning objective – just as an engaged human teacher would in a classroom.
Now, while Socrates was announced at the event, Blueprint was given a ‘soft’ launch about five weeks prior to PegaWorld. At the time of the event, clients and partners had already generated 35,000 process blueprints, which represents the fastest adoption and most excitement generated by any offering in the company’s history. It’s also a clear testament to its value.
Both of these announcements speak to making it easier to envision what’s possible, get started with Pega and maintain momentum by building internal capability.
This is completely aligned with recent research findings from Gartner, which found that the top two challenges to implementing AI solutions are finding ways to estimate and demonstrate value, reported by 49% of their survey participants, and a lack of talent/skills, reported by 42% of participants.
Overall, PegaWorld was a breath of fresh air. It wasn’t all about the technology. It spoke clearly to the problems that large enterprises face when it comes to buying and harnessing technology to help drive better customer, employee and business outcomes.
They did that by focusing on how to choose the right kit, imagine what to do with it, and then become better users of it.
That was welcome.

title: Council Post: AI: The Good, The Bad, The Real
text:
Founder and CEO, Pulse Creative.
Last year, I wrote an article discussing the importance of artificial intelligence in the social media sphere and the idea of leveraging it with human authenticity. Since then, AI has continued to be the talk of town. It’s exciting—but as creatives, we need to blend that excitement with practicality.
AI tools offer us efficiency and innovation, but with those opportunities come challenges. In the rapidly evolving landscape of digital content creation, we need to look at two challenges in particular: ownership and authenticity. To sustain the growth of AI in the creative industry, we must address areas where AI could be abused.
Licensing In The AI Space
One of the primary challenges stemming from AI-generated content is the licensing practices and updates that will be required of us. With AI algorithms churning out vast quantities of content, determining ownership and securing proper licensing becomes a nightmare. Before AI entered the picture, some content creators were already finding themselves entangled in legal disputes over intellectual property rights which diluted value and put revenue generation at risk.
Nowadays, with AI creating content, it raises the question: Who owns what? Is it the AI technology that owns what it creates? Is it the person who put in the content request? The lines of ownership are blurred, and the courts are figuring it out. Moreover, as we continue to tap into AI-generated content, ensuring authenticity and ownership becomes increasingly complex. Distinguishing between original and AI-generated content has become a daunting challenge in some instances. As marketers, we bear the responsibility of spearheading the conversation on authenticity in the digital realm. We should be exploring and implementing robust verification mechanisms. We must be vigilant about safeguarding the integrity of AI-generated content creation.
Authenticity Will Be At A Premium
Amid the licensing challenges of AI-generated content, marketers must do their best to adhere to authenticity and copyright integrity. Preserving authenticity and real-world human experiences must always be the core of marketing and messaging.
In a world inundated with AI-generated content, the ability to craft narratives with authenticity and emotion becomes a hot commodity. As such, content writers who can infuse their work with unique perspectives and genuine human experiences will rise in prominence, offering a counterbalance to the wave of AI-generated content. I believe that these new circumstances will force content writers not to rest on their laurels—they’ll be pushed and challenged to create and be truly unique in their voices.
However, the impact of AI on content creation extends beyond writing. In the entertainment business, for instance, AI can disrupt traditional roles. Disruption, as any agency knows, comes with innovation. While AI tools can streamline certain aspects of production, they cannot replicate the nuanced decision-making and creative vision of showrunners, directors, producers, cinematographers and other field-based professionals. As such, these roles remain indispensable in shaping the body of creativity, ensuring we get the perfect scene, the perfect shot. Creating, directing and capturing a moment to tell a story and bring a vision to life is an art that goes beyond the scope of AI. We need real artisans and craftsmen who put their hearts into what they do.
I don’t think AI will eat the jobs of all creatives in marketing or other fields. Rather, I think it will erode the jobs of those who refuse to evolve their craft. It will force us all to be better creatives.
Be Nimble, Open And Ready
In the marketing world, agility is our strength. I personally push every creative who works with me out of their comfort zone. We must adapt swiftly to technological shifts like AI. We must track changing consumer trends and adjust strategies to match. We must act fast to protect ourselves and our clients from AI-generated risks. Nimbleness should be in our DNA to drive success in a dynamic digital world. But differentiation? That’s the name of the game. So, as we embrace AI and incorporate it into our processes, we must never forget our role as marketers to ensure that our clients continue to stand out from the crowd. We must guarantee authenticity and always remain current and on-trend.
As marketers, we must harness the transformative power of AI to drive business growth and success in an ever-changing digital landscape. However, we must also be aware of the pitfalls. At this moment, it’s licensing and copyright issues. In the future, other challenges might arise. No matter what happens, we must always be nimble, open and ready.
