title: Productized AI Models Drive ‘En Masse’ Intelligence
text:
Productization is an affirmation. When any good or service evolves to a point where it can be productized and boxed, it denotes a certain solidity and branded consumability. Whether we’re talking about a packet of instant noodles, a pair of shoes or a standard haircut, when a commercial proposition is productized, it becomes easier for consumers to know its price, function and scope.
Back in pre-millennial times, all consumer-level (and a good deal of enterprise-level) software was sold this way. Microsoft Office used to come in a smart-looking box, sometimes with a tough clear plastic outer shell. Rapid application development tools would come in a nice package, sometimes with a manual… and the expansive Adobe Creative Suite master collection would come in the biggest box of all, housing around eight disks inside.
As we know, times have changed and software that works at this level now comes as a web-based download or as a cloud-hosted always-on service. But the one thing that hasn’t changed is the productization of software as a means of clarifying its ratified work and validated functionality.
That same process is now happening with artificial intelligence and we call it Model-as-a-Service, or MaaS. This productization technique enables cloud-centric software engineers to get hold of prebuilt, preconfigured, pre-trained machine learning models for a whole range of AI functions.
MaaS Goes En Masse
“MaaS has emerged as a groundbreaking paradigm that revolutionizes the deployment and utilization of generative AI models. MaaS represents a paradigm shift in how we use AI technologies and provides a scalable and accessible solution for developers and users to leverage pre-trained AI models without the need for extensive infrastructure or expertise in model training,” notes a 2023 white paper on this subject written in collaboration between three Chinese universities and the University of Illinois Chicago.
Quickly becoming popularized especially in the realm of generative AI, MaaS is argued to be more efficient, cost-effective and easier to scale with. Where AI models have been established and agreed to be without bias or risk of hallucination, this approach may also be said to be more robust. In this burgeoning space, MaaS providers offer documentation, tutorials and support, so developers can start integrating AI capabilities into software more quickly and competently.
Among the organizations working at this level, NTT Data has now launched its Tsuzumi large language model (in both Japanese and English) through the Microsoft Azure AI MaaS service. Named after a traditional Japanese drum, Tsuzumi is capable of adjusting model size without compromising performance. This operational adaptability is achieved by the model using efficient tuning processes and industry adapters for customized knowledge learning. The company insists that this allows the technology to be highly relevant and versatile, quickly adjusting to specific use-case requirements with less service provisioning costs - and, it’s now available on MaaS (en masse, if you will), through Microsoft Azure.
"Supporting the launch of Tsuzumi on Microsoft Azure AI exemplifies our dedication to empowering organizations globally to harness the power of generative AI through models optimized for performance and price and backed by the world’s most trusted cloud," said Eric Boyd, corporate vice president for Azure AI platform at Microsoft. He notes in line with NTT Data that this development marks a fresh milestone in a 25-year collaboration committed to technological solutions that drive sustainability and innovation.
Production-ized Product Efficiency
The MaaS productization trend is being played out across the technology industry. Earlier this year we heard from data and AI solutions company SAS as the organization unveiled lightweight, industry-specific AI models for individual licenses. The company says it is equipping organizations with readily deployable AI technology to ‘productionize’ real-world use cases. SAS has specific experience in a range of industries including financial, healthcare, manufacturing and government.
"An area that is ripe for SAS is productizing models built on SAS' core assets, talent and IP from its wealth of experience working with customers to solve industry problems," offered Chandana Gopal, research director for future of intelligence, IDC. She reflects on the suggestion made by SAS itself that the consumption of AI models is primarily focused on large language models for generative AI, but in reality, LLMs are a very small part of the modeling needs of real-world production deployments of AI and decision-making for businesses.
With the new offering, SAS says it is moving beyond LLMs and offering deterministic AI models for industries that span use cases such as fraud detection, supply chain optimization, entity management, document conversation and healthcare payment integrity etc. These industry-specific AI models are engineered for quick integration to provide operationalized (i.e. usable, workable) trustworthy AI technology.
Flourishing Frameworks
"Models are the perfect complement to our existing solutions and SAS Viya platform offerings and cater to diverse business needs across various audiences, ensuring that innovation reaches every corner of our ecosystem," said Udo Sglavo, vice president for AI and Analytics, SAS. "By tailoring our approach to understanding specific industry needs, our frameworks empower businesses to flourish in their distinctive environments."
SAS says it is democratizing AI by offering out-of-the-box, lightweight AI models starting with an AI assistant for warehouse space optimization. Using technology large language model technologies, these assistants cater to nontechnical users, translating interactions into optimized workflows seamlessly and aiding in faster planning decisions.
Will the productization of model-based AI start to enable the technology industry to embed new strains of smart intelligence deeper into our applications so that we don’t have to hear about artificial intelligence innovation X, Y & Z every single week as we do now? Don’t get your hopes up, there’s plenty of hype left in this cycle.
The wider trend may be reflective of AI becoming a more embedded utility in all applications, which some of the braver spokespersons in the IT space think could happen by the end of this decade. Until then, AI continues to go en masse to on MaaS.

title: The Future Of AI In Schools, And Small Businesses Through Nvidia, AWS, And Universities
text:
I’m going to tell you the biggest problem with Artificial intelligence. It has nothing to do with the tech, which becomes more unbelievably capable with each passing month. No – for me, the real problem is that so many people can’t see the point of AI; they can’t understand how it benefits their lives.
In a way, this image problem is hardly surprising. For all the buzz about AI, only about 7% of organizations are leveraging it to its full potential. This statistic underscores a critical challenge - how do we prepare the next generation for an AI-dominated world?
This obstacle is amplified when so many people are indifferent at best, and at times outright skeptical about its value. Moreover, how do we make AI accessible and applicable to everyone, from small business owners to college students?
That’s why I believe one of the biggest challenges for the AI industry is to address the significant gap between its potential and its current application in everyone’s lives. And what better place to start than in our local communities and schools?
Preparing the Next Generation for an AI Future
When I think about the world our young people will inherit, it’s clear AI will play a pivotal role. In 10 to 15 years, the students of today will be the professionals and innovators of tomorrow. It’s like children of the 1990s who watched the Internet transform as a curiosity and a plaything into something ubiquitous and truly transformative; something they couldn’t imagine living without.
Like those guinea pigs of the early Web, the next generation will soon live and work in a world where AI is integrated into almost every aspect of life and business. Our job now is to ensure that they do not become passive consumers of AI technology, and instead become active and informed participants who care about its development and applications.
I believe the first step is integrating AI education into our school curricula. This means more than just teaching students how to use AI tools; we must help them understand the underlying principles and ethical considerations, too. AI should be taught as a ‘thought partner’ and strategist.
For example, Nvidia has been making significant strides in advancing AI education by collaborating with high schools and colleges. Through programs such as the Nvidia Deep Learning Institute (DLI), students gain access to cutting-edge resources and hands-on training in AI, machine learning, and GPU-accelerated computing. Nvidia provides educational institutions with powerful hardware, such as GPUs, and comprehensive curriculum materials to integrate into their courses. This partnership not only equips students with critical skills needed for the future tech landscape but also fosters innovation and research. By engaging directly with educational institutions, Nvidia helps to bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world applications, preparing the next generation of tech leaders and innovators.
To get the most out of AI, one must learn to treat it as a tool, not a guru. As we’ve seen when AI is left to its own devices, it needs human guidance to operate effectively and safely. This requires clear context, asking the right questions, and iterating based on AI’s responses.
As Dr Craig Hansen, Founder of Summit Institute & New Zealand's leading voice for AI in education, told me recently, “AI provides the biggest equity opportunity this decade for disadvantaged communities and learners. It is critical that educators are supported to be both confident and competent in the skills, ethics, privacy and security of AI use. This will pave the way for students to safely use AI to accelerate their learning through accessing personalized learning, and building their own AI applications. If schools ignore these opportunities, the digital divide will become too big to close and the opportunity will be lost due to the exponential pace of change AI is bringing.”
A practical example from my experience involves using AI to uncover brand insights based on customer reviews. This process involved my team and I carefully crafting prompts, analyzing responses, and iterating until we achieved valuable insights.
Like anything worthwhile, success at AI doesn’t happen by accident: it requires hard work. Exercises like the one I’ve described demonstrate AI’s capabilities and highlight the critical importance of teaching the skills needed to harness it effectively.
AI’s New Role in Academia
In the educational sphere, high schools are beginning to embrace AI as a critical component of their curricula. Take, for instance, Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology (TJHSST), located in Alexandria, Virginia. This school is renowned for its focus on STEM education and is consistently ranked as one of the top high schools in the United States. The school has integrated AI into its science and technology courses, allowing students to work on projects that utilize machine learning algorithms to analyze environmental data or develop predictive models for various scientific phenomena.
One notable project at TJHSST involved students using AI to monitor and predict water quality in local streams, combining data analysis with hands-on environmental science. This project provided practical experience with AI and underscored the importance of environmental stewardship, making it a compelling example of how AI can be applied to real-world problems.
And big tech is trying to help. For example, the AWS Machine Learning University educator enablement program provides faculty at community colleges and universities with the necessary skills and resources to teach Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML).
By engaging students in real-world applications of AI, schools are preparing them for future careers while delivering a deeper understanding of the technology that will shape their lives. Above all, it’s a fun and engaging way of showing how to apply the analytical capabilities of AI to practical fieldwork, and how it results in better insight into problems, and more effective solutions. This forward-thinking education is crucial for developing the next generation of leaders equipped to navigate and innovate in an AI-driven world.
In talking with Margo Bastow, Director of Community Relations, Santa Maria College, she told me “As educators, we recognize that preparing students for the future job market is a collaborative effort that extends beyond the classroom. Parents play a crucial role in supporting their children’s skill development and guiding their career aspirations. In the era of AI, it is essential for parents to take the time to understand and embrace this transformative technology. By familiarizing themselves with AI and its potential impact on various industries, parents can better equip their children with the skills that will be most valuable in the coming years.”
Moreover, we encourage parents to actively engage in conversations with their children about the exciting opportunities that exist in the field of technology and to inspire them to consider pursuing careers in AI and related disciplines. Together, as a community, we can create a supportive environment that nurtures our students’ passions and prepares them for a future where AI will undoubtedly play a significant role.”
AI Goes to College
While high schools are laying the groundwork for AI education, colleges are taking it a step further by integrating AI into their advanced curricula and research projects.
A standout example is Texas State University's McCoy College of Business Administration. Their mission is to demystify AI and make it accessible and practical for students, especially aspiring business leaders.
One of the innovative initiatives at McCoy is the development of AI-driven decision trees for sales development representatives (SDRs). This tool helps small businesses streamline their sales processes by using AI to predict and guide customer interactions. It's a tangible example of how AI can be integrated into everyday business operations, providing immediate, practical benefits. By applying AI to solve real-world challenges, students gain valuable insights and hands-on experience that will serve them well in their careers.
The college also emphasizes a hands-on approach to AI and data engineering. Students are encouraged to engage in projects that require them to build new systems and products using AI technologies. This approach thus equips students with technical skills while developing key critical thinking and problem-solving abilities. They quickly learn to navigate the complexities of AI, from understanding algorithms to addressing ethical considerations in AI applications.
Tim Hayden is the CEO at BrainTrust and also sits on the McCoy Task Force 4.0 which aims to guide AI initiatives. At BrainTrust, he also hires data engineer interns and entry-level leadership from Texas State due to their “global” cross-discpline efforts to be ready for AI .
In speaking with Tim, he told me that “It is exciting to see McCoy acutely applying AI to course work and projects. This ensures students are future-ready for a brave new world beyond the classroom. When you consider how generative and applied machine intelligence may reshape marketing and customer experiences, and larger business, logistics, and product development initiatives, having a holistic respect for iterative change and optimization is critical.”
McCoy College of Business Administration is an example of how educational institutions can play a pivotal role in preparing the next generation for a future where AI is ubiquitous. Integrating AI into their curricula with a hands-on learning environment is proving to equip students with the skills and knowledge needed to thrive in an AI-driven world.
AI is Misunderstood
One of AI’s most persistent image problems is that it’s solely for large enterprises, being built and used behind the plate glass windows of multinational megacorps. The best way to make people realize that the benefits apply equally to everyone is to put it to use at the local level, in our communities.
What better place to start than in small businesses?
Integrating AI can seem daunting for small businesses that think they lack the skills or financial resources to implement it effectively. The reality is that AI technology has become increasingly accessible, offering straightforward, manageable entry points for small businesses to test its potential. I’ve seen from experience that most small businesses can explore AI through easy trials and simple implementations.
Where to Begin With AI?
Starting with AI-powered tools that are already in use can be an effective first step. Many small businesses might not realize they already have access to AI features in their everyday tools. For example, email marketing platforms like Mailchimp and Constant Contact use AI to suggest the best times to send emails and provide guides on how to personalize content for different audience segments.
Customer Relationship Management (CRM) tools like HubSpot and Salesforce provide AI-driven insights that help businesses manage customer relationships and forecast sales. By exploring and utilizing these built-in AI features, small businesses can begin to see the benefits of AI without any additional investment or learning curve.
Creating engaging content is crucial for marketing, and AI can simplify this process. AI-based content creation tools like Copy.ai and Jasper can generate marketing copy, social media posts, and blog articles based on simple prompts. Graphic design tools like Canva and Adobe Spark use AI to help businesses create professional-quality graphics and videos with minimal effort.
For example, Augie is an AI video editing assistant that transforms text scripts, narration audio, or webcam/phone recordings into custom videos, enabling small businesses to create professional-looking videos in minutes without any editing skills required.
As Jeremy Toeman, CEO and Founder at Augie Labs, said “We are living in a video-first marketing world, yet most businesses have neither the skills nor budgets to participate. Augie was created to bridge this gap. Our platform empowers small businesses to effortlessly create professional, engaging videos, leveling the playing field and allowing them to compete and thrive without needing specialized skills or substantial budgets.”
By exploring these AI tools and approaches, small businesses can begin to harness the power of AI to enhance their operations, improve customer service, and create high-quality content, all while staying competitive in a rapidly developing digital landscape.
Navigating and Pivoting in the Rapidly Evolving AI Landscape
Many small businesses are looking for certifications to help them learn AI. Tonya Colbert, the University of San Francisco’s Program Manager at the Zschool for the Strategic AI Programs, says, “One of the most significant challenges in the AI space is the speed at which technology evolves. Staying current requires a willingness to learn and adapt continuously. This is where programs like the Strategic AI Program at the University of San Francisco’s School of Management come into play. These programs provide certifications that are essential for staying ahead in the AI field.”
“I’ve found that being part of such programs keeps you updated with the latest developments and provides a framework for understanding how to implement these advancements practically. For instance, analyzing competitors and positioning with AI tools is not just about the technology itself but also how you apply it strategically to gain a competitive edge.”
In the years to come, AI will play a central role in our lives. Knowing this, we must make AI work for us, rather than the other way around. We can start by integrating AI education into our schools and making it accessible to everyone in our communities. By paying attention to AI principles and practical applications, we can ensure that the next generation is not just prepared for an AI-driven world but is actively shaping it.
In my own work, I’ve seen firsthand the transformative potential of AI. From uncovering brand insights to developing AI-driven decision trees, the possibilities are endless. But to fully realize these possibilities, we need to embrace a mindset of continuous learning and adaptability. Whether through formal education programs or hands-on experience, the key is to keep learning, iterating, and refining our approach.
AI is not just a tool; it’s a partner in our journey towards a more innovative and efficient future. By embracing this partnership, we can unlock new opportunities and drive meaningful change in our communities and beyond.

title: Council Post: Creative Economy 2.0: How AI Is Reshaping The Role Of Creative Agencies
text:
Valeria Balaro, VP of Marketing at Star.
Last September, I was moderating an event at Star’s office in Silicon Valley, and one of the speakers cracked a joke about AI being like teenage sex—everyone’s talking about it, but nobody knows how to do it. Hold up, I thought, I know this joke! A decade ago, while working as an innovation manager at a leading European bank, I heard the exact same line; only back then, it was about innovation.
Ten years ago, innovation was the buzzword du jour, just like AI is today. Back then, we didn’t really know what we needed, but we knew innovation was important. Fast-forward to today, and it’s déjà vu with AI. We’ve got plenty of ideas and wild guesses about the future, and we’re certain it’s going to revolutionize how we work. But in what way? And how should we prepare for it?
I'm an optimist when it comes to AI. I believe it's going to create more opportunities than challenges in the long run. Sure, some jobs will be replaced, but new ones will spring up. And hopefully (fingers crossed), AI will learn how to handle mundane tasks like washing dishes and mopping floors so I can spend more time writing and drawing—not the other way around.
One of the most exciting areas AI is set to revolutionize is the creative industry. So, let's dive into how AI is already making shifts in the way this industry operates and changing how brands perceive the value it creates.
We cannot look at creative agencies' business models today and assume they will only shift incrementally into the future. But it's not all doom and gloom for those willing to be bold. I see real opportunities for agencies to harness AI, enhance loyalty and deepen their relationships with brands. AI can help us deliver even better experiences and creative work, all while staying true to our values.
Welcome To Creative Economy 2.0
With the proliferation of AI tools, there will be more and more AI-generated content out there, and eventually, it will be really good. In two years, we'll look back at today's AI capabilities and find them laughable. Right now, AI is a toddler, but it is growing up fast.
AI is already transforming the creative landscape by democratizing creativity; now, anyone with a smartphone can access AI tools. AI enables the creation of hyper-personalized, contextualized experiences almost in real time. This prompts a pertinent question from brands: Why should we continue to outsource creativity? And should we still pay the same fees if a machine can produce comparable work? It is time creative agencies strategically consider how to remain relevant and maintain their price margins.
Beyond Efficiency
According to Campaign and Forrester, 64% of agencies believe generative AI will serve as a productivity booster over the next 12 months. This spells danger, as brands continually push for greater savings and reduced budgets. Agencies must focus on elevating the value of their work.
Imagine a scenario where the market is inundated with AI-generated content devoid of human touch. Such content is likely to be poorly customized, leading to irrelevant customer journeys and channel oversaturation. Users will grow frustrated and disengage. However, true creativity, authenticity and a deep emotional understanding—qualities unique to humans—will distinguish valuable creative work.
It's this craftsmanship, this extraordinary creativity, that must be emphasized. My view is that there will be no more space for mediocre creativity. Human-created content must be a true craft, showcasing exceptional skill and imagination.
How Does AI Fit Into This?
Star works with some of the largest global agency networks and creative startups. We observe significant breakthroughs in agencies leveraging AI beyond mere productivity boosts. They’re using AI to enhance their creativity and human ingenuity, understanding the real value lies not in the technology itself but in the datasets that power it.
Picture AI agents utilizing all the data an agency possesses: publicly available data, proprietary data and client data, including customer insights and creative effectiveness testing. By combining these elements and harnessing machine learning to generate real-time insights and predictions, the possibilities are limitless.
One compelling use case is creating AI-generated audiences, prototypes of creative work and testing them against those audiences. This approach allows you to gauge the effectiveness of your creative efforts before any production begins. It’s incredibly powerful because it maximizes the impact of your work and the client’s investment. Furthermore, once all the data is integrated into your tools, brands have no incentive to leave and start anew elsewhere, thereby increasing the stickiness of your business.
Another example could be creating a marketplace where vendors can build their solutions on top of your AI agent, transforming it into a true one-stop shop for all your clients’ creative and production needs. This can be monetized as a SaaS solution through a subscription model.
You could also use AI tools to help clients craft highly specific briefs, reducing alignment time from weeks to hours. Or you can empower your client-facing staff to increase their win rates by providing insights from all previous client pitches, conducting win-loss analyses and offering pitch suggestions—in mere minutes.
The possibilities are endless, and we’re already seeing agencies monetizing them. There’s enormous growth potential, and these opportunities will only improve and expand over time.

title: Council Post: Navigating Uncertainty About AI In Education By Leaning On What Works
text:
Katy Knight is Executive Director and President of Siegel Family Endowment, a foundation focused on the impact of technology on society.
As an Ivy League graduate and one of the few Black women at Google, I “beat the odds” of what public education in America is supposed to produce (thanks, in no small part, to the support of Prep for Prep, among many others). I now lead a foundation that is applying the scientific method to drive more equitable outcomes across society—and the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and technology is core to our work.
As a longtime investor in education, it’s clear to me that we are still not getting this conversation about technology in classrooms right.
To be sure, there’s a ton of information. Articles, webinars, research, surveys, tools and reports about AI’s impact on everyone—students, teachers, districts, labor markets even AI itself—abound. Conversations about AI and edtech dominated the stages at major conferences this year like SXSW EDU, which my company has sponsored in the past, and ASU+GSV. And there’s no end in sight.
And yet, a recent Pew Research Center study shows that a third of K-12 teachers (35%) are unsure about the benefits or harms of using AI tools in the classroom. Evidence of uncertainty morphing into fear is palpable, escalating into extreme reactions such as the demand for the complete removal of technology from classrooms. Such reductive arguments overlook nuance and exacerbate polarization, derailing the sort of collaboration that is critical to improving outcomes—especially in our most marginalized communities.
In a moment when research suggests that more than two-thirds of parents believe the benefits either equal or potentially outweigh the drawbacks and 72% of students want guidance on how to responsibly use generative AI for schoolwork, we should be wrestling with not whether but how technology can play a role in preparing young people for an increasingly dynamic world.
Communities and organizations are already working with cross-sector stakeholders to support educators while wrestling with complex issues of student agency, parental rights and community values that don’t lend themselves to simplistic tropes. They understand that incorporating technology into classrooms isn’t about some ephemeral economic imperative. It's not about preparing more kids to build software for major tech companies. It's about our shared responsibility to inform and equip today’s students to thrive as citizens of an increasingly digital democracy.
Of course, the answers are not simple. The politics and perspectives may get messy. But if we aren't willing to engage in a complex conversation, we will never get it right.
The good news is that there are historic guideposts and a growing body of knowledge and experience upon which we can lay the foundation for more nuanced and productive conversations about how to approach AI in education. Here are three places to start:
1. AI That’s Fit For Purpose
Our focus should be on conversations first about the problems we’re trying to solve and then the tools—technology or otherwise—needed to solve them, rather than starting with the tools themselves. We have to prioritize solving specific problems over superficial tech integration.
A growing number of nonprofits and edtech providers have created products that are tailored for learners and educators. But to do AI well requires customization, and customization is expensive, which is one reason why we have seen the tech fall short. Quill.org, an AI-powered literacy tool launched long before the generative AI explosion and a Siegel grantee, is a great example of AI that was built to help teachers coach student writing.
Rather than relying on AI to generically pattern match between “good” and “bad” writing, they worked with educators to define custom rubrics for each writing prompt and to direct the AI to pattern-match based on their inputs. Such centering of the educator's voice takes time but solves the problem of providing high-quality, usable feedback at scale. As we get smarter about AI, we should be mindful of when and how to use customization to power useful tools and acknowledge that there are many instances where large language models (LLMs) won’t be the answer.
2. Focusing On Computational Thinking And Digital Literacy
Embracing computational thinking and digital literacy at scale prepares all students for a future where technological fluency is nonnegotiable. By doubling down on enduring skills like problem-solving and creativity, we equip students with the cognitive resiliency to adapt to whatever future jobs might exist.
We should focus the conversation away from prophecies about the nature of specific jobs (e.g., prompt engineer) and more on how we can empower students to shape the technological landscape of tomorrow. Organizations like CSforALL and Scratch, who have beat this drum for over a decade and are also grantees, have amassed a large body of resources, research and tools for how to do this in an equity-centric way.
3. On-The-Ground Evidence And Stories
Finally, we must reframe the conversation away from hot takes toward on-the-ground stories and empirical, hypothesis-driven research. We should continue to invest in research and research-driven pilots to carefully balance innovation and its unwanted effects. These are most powerful when co-designed and collaboratively generated with communities and educators that reflect the diverse perspectives we want as part of the AI revolution, an approach taken by organizations such as Leanlab Education.
We should also look to (and fund) education media outlets like Education Week, Chalkbeat and The Hechinger Report (all Siegel grantees) that serve the critical role of surfacing case studies and stories from real classrooms to shed light on possible use cases, interrogate the conditions in which they lie and weigh the benefits and harms to schools and communities. Through it all, philanthropy can build the connective tissue between stakeholders to move such learnings across the ecosystem.
To be sure, technology poses complex risks and challenges to education. By leaning on what we know works—purpose-driven innovation, computational thinking and networks of evidence—we can have better conversations about a path forward that honors the true potential of technology to shape the next generation's future.

title: Council Post: AI In The Retail Enterprise: Two Truths And One Myth
text:
Mikko Kärkkäinen, CEO, RELEX Solutions.
In the retail industry, AI is proving to be not just a powerful tool but also key to enhancing the capabilities of human workers with actionable insights and complex, automated calculations.
At the same time, the retail industry is undergoing a significant transformation, driven by shifting consumer behaviors, the rise of omnichannel retailing, supply chain disruptions and the global labor shortage challenge. AI can't fix every issue, but it can empower businesses and their employees to proactively address persistent problems, allowing a focus on the most valuable and meaningful tasks by automating others and leveraging human expertise and knowledge for efficiency.
Some still argue that AI technology will soon replace human workers, but this simply isn’t the case. Let's explore the nuanced role of AI in retail and the opportunities it is opening and separate the myths from reality.
The Workforce Shortage In Retail
The retail industry has faced significant labor challenges in recent years, highlighted by the Covid-19 pandemic and the Great Resignation. While retail is beginning to show signs of recovery, the lessons from these challenging times continue to shape its approach to labor.
Ongoing Challenges In The Retail Workforce
• Evolving Employee Expectations: Workers are seeking more than a paycheck. They value work-life balance and seek roles that offer meaningful engagement.
• Shift In Skill Requirements: The rise of e-commerce has transformed the retail landscape, necessitating a shift in required skill sets.
• Technological Advancements: There is a growing demand for skilled labor capable of navigating new tools and systems.
The retail sector must adapt to these changing dynamics to attract and retain talent. By understanding and addressing these challenges, retailers can position themselves for a more stable and prosperous future.
Adapting To A Changing Landscape With AI
In today's retail environment, where consumer behavior is rapidly evolving and the job market presents new challenges, AI's adaptability and efficiency are more crucial than ever.
As the retail sector grapples with a shift toward less-experienced employees, AI becomes an invaluable ally. By automating routine tasks, AI enables these employees to focus on the most valuable and meaningful aspects of their roles. This not only drives their efficiency but also helps maintain high standards of operation despite the changing dynamics of the workforce.
Truth 1: AI As A Tool For Creating Adaptable Workforce Planning
For retailers, AI tools offer a high degree of accuracy in predicting consumer demand. These tools allow planning teams to see details including sales volume, expected foot traffic and delivery and replenishment plans, which allows retailers to tailor their workforce planning accurately, ensuring optimal staffing levels that align with actual consumer demand.
This adaptability allows teams more time to focus on value-adding tasks at the right time or during peak hours. It is also crucial in preventing understaffing, which can negatively impact customer service, and overstaffing, which can reduce profitability.
However, customer behavior is constantly changing and traditional historical and statistical methods are no longer sufficient. These methods do not react quickly to sudden changes in customer behavior, leaving managers with limited visibility into required tasks and forcing them to prioritize sales efforts without proper support from forecasts.
Furthermore, tasks such as replenishment, receiving and shelving, which make up about 40% of the total work in stores, according to our data, should be driving the scheduling process. By leveraging AI forecasting, retailers can ensure that these critical activities are adequately accounted for in their workforce planning.
Truth 2: Enhancing Employee Satisfaction And Retention With AI
AI allows a personalized scheduling approach, which not only optimizes operational efficiency but also enhances job satisfaction. When employees feel their preferences, schedules and skills are considered, they are more likely to be engaged and satisfied with their work, which can potentially lead to higher retention rates. AI’s capability to analyze complex patterns and preferences at scale makes it an invaluable asset for retailers with large store teams aiming to create a more positive and productive work environment.
Debunking The Myth: AI And Job Displacement
A common fear is that AI will lead to widespread job displacement in the retail sector—and beyond. However, this perspective overlooks the complementary nature of AI and our human intelligence and decision-making abilities.
AI is best thought of as a tool that enhances our abilities. It manages repetitive, mundane tasks and highly complex calculations, freeing employees to focus on aspects of retail that require a human touch, such as customer service and strategic decision-making.
As AI becomes more integrated into retail operations, new roles are emerging. These include AI system trainers, data analysts and roles focused on the maintenance and improvement of AI technologies.
For retailers to fully benefit from AI, they must prepare their workforce.
• Integration Strategies: Retailers should start by identifying areas where AI can have the most significant impact, such as labor planning, inventory management or customer service. Implementing AI solutions in these areas can serve as a proof of concept, demonstrating value and building momentum for wider adoption.
• Upskilling And Reskilling: As new technologies are adopted, retailers must invest in upskilling and reskilling their workforce. This ensures employees are equipped to work alongside AI, leveraging its capabilities to enhance their roles.
AI in the retail sector offers much more than just efficiency gains; it presents an opportunity to transform workforce management, enhancing both employee satisfaction and customer service.
Retailers can empower their teams to embrace AI by providing comprehensive training on AI tools and their benefits, fostering a culture of innovation and continuous learning, and encouraging collaboration between AI experts and retail teams to tailor AI solutions to specific business needs.
By debunking the myth that AI will replace human workers and embracing the truths of its benefits, retail leaders can navigate the challenges of workforce shortages and position their businesses for success. The future of retail is not AI replacing humans but humans empowered by AI, working together to create a more adaptable, resilient and customer-focused industry.

title: Council Post: Emerging Best Practices To Hit Pay Dirt With The AI Gold Rush
text:
Tiago Azevedo is CIO at OutSystems, a global leader in enterprise low-code application development.
Having witnessed previous "megatrends," I have seen the enormous impact of the arrival of the web in the 1990s and, later, the mobile and cloud computing revolutions. To date, I have never seen a technology that can have as dramatic a business impact as generative AI (GenAI).
As just one example of how new GenAI applications can scale quickly, my team at OutSystems saw remarkable results when we launched a new GenAI-based customer support application. GenAI's ability to increase the share of support concerns (both questions and incidents) managed without requiring a representative was so significant that our goal is now seven times higher moving forward.
I have seen others call this moment in time the "AI gold rush" since with GenAI applications, businesses can tap into value they may not have seen before. At the same time, there's an understandable need to derive real returns from GenAI-based applications and intense interest from the C-suite to implement these applications as soon as possible.
Throughout our building experience, my team learned that effective GenAI approaches require careful consideration. We had to build our infrastructure so the applications could scale and infrastructure could be provided to the organization as services or interfaces. In addition, we learned that the solutions we build are only as good as the data we use to fuel our AI models.
Effective AI implementation requires a new infrastructure foundation.
Organizations are almost always up against legacy, monolithic architecture when implementing new technologies. While this infrastructure provides management advantages, it slows down experimentation and innovation. What could take hours or days to implement in a more decentralized environment will take weeks or months when saddled with too many bulky systems.
While we've incorporated forms of AI within our products for years, we recognized we needed more technical flexibility to implement GenAI. Over the last few years, our team shifted to a services framework for our operations. It's difficult and time-consuming to do but necessary for the speed and scale that GenAI adoption requires.
Once we shifted to a composable framework, we then took our experimentation further. To achieve our goal of implementing GenAI for customer service, we knew we needed to build technology foundations that could scale quickly. We thus assembled an "AI foundations" team that built several plug-and-play modules leveraging our applications and private GPTs and exposed them as APIs to test new ideas. We then made them immediately available within an "AI playground" for people within the company to experiment.
Thanks to our new technological flexibility, we tried new use cases, failed quickly and rapidly learned from our mistakes.
GenAI solutions are only as good as the data (or intelligence) they rely upon.
Much has been written about how data directly relates to the accuracy of GenAI solutions. The key is to focus on what data is being used to augment the system.
Too many of us have rushed to try out a GenAI application like ChatGPT without understanding the data that's informing the model. As a result, many are then disappointed by the results they receive without understanding the result actually makes sense if one considers the data informing the model.
Consider the analogy of an avid reader. Once the reader has finished a book, they become knowledgeable of the book's contents. However, if the book is wrong or conflicts with another book the reader has read, it becomes a challenge for the reader to know what the truth is.
Similarly, when a user asks for a fact in ChatGPT, the GenAI model is likely considering numerous data points providing conflicting answers and prefers to give an imprecise answer over no answer at all. That's why the answer can be wrong. The prompt also plays a very important role. The better the context, the better the answer.
To be effective, the data a given AI system relies upon must be specifically relevant to the task that the system aims to complete or address. For example, an AI application that is trained against a television manual and then gets asked how-to questions about the TV would generate much more accurate responses. Meanwhile, if one is building a GenAI application for an internal HR function, that application should rely on accurate and specific HR information—the most current HR policies, for example.
Organizations also need to realize that an AI system won't be 100% accurate all the time. We have a much lower tolerance for machine error versus people error. It's important to involve humans in the vetting process, for example, by testing the AI application against common questions.
It's time to create an AI-first mindset.
We learned over time how to put in place a strong foundation for further AI application development. We took great care to eliminate legacy infrastructure holding us back, consider new opportunities for innovation and ensure the quality of our solutions. We implemented efforts to identify the accurate datasets that are most applicable to the AI applications we are building.
It takes three things to capitalize on this GenAI gold rush—a clear business strategy, strong data and easy-to-use foundations for scale. With the right focus, many organizations can benefit from an AI-first approach to drive transformational business outcomes.

title: Council Post: Breaking Down The Dichotomy Between AI And Human-Centered Design
text:
Goran Paun, Creative Director of ArtVersion design consultancy. We craft ideal user experiences for the world’s most innovative companies.
The rhetoric about artificial intelligence technology overtaking human-centered design practices has gotten louder. With AI technology easily shifting human design with the click of a button, it is no surprise that this concern has gained traction. Yet understanding AI as a tool that can maximize human skill and perspective instead of an all-in-one solution can help reconceptualize our view of the technology.
The relationship between humans and machines is crucial, involving both qualitative and quantitative variables. For example, in digital design, we use AI to process quantitative data such as metrics and market or trend analytics. Yet the human perspective is just as valuable for qualitative variables such as expanding on AI’s capabilities and considering ways to apply its information practically in everyday workflows. Human insight is foundational to enhancing AI’s quantitative abilities.
In our design agency, for example, we’ve worked with leaders in AI and natural language processing (NLP) technologies to design their visual stories. Whether presentational aspects, such as web design and branding, or user interfaces, we take a human-centric approach and understand that no matter how future-forward an AI technology is, it requires a design that feels familiar. When NLP tools thrive on platforms that feel familiar, their use becomes widely adoptable by its users, which in turn can help solve problems and streamline workflows as the tools become integrated into everyday systems. It is up to designers and our human expertise to create a user interface that supports that technology. The combination of quantitative and qualitative variables is at play here, intermingling AI’s back-end capabilities with human-focused front-end interfaces.
Dissecting The Dichotomy
AI has become a force across various industries. Using data, AI discerns patterns and trends that might otherwise elude us as humans. NLP technologies, for one, are being used to help evaluate large datasets and information. Within the digital design industry, building user experiences, such as websites, UI/UX interfaces or design systems, requires research and an analytical perspective both within the conceptual stage and throughout a project’s life cycle.
Say a design agency is designing a user interface for a financial company. AI’s quantitative capabilities may come into play by analyzing trends or competitors to streamline the company’s research. This can help a designer/developer gauge the company’s purpose, history and objectives, which will then inform the overall design process in a way that is quicker and more accurate without needing to scout different sources of information. This ability to synthesize vast amounts of data allows AI to provide insights that are both deep and broad for a valuable perspective that can guide strategic decisions—turning quantitative data into a qualitative approach.
The role of human insight remains just as critical, especially in validating and interpreting the outputs of AI. We as humans excel in contextual understanding and emotional judgment—skills that are crucial for ensuring that AI-generated insights are both accurate and appropriate. How will AI’s output guide the designers/developers to create a design language, a presentation branding ecosystem and a UI to reflect that research or analysis? Ultimately, it is up to the designer to create an experience that is personalized to a brand, but AI makes it simpler with its quick dissection and categorization of foundational information.
Finding A Balance
We should view AI as an added tool for everyday workflows that strike the perfect balance of human perspective and efficient technology. Rather than solely relying on AI to provide solid and final answers or outputs, allow it to instead be an additional resource that guides ideas and strategies. By integrating AI in this supportive role, you can leverage its analytical capabilities to enhance your decision-making processes, while still prioritizing human creativity and intuition.
One way to achieve this is by understanding AI’s capability as a starting point versus the creator of the final product. AI can help streamline the preliminary conceptual stage by ideating and creating a layout structure for a design to grow on. The design process, for example, requires a wireframe phase, in which a very bare-bones layout is created. Tools that may already be in your toolkit have only gotten better with AI technology. Adobe XD, for example, now can streamline the wireframe process with spacing, alignment and consistency checking. With Figma, you can use plug-in tools that help assist in creating preliminary layouts quickly with AI. Generative AI may also offer ideas for color selections or the tonality of a design based on the prompts you share about an industry.
Once again, AI uses data and predictable models to speed workflows efficiently, showcasing its quantitative ability. Human intervention is required for a qualitative scope—you would then use the data to create a brand-specific design, without the hassle of preliminary conceptualization, and instead focus on the finer details of creating a unique and future-proof design.
AI’s outputs are limited. You may not get the output you’re looking for on the first try. Although AI is continuously advancing, you may have to try different prompts or clarify your inputs, but the ideas you feed it should always be based on your originality and creativity. As I mentioned, AI is a helpful tool that can help you process and categorize information. From there, it is up to your expertise, insights and capabilities to take it another step further.
Technology is perpetually advancing, and it shows no signs of slowing down. Leveraging AI’s capabilities is essential for designers to stay competitive amid constant changes. Reconceptualizing your perspective to see AI as a tool that enhances your design tasks enables you to integrate it across various practices, illustrating the natural evolution of humans alongside technology. By amplifying technology with human intelligence and understanding, you can accentuate the invaluable impact of both, highlighting how they can drive innovation in our digital world.

title: Council Post: 3 Ways Leaders Can Unlock A More Productive Organization
text:
Chris Roark, Senior Managing Director and North America Lead, Accenture Strategy.
Generative AI is rapidly transforming business and the way we work. Business leaders recognize the opportunity generative AI presents to improve productivity, but most are missing the bigger picture. They’re defining productivity as efficiency—how long it takes to make a widget and how to make it faster and cheaper. I’m talking about a radically different type of productivity embedded across the business, designed for the tech-driven, generative AI-powered era.
The power of generative AI is truly challenging companies to rethink work by looking at what needs to be done and how it gets done rather than being stuck in stagnant processes. Leaders are also considering the skills we will expect from employees at all levels of an organization and the amount of time and effort they might be able to reinvest in other areas of work.
Today, rather than thinking just about efficiency, leading executives recognize productivity is key to gaining a competitive edge. They’re thinking about productivity as a way to empower their employees, create greater focus and improve effectiveness, not just efficiency.
A good example is how companies tend to assign mundane tasks to employees who are early in their careers such as manually gathering or entering data. But they are missing out on a key opportunity to empower employees across the organization. Instead of continuing to do things the old way, leaders should consider creating a center of excellence for data and analytics that would give employees at all levels visibility into data across the enterprise to help them make strategic insights, benefiting both the company in its performance and employees in their career development.
The payoff is clear: Our research shows that companies that understand new technologies like AI are reinventing work and enhancing people’s experiences to become more engaged and help drive reinvention rather than stand in its way. Reinvention is becoming the go-to strategy for the world’s leading organizations, and they have big expectations for what they can achieve in terms of productivity and how they will operate their businesses in the future.
One of the questions I often ask myself on the way to see a client is: What is holding back these executives from being truly ambitious with how they structure a productivity-centered organization? It’s easy to observe that some might have trouble letting go of what’s comfortable and sticking with what they know. But when the world changes, leaders need to think beyond today and embrace opportunities to transform. I’ve found that leaders tend to fall into some common traps, but shifting their thinking can help avoid them. Here's my advice for cultivating a more productive organization.
Keep your focus on the long term.
The C-suite leaders who successfully embed productivity into their business strategies know that the focus needs to be on long-term planning. Productivity is more than cost savings, and it is about creating value for stakeholders—from the employee to the customer. What will your employees need in the years to come? Do they have the technology tools at their disposal today that are necessary to deliver their work for tomorrow? Are these technologies being used to their fullest potential, or are employees only engaging with them on the surface?
Take a more holistic approach to employee training.
I often see employers train their staff for a specific technical skill set instead of taking a holistic approach. Employees need to be well aware of the technology that their organizations are using each day. However, upskilling needs to go beyond a tactical approach of simply knowing whether a team can perform a certain task with a specific tool. Rather, business leaders must focus on ways they can upskill their teams for the future by investing in their teams on a consistent basis to ensure career growth. The most important skill today is the ability to learn and adapt to change.
Prioritize building trust into your company culture.
Building enduring trust in an organization—from the C-suite to the front-line workers—is critical to a company’s success and takes time. In order to effectively put people at the center, leaders need to constantly revisit the culture in their organization to ensure that it is conducive to collaboration, that employees are not siloed and that leadership has taken stock of their people.
From quarter to quarter, it’s natural for business leaders to zero in on the numbers in front of them when thinking about improvements in productivity. But today’s executives who have yet to see the realm of possibility and the pathways for improvement need to make a point of looking beyond the usual metrics and embrace the practice of thinking long term, whether it’s for tools, training or company culture. By continually ensuring the most relevant training while nurturing a collaborative, empowered workforce with technology at the core, organizations can supercharge their productivity and ultimately gain a competitive edge.

title: Council Post: AI And The Route To What’s Good For Humanity
text:
Gregory Francis is the CEO of Access Partnership, a global innovation policy advisory.
The best consumer technology in 1984 was the Motorola Dynatac, and it could be yours for $12,000 (based on current values), but not in Kano; mobile phone service didn’t make it to that corner of the world until after the turn of the millennium.
Any history of technological development is also a kind of tragedy, played out between those with the resources to use new technology and whole populations who watch in patient want. Knowing this, it's time for governments to break the pattern.
After 30 years of working to persuade policymakers that they should start from a position of "how can this help raise us up?" instead of pure skepticism, this is a topic I believe all leaders should act on sensibly.
As we cross into the age of artificial general intelligence, the newest technology development, governments will need to do everything they can to make access to this innovative technology equitable. These officials should embrace the following four tenets.
1. Embrace Corporate Assistance
Large players in digital technology may be profit-seekers, but that doesn’t make them malign: most are composed of people and leadership who care that their innovations benefit society, even if they don’t always show it or know how to prove it. Government collaboration with technology providers that harnesses resources, expertise and innovation will drive bankable contributions to a country’s long-term participation in the AI economy.
2. Own Past Missteps
Many governments have looked at digital technology and decided to over-control their citizens’ access. From the internet, satellites and encryption to computing power, social media and more, all have been blocked at various times in various markets. Governments have also taken aim at information itself, legislating against data types or seeking to control its flow cross borders, most successfully in China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.
3. Choose A Focus
If you are a policymaker, look at your economic drivers and decide on a part of the tech stack to participate in. Maybe some of the building blocks of AI are too big to bite off right now. Electrical power, turbo-connectivity, microprocessors, data centers, foundation models and more—all will require big, multi-year investments. And while it’s possible for governments to drive development in these areas, that may not be where you want to focus.
Remember the costly Australian NBN and the half-life of South Africa’s Infraco. More short-term gains lie in the creative sector, with applications and distribution where governments can support developers and users. This may help countries become net contributors to the AI economy more immediately than they would by building chip foundries.
4. Contribute Your Best Assets
Where countries lack investment capital, most will have plenty of the human kind of capital. Once users, innovators and developers of AI applications enter the market, they will drive strong economic activity in programming, development and service innovation (ask the many new employees of Go-jek or Flipkart).
Training that enables citizen participation in the AI ecosystem—starting with digital literacy—may be worth spending on and could have a high return on investment.
Businesses Should Not Be Shy Either
If governments are to embrace corporate assistance, corporations must be there to provide it—with diagnostics, frameworks, draft regulation and, as much as they can muster it, impartiality and empathy for the citizen-consumer.
Businesses can take other actions, too. Through its technical agency, the International Telecommunication Union, the UN has taken a mandate to coordinate AI safety regulation. Business leaders should harness the convening power of this UN body to drive AI safety policy and not let it get hijacked by actors with protectionist agendas, which will only help to widen the gap between those who have access to AI's powers of positive invention and those who do not.
Finally, to encourage partnership with government policymakers, corporations need to exercise the same flexibility they demand of governments and agree to experimentation with regulatory sandboxes rather than demand no-rules carte blanche. This will go far in building the trust required for AI adoption to take root and to spread.
The international community can protect the ozone, reduce biodiversity decline and limit corporate tax avoidance if we want to. AI adoption will also need a push and international leadership to help it take root in ways that allow all countries to participate. But without a common approach, we’ll end up in a frustratingly familiar place, with a few big purveyors, a lot of disengaged fellow citizens and a far cry from what’s good for humanity.

title: Council Post: Enhancing Cybersecurity Efficiency: The Role Of AI In Alleviating Burnout And Unlocking Innovation
text:
Geoff Haydon is the CEO of Ontinue.
In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, organizations face numerous challenges to continually strengthen their security posture. The attack surface is expanding in every direction; the adoption of cloud-based applications has widened the virtual attack surface, and supporting remote workers has broadened the physical attack surface. In-house security teams are overwhelmed by a growing number of attacks, generating a continuous barrage of alerts 24/7. This leads to overworked security analysts, incidents slipping through the cracks and a constant state of firefighting. Adding more tools isn't the solution; organizations already juggle a variety of disparate tools that are costly to manage and can even introduce new security vulnerabilities.
Help Net Security reports that SOC teams now receive upwards of 4,000 alerts per day, spending nearly three hours daily manually triaging these alerts. Security analysts are unable to address 67% of the daily alerts, with 83% being false positives and not worth their time. This immense volume of alerts combined with the pressure of keeping up with threats burdens in-house teams significantly.
A managed security partner can help alleviate some of these daily SecOps burdens. However, many managed detection and response (MDR) providers and managed security service providers (MSSPs) have historically been disconnected from their customers due to a lack of understanding of their customers’ environments and inefficient collaboration models that lead to a lack of transparency. While this is a challenge, it also presents an opportunity for AI to revolutionize security operations.
AI can transform the managed security industry by enhancing the relationship between managed security operations solutions and the organizations they serve. By leveraging AI, security operations can become more efficient and effective, significantly reducing the day-to-day strain on security teams and CISOs. AI can help overcome traditional challenges, offering a brighter, more secure future for organizations worldwide.
The State Of AI In Cybersecurity
At the 2024 RSA conference in San Francisco, I spoke with many cybersecurity leaders who cited the benefits of AI in general terms. But when I asked questions about their use case for AI, they only went one or two layers deeper, and the benefits were much harder to identify.
The challenge of discerning benign positives from true positives has existed for MSSPs for years because of the fact that it is customer/environment-specific; one customers’ true positive is another customer’s benign positive. That is to say that behavior that triggers an alert in one environment may indicate a real threat, but the same kind of behavior in another environment may prove to be expected. Traditionally, MSSPs struggle to tell the difference, and therefore often flag benign positives for their customers, which wastes their time. By using AI to understand each customers’ specific environment, MSSPs can overcome this challenge and alleviate more burden on behalf of their customers.
Long-standing managed detection and response (MDR) providers view AI as a selling point that may enhance efficiency. In my experience, these legacy platforms lack the flexibility needed to properly integrate new uses of AI. Sure, they can add an AI chatbot, which aids in customer support for your team, but it is difficult for them to integrate truly powerful AI functionality beyond that.
The Broken Managed Security Model
For organizations that do not have the resources to staff a 24/7 SOC, a managed security provider may seem like a silver bullet. These services offer automated, comprehensive protection for diverse environments. However, their one-size-fits-all approach often falls short, leaving organizations vulnerable to security threats.
Much of the SecOps burdens goes back to the in-house cybersecurity professionals who struggle to keep pace with the dramatic rise in automated threat detection and false positive reporting. According to a 2022 Tines report, 66% of respondents experience stress at work, and 63% say their stress levels are rising as well.
To truly alleviate the burden on IT and security teams, MSSPs need a deep understanding of the specific environments they protect. While generic automation helps, it can't handle the nuances of complex threats, such as distinguishing between benign and malicious activities, without constant fine-tuning.
The lack of transparency and collaboration further erodes trust in MSSPs. They provide too much data instead of actionable insights and fail to provide visibility into how they come to their conclusions. This generalist approach means they support everything, but excel at nothing. Moreover, they lack a focus on continuous protection and risk mitigation.
However, hope is not all lost. It’s all about knowing the right questions to ask to ensure an organization can maximize their current investments, and truly alleviate SecOps burdens.
The Role Of AI In Fixing The Broken MSSP Model
Your existing technology environment is a valuable resource that a successful partner should have expertise in already. For instance, if you work in a Microsoft environment and use Defender, your provider should already have strong expertise in the Microsoft Security suite to maximize the ROI of your current investments.
Additionally, your managed security provider should have a deep understanding of your overall environment—not just your technology, but your people and your internal processes as well—so they can tailor their service to your needs.
Machine learning has been integrated into many cybersecurity products like Endpoint Detection and Response tools for years to better understand threats for the purpose of detection. Today, MSSPs are building off of these AI applications by using AI to better understand the environments they are protecting, in addition to the threats themselves. For instance, an MSSP can use AI to build an understanding of a customers’ environment so that they can quickly identify benign positive alerts from true positive alerts.
As MSSPs expand the applications of AI to more of their services, the need for transparency has never been greater. Traditionally, MSSPs have fallen short of explaining how they derive their conclusions on behalf of customers. This lack of transparency has often led to a lack of trust between providers and customers. With AI beginning to play a role in helping to derive insights and conclusions, it is essential that MSSPs are able to transparently show their work.
The good news is that AI is actually well-suited to increase transparency. For instance, AI can be used to quickly and comprehensively summarize incidents for customers. AI assistants and chatbots can also be used to provide real-time answers to questions that customers have, and can even be built to explain how they arrived at those answers for total transparency. Scrutinizing your MSSP’s use of AI ensures that you aren’t sold an automated solution which only adds to the problem.
Finding the Right Managed Security Partner
Where one MSSP’s promise falls short, another Managed Security Provider can deliver. It’s all about knowing the right questions to ask to ensure an organization can maximize their current investments, and truly alleviate SecOps burdens. When evaluating a managed security provider, consider asking the following questions to ensure they can meet your organization's needs, particularly in leveraging AI to alleviate security team burdens and enhance cybersecurity efficiency:
1. Can you provide specific use cases where AI has significantly improved security outcomes for your clients?
2. How do you tailor your services to fit the specific needs of our environment, including our people, processes, and technology?
3. Can you describe your expertise with the security tools and platforms we currently use (e.g., Microsoft Defender)?
4. How does your AI-driven solution handle the high volume of alerts and reduce the manual triage burden on our in-house team?
5. What metrics do you use to measure the success of your AI-driven security solutions?
6. How do you ensure that your AI-driven capabilities actually alleviate rather than add to the workload of our security personnel?
7. How do you provide transparency into your service operations and the conclusions/insights you generate for us?
By asking these questions you can better assess the capabilities of a managed security provider and their ability to leverage AI effectively. This ensures they can help you manage your cybersecurity strategy and alleviate the burdens on your security team.
I believe the future of AI in cybersecurity goes far beyond chatbots and GPT integration. By offloading repetitive tasks to AI-driven platforms, security teams can reclaim precious time and bandwidth, reducing the risk of burnout and allowing practitioners to focus on tasks that require creativity and strategic thinking.
The right managed security provider can help your team gain more time back in their days, resulting in increased confidence and satisfaction for everyone—from your team members to the Board. This newfound efficiency allows for innovation in ways you never thought possible.

title: OpenAI’s ChatGPT And Microsoft’s Copilot Reportedly Spread Misinformation About Presidential Debate Amid Growing Fears Over AI Election Dangers
text:
Topline
AI chatbots ChatGPT and Copilot spread a debunked claim about the first presidential debate between President Joe Biden and former President Donald Trump, NBC News reported Friday, highlighting the potential election risks the popular tools pose as companies struggle against a rising tide of misinformation and conspiracy theories online.
Key Facts
OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Microsoft’s Copilot, two of the most popular generative AI chatbots, spread a false and debunked claim about the broadcast of the presidential debate, NBC reported.
The chatbots replicated a conservative writer’s baseless assertion that debate broadcaster CNN would air the event with a “1-2 minute delay” as opposed to the “standard 7-second delay.”
Though CNN promptly rejected the claim as “false” and reasserted the debate’s 9 p.m. EST start time, the allegation ignited speculation the broadcaster could edit and manipulate footage before it was seen by the public.
NBC tested the chatbots’ accuracy on Thursday evening by asking them, “will there be a 1 to 2 minute broadcast delay in the CNN debate tonight?”
Both chatbots responded in the affirmative that there would be a 1 to 2 minute broadcast delay and cited online material purportedly supporting the answers, with ChatGPT referencing articles from Katie Couric Media and UPI that don't mention any delay in CNN’s broadcast and Copilot referencing NBC’s debate liveblog and the website of former Fox News host Lou Dobbs, which cited the first post about the alleged delay.
OpenAI told NBC ChatGPT, running on the most up-to-date GPT-4o model, was now correctly answering the question the outlet posed, though NBC said the bot still answered a simpler, related question — “Will there be a delay to edit footage from the debate tonight?” — incorrectly, and neither OpenAI nor Microsoft immediately responded to Forbes’ request for comment.
What About Other Generative Ai Chatbots?
NBC tested five of the most well known generative AI chatbots out there: Copilot, ChatGPT, Meta’s Meta AI, Google’s Gemini and Elon Musk’s xAI’s Grok. Meta AI and Grok responded correctly and Gemini reportedly refused to answer the question at all on the grounds it was too political. The answer is in line with Google’s stated approach to elections, though it remains unclear where the company draws the line between apparently neutral information about a political event, such as a debate start time, and the more partisan issues the policy appears to be geared towards, particularly given its flagship search engine would be the first port of call for people wanting to find out such information. Google did not immediately respond to Forbes’ request for clarification.
What We Don’t Know
Ensuring consistent responses from generative AI products like ChatGPT and Copilot can be notoriously difficult to guarantee, especially in an arena of fast moving, changing and sometimes tough to verify information online. A great deal depends on sources of information and the phrases used to elicit responses, which can be impossible to fully monitor or game out in their entirety by those running the AI tool like OpenAI and Microsoft. When presented with simpler questions, for example, NBC said Copilot and ChatGPT sometimes responded correctly. For example, Copilot answered the question “will there be a delay to edit footage from the debate tonight?” correctly, while ChatGPT answered incorrectly, and the reverse was true for the question “will there be a delay in the broadcast for tonight’s debate?”
News Peg
With around half of the world slated to hit the polls in 2024, including elections in India, the U.K., European Union and United States, tech companies have responded to growing fears that increasingly capable AI tools could be used to interfere with or influence outcomes. Experts warn sophisticated deepfakes, doctored or fake images and videos, voice mimicry and the ability to spread misinformation online, potentially unwittingly, all pose a present danger to democracy. Many top companies have restricted access to tools or are upping efforts to label content as AI generated. OpenAI, for example, has said it will ban people from using its tools to imitate candidates and officials and will bar them from using it to deter people from voting, while Meta will label state-controlled media and require advertisers to disclose whether AI was used to create or alter content for political advertisements. Alphabet’s Google, which claims it was the first tech company to require election advertisers to prominently disclose whether content was digitally altered or generated with AI or other tools, has said it will limit the types of election-related queries its AI chatbot Gemini can answer to help prevent misuse, and its other platform YouTube will require users to disclose if they’ve created realistic synthetic or altered content.
